# MARSILIO FICINO OF FLO-
## rence humbly commends himself to the Most Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Giovanni de' Medici, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.

<note>Giovanni de' Medici (1475–1521) was the son of Lorenzo the Magnificent. He was appointed a Cardinal at the remarkably young age of thirteen and later became Pope Leo X. Marsilio Ficino was the tutor and philosopher-priest of the Medici family.</note>

*When I had decided to write a letter to you to congratulate you on the Cardinal’s dignity recently conferred upon you, and when I was considering to whom I should best give it to deliver to you—someone who might make our congratulations much more pleasing—I suddenly took myself to the academy. I hoped that in its innermost sanctuaries, at least, some greeter most acceptable to you would not be lacking. There, by some divine fate, I first encountered Iamblichus among the academicians, surnamed "the Divine," and a great priest there. To him indeed I said: "Hail, Iamblichus, great priest! At present (as you see), I have congratulated Giovanni de' Medici, the new <term>prelate</term><note>original: "antistiti." A high-ranking religious official or priest.</note> of the Christian religion. I pray you—if my request is just—that you will make our congratulations, which are otherwise meager, fuller with your divine words and mysteries." He nodded to my prayers, and so, with this sentiment, O Giovanni, great priest, that great priest comes to you. Receive, therefore, such a greeter with joy; and after the first greeting, after the letter has been read, listen more attentively, if you please, to what that divine man says. For he promised that, so he might say things worthy of both his persona and yours, he would express to you in brief what the Egyptian and Assyrian priests thought about religion and divine matters.*

<note>Ficino uses a literary device here, imagining that he met the ancient philosopher Iamblichus in his "Platonic Academy" in Florence. By "delivering" Iamblichus’s book to the young Cardinal, he is presenting the wisdom of the ancient world as a gift for the new leader of the Church.</note>

<summary>In this dedicatory letter, Marsilio Ficino presents his translation of Iamblichus to the young Cardinal Giovanni de' Medici, framing the ancient philosopher as a "divine priest" whose wisdom on Egyptian and Assyrian mysteries is worthy of a prince of the Church.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Giovanni de' Medici, Iamblichus, Neoplatonism, Renaissance Humanism, dedication, Cardinal, Egyptian mysteries, Assyrian mysteries</keywords>

### Summary of the book of Iamblichus.

*Porphyry, who is called "the philosopher" among the Platonists because of his excellence, sent a long letter to Egypt to Anebo, a priest. It was full of various and weighty questions regarding all parts of philosophy, especially regarding God, as well as angels, demons, souls, providence, fate, prophecy, <term>magic</term><note>original: "magicen." Here referring to theurgy or ritual practice rather than stage magic.</note>, miracles, sacrifices, and vows. Iamblichus, his pupil, responded to Porphyry's questions. However, he introduces Abamon, an Egyptian priest, as the one responding on behalf of his disciple Anebo, to whom Porphyry had sent the letter. Therefore, concerning this entire inquiry and the truly divine response, as if I were still too much occupied with <term>Plotinus</term><note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism. Ficino had previously translated his massive "Enneads."</note>, I have translated almost every thought rather than every word. Thus, it should not be thought a marvel if the speech seems fragmented in some places, especially during the principles of the debate themselves, where the loss of words is of less consequence. From this point forward, the context of the words will appear more continuous. I have, however, been forced at times to insert some word for the sake of either continuity or understanding. Furthermore, the reason for this swifter edition was <term>Pierleoni</term><note>Pierleone Leoni (died 1492), a celebrated physician and scholar who served the Medici family and was a close friend of Ficino.</note>, a man most eager for all secrets. Indeed—and this is what I admire most of all—he always seems to strive for those things which he already possesses. For, through a certain divinity of character, he attains the secrets of the Philosophers, both Greeks and <term>Barbarians</term><note>original: "Barbarorū." In a classical context, this refers to non-Greek cultures, specifically the Egyptians and Chaldeans in this text.</note>, even those not yet read.*

<summary>Marsilio Ficino provides a summary of the upcoming text, explaining that it is a response by Iamblichus (writing as the priest Abamon) to a letter of philosophical questions from Porphyry. Ficino also notes his translation style—focusing on the "sense" of the text—and credits his friend Pierleone Leoni for encouraging the work.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, Iamblichus, Anebo, Abamon, Plotinus, Pierleone Leoni, Neoplatonism, Translation theory, Egyptian priesthood, Theurgy</keywords>

### *On the knowledge of divine things.*

The Egyptian writers, believing that all things had been discovered by <term>Mercury</term><note>original: "Mercurio." In this context, Mercury refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure conflated with the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with the invention of writing and all sacred sciences.</note>, dedicated their books to Mercury. Mercury presides over wisdom and eloquence. Pythagoras, Plato, Democritus, Eudoxus, and many others went to visit the Egyptian priests. The doctrines of this book belong to the Assyrians and the Egyptians, and are drawn from the pillars of Mercury. Pythagoras and Plato learned philosophy from the pillars of Mercury in Egypt. The pillars of Mercury are full of teachings. Before any use of reason, there is naturally implanted in us a notion of the gods; indeed, there is a certain touch of divinity that is better than mere knowledge, from which the natural appetite for the good, as well as reasoning and judgment, is stirred. There is an essential knowledge of divine things which is perpetual to the soul, and in truth, this is not the kind of "knowledge" by which we simply know about God, but that by which we enjoy Him. In the knowledge...

<summary>This page introduces the origins of the text's wisdom, attributing it to the Egyptian god Mercury (Hermes Trismegistus) and noting that Greek philosophers like Plato studied these Egyptian teachings. It argues that a fundamental "touch" of the divine exists in humans even before they begin to use reason.</summary>
<keywords>Mercury, Hermes Trismegistus, Egyptian priests, Pythagoras, Plato, pillars of Mercury, divine knowledge, Neoplatonism, innate ideas</keywords>

...for there is no <term>otherness</term><note>original: "alteritas." In this philosophical context, otherness refers to the gap or separation between the knower and the known. Iamblichus argues that at the highest level, this gap disappears.</note>, but a certain essential and simple contact. For we cannot reach unity itself except by something most unified, and by a unity of the mind which stands above the specific properties of the soul and the mind. The unity of the gods itself unites souls to it from eternity through their own unities, according to a proximity so intimate and effective that it appears to be a continuity. The divine intellect gives being to the soul through its own essential act of understanding. Therefore, the being of the soul is a certain way of understanding—namely, understanding God, upon whom it depends. 

Our very being consists in knowing God, because the primary being of the soul is its own intellect, in which being is the same as understanding divine things in a perpetual act. From that primary being are derived the <term>discursive powers</term><note>original: "potentiæ... discurrentes." These are the logical, step-by-step reasoning processes of the human mind, which Neoplatonists viewed as inferior to direct, intuitive divine intellectual grasp.</note> of the soul. After the gods, we place <term>daemons</term><note>original: "daemones." These are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or guiding entities that exist between the divine and the human realms.</note>, <term>heroes</term><note>original: "heroës." In this hierarchy, heroes are elevated souls or semi-divine beings that serve as a bridge to the gods.</note>, and pure souls; these three orders are the attendants of the gods. 

We cannot reach these attendants of the gods—the daemons, heroes, and pure souls—by the usual discursive reasonings of human logic. Instead, it is necessary to rise to an essential and eternal intelligence. Just as the gods are always reached through an innate notion, so the divine powers that follow the gods are only reached when the soul has laid aside its shifting mode of knowledge, which belongs to the rational power, which [intellectually...] <note>The text ends mid-word, "intelligit" (understands), corresponding to the catchword "lectu" for the following page.</note>

<summary>This page describes the metaphysical hierarchy and the soul's essential connection to the divine, arguing that true being is found in knowing God through an intuitive, unified intellect rather than human logic. It introduces the hierarchy of attendants to the gods: daemons, heroes, and pure souls.</summary>
<keywords>alterity, essential contact, unity of the soul, divine intellect, daemons, heroes, pure souls, discursive reasoning, innate notion, Neoplatonic hierarchy</keywords>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...is formed by intellect <note>original: "intellectu." The text begins mid-word, continuing from the previous page's discussion on the formation of the soul's understanding.</note> and intelligence, which he calls the <term>acquired intellect</term><note>original: "intellectus adeptus." In Neoplatonic thought, this is the human intellect when it has successfully received or "attained" universal truths from a higher source.</note>. For the primary knowledge resides in the <term>active intellect</term><note>original: "intellectus agens." This refers to the part of the mind that actively processes and illuminates knowledge, rather than just receiving it.</note>. Since knowledge is achieved through <term>alignment</term><note>original: "adaequatio." The philosophical principle that truth is the correspondence or "equalizing" of the mind to the object being known.</note>, it follows that we reach even the smallest eternal and immovable things through a concept that is itself eternal, immovable, and simple.

The knowledge by which we know <term>separated substances</term><note>original: "substantiae separatae." These are entities that exist independently of physical matter, such as divine minds or angels.</note> belongs to a different category than the knowledge by which we use to know other things. Knowledge of the divine has always existed in the soul through a simple <term>intuition</term> or "touch." Some people believe they can reach these separated substances through a method of opposition: namely, that material things are mobile, located in specific places, and subject to change; therefore, separated substances must be immovable, and so forth. 

In this way, one certainly learns what they are *not*; but what they *are* is known through the alignment of our knowledge with that which is naturally present in the soul through the intellect. This is acquired within the rational faculty through a kind of dedicated study—not so much through comparison and guesswork, but through the work of <term>separation and purification</term><note>original: "separatio et purificatio." The spiritual and intellectual process of stripping away material concerns to reveal the divine core of the soul.</note>. There was also a method of logical division: namely, that the gods and divine things are either temporal or eternal. They are not temporal; therefore, [they are eternal], and so on. Yet this method, because of its own "movement" <note>The author argues that step-by-step logical reasoning is a "moving" process and therefore cannot fully grasp the "immovable" nature of the divine.</note>, is not suited to things that are truly immovable.

...from a <term>genus</term><note>original: "genere." A general category or "family" of things.</note> that is indeterminate by itself, and a <term>difference</term><note>original: "differentia." The specific characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within the same genus.</note> that provides a boundary. For those <term>substances</term><note>original: "substantiae." In this context, these are higher, non-physical beings.</note> are complete <term>species</term><note>original: "species." The specific form or type of a being.</note> in every way, existing as a determined and finished <term>act</term><note>original: "actu." In Aristotelian and Neoplatonic thought, "act" or "actuality" refers to something being fully realized, rather than just having the potential to exist.</note>. If these <term>separable substances</term><note>original: "substantiae separabiles." Divine or angelic beings that exist independently of matter.</note>, being simple, do not differ among themselves by specific differences within the same genus, it follows that they do not differ as individuals within a single species either. Therefore, each one is, as it were, its own unique genus or species existing by itself. They differ from one another by their own inherent natures, by their rank in the hierarchy, and by the fact that they relate to the <term>First Principle</term><note>original: "primum." Referring to the ultimate source of all existence, or God.</note> in different ways.

These pure <term>Intelligences</term><note>original: "Intelligentiae." Non-physical, purely intellectual beings.</note> do not share a common category nor are they distinguished by any specific traits—for they are perfectly simple—but rather they are defined by the manner (either the same or different) in which they relate back to the First. Some are arranged in the higher ranks of perfection, while others follow in the lower degrees. Everywhere, the differences we see between things in their actions and how they are acted upon must be traced back to differences in their <term>powers</term><note>original: "iurium." Literally "rights" or "laws," referring here to the governing capacities or authority of a being's nature.</note>, and these in turn must be traced back to differences in their <term>essences</term><note>original: "essentiarum." The fundamental nature or core being of a thing.</note>. We must never stop at the outward effects but must always look toward the primary causes.

Neither in the substances higher than our soul, nor in the soul itself, is there any "passive motion" <note>original: "motio passiva." Being moved or changed by an external force.</note>; instead, everything is an effective act. The motion of the soul, by which it moves itself, is not divided into a "mover" and a "thing being moved," or into "moving" and "being moved." Rather, it is an essential act proceeding

...temporally. <term>Accidents</term><note>original: "accidentia." In philosophy, these are non-essential qualities (like color or position) that can change without changing the nature of the thing itself.</note> belong to composite things and to <term>forms</term><note>original: "formis." The defining characteristics or "blueprints" of things.</note> that exist within a subject, but they do not apply to immaterial forms. Whatever exists in <term>separable forms</term><note>original: "formis separabilibus." Beings like gods or angels that exist independently of matter.</note> is purely its own being; it is essential by a certain special and equal destiny. Neither "accidents" nor "consequences" are found there. Their motions and actions differ because their inherent natures are different, not the other way around. If we were to claim there is only one single <term>genus</term><note>original: "genus." A broad category or family of things.</note> for all separated beings, we would throw <term>theology</term><note>original: "theologiam." Here referring to the systematic study of the divine hierarchy.</note> into confusion. Separable substances do not belong to one common category in which they are distinguished by specific differences; instead, they are distinguished by themselves and by the order of their ranks, insofar as they are related to the <term>First Principle</term><note>original: "primum." The ultimate source of all existence, often identified as the One or God.</note> through different degrees of perfection. However, those beings that relate to the First and the Last in a similar way have more in common with one another.

Goodness is twofold: that which is <term>above essence</term><note>original: "super essentiam." Refers to the absolute Good (The One) which is so perfect it transcends the very definition of "being."</note>, and that which is according to essence. <term>Essence</term><note>original: "Essentia." The fundamental nature or "what-ness" of a thing.</note> is the defining property of all the Gods. But the Good itself is above essence and is called the cause of good—that is, the principle of essential good. Accordingly, the ranks of the Gods are distinguished from one another according to their degrees of essence. In the lowest <term>rational souls</term><note>original: "Animabus rationalibus." Human souls or similar intellectual beings that occupy the boundary between the divine and the material.</note>, essential good is not present in the same way it is in the gods; instead, they possess a participation in the good according to <term>intellectual beauty</term><note>original: "pulchritudinem intellectualem." A non-physical beauty found in truth and divine order.</note>, though this participation is present in them immovably.

### On the Order of Superior Beings.

Our souls are counted among the divine classes. <term>Heroes</term><note>original: "Heroës." In Neoplatonism, these are beings intermediate between humans and spirits, often associated with the purified souls of great figures from the past.</note> are greater than humans; therefore, <term>daemons</term><note>original: "dæmones." In the context of ancient philosophy, these are not "demons" in the modern evil sense, but intermediary spirits that guide and bridge the gap between gods and men.</note> are much greater still. The first of the divine is the **Good** itself, with the gods following after. The last are the individual rational souls. Between these two extremes are two intermediate ranks: namely, the heroes, who are close to souls, and the daemons, who are close to the gods—just as air and water exist between fire and earth. Even though heroes surpass us in power, virtue, beauty, and greatness, they still share much in common with our soul and its way of life.

Daemons are superior to heroes and act as ministers to the gods, who serve as architects in the <term>crafting of the world</term><note>original: "opificio mundano." This refers to the creation and maintenance of the physical universe by divine forces.</note>. What is inexpressible and hidden within the gods, the daemons express and reveal. Daemons and heroes adapt the universal, simple, and unchanging gifts of the gods for the benefit of lower beings; they reconcile all things and are the authors of harmonic agreement and mutual <term>sympathy</term><note>original: "compassionis." In ancient science, this refers to the natural "resonance" or interconnectedness of all parts of the cosmos.</note> between all things. They bring divine things down to us and, in turn, lead our concerns up to the divine. Furthermore, they equally organize the degrees of the gifts given by superiors and the preparation of those who are meant to receive them.

The property of the **gods** is **unity**, a permanence within themselves, the immovable cause of all motions, and an eminent providence that has nothing in common with those beings for which it provides. This characteristic is preserved in them according to their <term>essence</term><note>original: "essentiam." In this philosophical context, essence refers to the fundamental nature or "whatness" of a being.</note>, their <term>power</term><note>original: "virtutem." This refers to the inherent capacity or potential for a being to exert influence.</note>, and their <term>action</term><note>original: "actionem." The property of **souls** is a leaning toward multiplicity and motion, a connection with the gods, and the capacity to receive something from other sources. They fill these things with vital motion and harmonize everywhere with all things—partly with those that remain stable and partly with those that are in flux—tempering all things within themselves and through their own nature. This property is likewise preserved in them according to essence, power, and action. 

The properties of **daemons** consist in containing within themselves the gifts of the gods, though in a lower manner than the gods themselves. Under the governing <term>form</term><note>original: "idea." The divine blueprint or rational principle that shapes reality.</note> and reason of these gifts, they also contain the conditions of lower things; thus, while they are indeed multiplied, they are also joined in unity. They are mixed, yet remain unconfused; finally, they move, but they do so with stability. 

**Heroes**, on the contrary, possess unity, identity, stability, and excellence while operating under the conditions of multiplicity, motion, and mixture. 

Daemons and heroes are closest to the extremes: the former to the gods, the latter to souls. The differences between daemons and heroes are primarily that heroes sometimes lean more toward particular and changeable things than daemons do. These two intermediaries—namely, daemons—

### How the actions of superior beings are distinguished from one another.

**G**ODS occupy the highest rank of beings, and souls the lowest. The gods are capable of all things, united in a single moment; souls, on the contrary, are neither capable of all things, nor do they act in a single moment, nor are they united. The gods perform and care for all things without being inclined <note>original: "non inclinati." In Neoplatonic philosophy, this suggests the gods act upon the world without being "bent" or affected by the material things they govern.</note>; souls act with a certain inclination and a turning toward their objects. The gods are the primary causes; souls depend perpetually upon the will of those gods. The gods, with the swiftest vigor, grasp their innermost ends simultaneously with their principles; souls proceed from one thing to another, moving from the imperfect to the perfect. The gods cannot be comprehended by any measure or form; souls are held back and overcome by inclination, by <term>disposition</term><note>original: "habitudine." This refers to the state or condition a soul takes on when it relates to the physical world.</note>, and by an impulse toward the lower. They are touched by a desire for lesser things and by a familiarity with them, and from this they contract certain qualities.

### On the Intellect and the Soul.

**I**ntellect, the maker of all things, is always present to all gods in the fullest sense through a single <term>act</term><note>original: "actum." The internal operation or "energy" of a being.</note> remaining within itself. The Soul is a participant in the <term>Intellect</term><note>original: "intellectus." Often referred to as "Nous," this is the divine Mind that contains the blueprints of reality.</note>, though it participates in a more divisible and multiform way.

Therefore, if you wish to understand the form of the gods, consider the properties of the lowest rational soul, and attribute the opposites of these—in their highest perfection—to the gods. If it pleases you to compose the form of a **daemon**, compose it from both, but for the time being attribute more of the divine to it. Finally, if you seek the form of a **hero**, it is truly derived from both, yet brings in more of the conditions of the soul. 

He <note>The author, Iamblichus, writing under the persona of the Egyptian priest Abammon.</note> criticizes <term>Porphyry</term><note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and the teacher of Iamblichus. ...[impulses], which if they are restrained more violently and suddenly from the beginning, eventually burst forth more fiercely, like a stifled flame or suppressed laughter; therefore, they should be corrected more gently. **Heraclitus** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for his doctrine of change and "fire" as the fundamental essence.</note> calls sacrifices "medicines," because they purge the soul of the diseases that have grown together with it in this <term>generation</term> <note>Latin: "generatione." In Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to the material world of "coming-to-be," where souls become entangled with physical matter and suffering.</note>. **Porphyry** <note>The student of Plotinus whose "Letter to Anebo" raised many of the questions Iamblichus is answering here.</note> suspected that not only daemons, but even the gods themselves, were touched by some <term>passion</term> <note>Latin: "passio." Again, this refers to being "acted upon" or changed by an external influence, such as a human prayer.</note>, since they are seemingly "moved" by invocations. But the will of the Good in God, and in the gods (who are the very essences of "Goodness"), is more excellent; and therefore, it is freer than our own "elective" life concerning the good. 

Therefore, the gods are not moved to provide good to men because they are "invoked" <note>Meaning, they are not compelled or forced to act by the ritual.</note>; rather, they spontaneously provoke us toward the good. When we turn toward them by invoking them, they meet us of their own accord, and they reveal and bestow something. Indeed, men think they are free to ask; let it be so, then—the gods are even freer to give. Because of their free will toward the good and their perennial and perfect action, the gods benefit all things as soon as people are turned toward them through invocation. 

In these supplications, the soul reaches a <term>contemplation</term> of divine things and transforms its former life—which was liable to passions—into a life free of passion, provided it enters into the activity and the life of the gods. How, then, can our supplications touch the gods with passions, when the rituals actually make the previously "passive" souls...

### *On the Anger of the Gods.*

**W**hen we turn away from the beneficent care of the gods, as if turning away from the light of the sun, we are immediately in darkness, and it is said of us that the god is "angry." To appease the "anger" of the gods, therefore, is simply to return to them through supplication. Appeasement of this kind does not bring a passion to the god; rather, it frees our own soul from its previous passions. The gods and divine <term>daemons</term> <note>Not "demons" in the modern evil sense, but "daemones": intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between the high gods and humanity.</note>, when humbly adored and worshiped, repel many evils that would otherwise happen naturally.

### *On the Necessity and Liberty of the Gods.*

**I**t is necessary that the gods be as they are, not because of a necessity imposed upon them from the outside, but because of a necessity that is natural and best for them. Therefore, their state is entirely voluntary, such that they would never wish to be otherwise even if a choice were offered. **Porphyry** <note>The scholar whose skeptical questions prompted this book.</note> and many other philosophers say that the gods are indeed "pure intellects," while daemons are "intellects" (or sharers in intellect) that are in some way connected to souls. But **Iamblichus** objects that this definition of the nature of daemons is not quite correct; for even souls [that are] intellectual...

### *On the difference between Gods and Daemons*
### *according to the Greeks and the most devout.*

**G**ods are rightly defined not according to the principle of the intellect itself, but according to unity, and goodness, and the <term>intelligible object</term> <note>Latin: "intelligibilis obiecti." In Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to a reality that can only be grasped by the mind, existing beyond the reach of the physical senses.</note>. Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century scholar who wrote a famous letter questioning the logic of religious rituals; Iamblichus is responding to those questions here.</note> suspects that pure and separate intellects have no relationship to sensible things <note>Physical things we can see or touch.</note>, and that they do not hear prayers. Nevertheless, a principal worship must be offered to these separate substances. In this worship, the highest part of the soul is awakened and joined to the highest beings; these supreme beings comprehend and know all our affairs within their own "One," and they contain within themselves the actions of religious prayers. They do not depart from themselves, but remaining in their own nature, they are fully present to the intention of those praying. Indeed, it is fitting to supplicate most humbly. For recognizing our own unworthiness, when compared to the beings above, causes us to supplicate most earnestly, to turn toward them completely, and through constant habit, to become like them. Prayers sent from a divine source, which contain a divine power, are especially beneficial. These points are made against Porphyry, who thinks that we should specifically worship the <term>mundane gods</term> <note>Latin: "mundanos deos." **P**orphyry says that certain material things are used in supplications, and for that reason, they are used only for those gods who are animate <note>Latin: "animalia." Iamblichus says that their essential substances and properties cannot be discerned through these distinctions alone.

### *Concerning the difference between gods and demons,*
### *and also concerning celestial beings.*

**C**elestial gods can be called incorporeal <note>Latin: "incorporei." In this Neoplatonic context, it means they are not restricted by the density or limitations of physical matter.</note>, because no hindrance from physical bodies affects their more excellent action and the happiness of their lives. But insofar as the gods tend toward the One <note>The "One" is the ultimate, absolute source of all existence in Neoplatonic philosophy.</note> itself, their bodies spontaneously strive toward that same goal; they do not confine souls, but are themselves most excellently contained by those souls.

The celestial body is most closely related to incorporeal things because of its simple, undivided, and constant nature, and its single action—which is its circular motion—as well as its innate life and light. In the heavens, there is no composite mixture of soul and body into a single "third nature"; instead, the body is drawn entirely toward the nature of the soul. It is, as it were, a kind of visible soul. Perhaps heaven is light itself without matter and without dimension. 

Dimension appears there only because of the soul's vast presence. Hence, heaven is the soul of heaven accommodating itself to our eyes and to perishable things; that great circle is the revolution of the soul, and the light is the <term>intellect</term> <note>Latin: "intellectus." For Iamblichus, this is the highest faculty of the soul, capable of direct spiritual perception.</note> of that same soul. Just as in the lowest of bodies the "form" <note>The organizing principle or "shape" of a thing.</note> becomes material, so in the highest realms matter becomes "formal." Thus, we have an "ensouled body" rather than a "bodied soul"—if indeed there is any matter at all in the heavens. Just as the highest part of the air becomes fiery, so the celestial

### *On the closeness of celestial bodies to incorporeal forms.*

### *On Providence, and on Gods and Daemons.*

The **providence** <note>The divine care or guidance of the universe.</note> of the gods is **universal**, but that of the **daemons** <note>original: "dæmonum." In the Neoplatonic tradition of Iamblichus, daemons are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits that serve as bridges between the high gods and the human world.</note> is **particular**. The **First God** <note>The ultimate source or "The One" from which all existence flows.</note> gives all things to all; the following gods bestow some things on all. Daemons and souls give only to some, and only some things.

There are invisible gods, and there are visible gods in the heavens <note>Visible gods refer to the celestial bodies—the sun, moon, and planets—which were considered divine beings.</note>, and there are also daemons. Indeed, the gods visible in the heavens exist within that very union with the hidden gods. Daemons, however, are far distant from them; they are more inclined toward action, whereas the gods are pure **contemplators** <note>original: "contemplatoribus." In this philosophy, "contemplation" is the highest state of being, involving a direct, non-discursive understanding of divine truth.</note>. Therefore, they are also far distant from the visible gods. Furthermore, the essence of both types of gods—as well as their power and providence—is universal, extending through all things. The nature of daemons, however, is a particular providence concerning certain matters and provinces <note>original: "prouincias." This refers to specific spheres of influence or jurisdictions in the natural world.</note>. Also, the gods so far transcend their bodies, and their bodies are so obedient to them, that they are said to be separated from their bodies. Daemons, on the other hand...

...by their own nature <note>The Latin "ria" likely completes "propria" (one's own) from the previous page.</note> they are more affected and joined to bodies. Likewise, the **gods** are the **architects** <note>The designers or master-builders of the universe.</note>, whereas the **daemons** are the **ministers** <note>The servants or agents who carry out the divine plan.</note>. Daemons are hidden from the senses, and the gods are also hidden from human reason; yet if it should happen that the gods appear, they will still be superior to the daemons of the air near the earth. For a change of location or duty does not change the divine nature. He refutes the examples that **Porphyry** <note>A Phoenician philosopher and student of Plotinus who questioned the efficacy and morality of religious rituals.</note> had brought forward from history—namely, the claim that many things are done toward the gods as if they were **subject to passions** <note>original: "passibiles." In ancient philosophy, "passion" refers to being "acted upon" by external forces, including emotions, suffering, or physical needs.</note>. He argues this because the law of sacred rites commands that one must be free from passions during sacrifices; this law was divinely given by the **First Father** of the world, from whom all symbols in sacrifices signify something most hidden. Ultimately, those things which are performed correctly in the sacred rites have a divine cause so far removed from passion that human reason cannot even grasp it.

The **common people** <note>original: "Vulgus." The uninitiated or those without philosophical training.</note> cannot grasp the reason for ceremonies that are divinely instituted, yet they attempt to assign a reason anyway. By assigning reasons based on their own passions, they attribute those same passions to the gods.

The common people use gestures of veneration toward the powerful and offer the same gifts to the gods. They do this toward men, both because of their own passions and because of the passions of their superiors. Thus, they believe that similar passions exist within the gods as well...

### *How Daemons, Heroes, and Souls Differ.*

**T**here are in the gods **generative** <note>Powers related to the creation and "bringing forth" of the world.</note> and **demiurgic** <note>original: "opificesque." Refers to the "Demiurge," the divine craftsman or master-builder of the universe.</note> powers; there are also **life-giving** powers, which are contained more sublimely in the higher gods. The first [generative] powers are spread more widely than the second [life-giving] ones. The second are defined by the first. **Daemons** emerge after a long progression of these powers, at the point where they are already diverted into the greatest degree of division. **Heroes** are defined by the second—that is, the life-giving powers—before they reach the final stage. For in the final stage of these powers, **souls** emerge.

Therefore, the **duty** <note>original: "officium."</note> of daemons is the work of craftsmanship regarding worldly natures, to carry through and complete all things down to individual details simultaneously, and to bind souls to bodies. But the duty of heroes is to give life, to reason, and to guard souls, and to release them from bodies. The duty of daemons is wider than that of heroes: the former work more regarding the universe as a whole, while the latter work rather regarding individual souls. We do not say that souls are "made" [by them], but that they receive something from daemons and heroes, and add many things from themselves besides, and begin their own <insert>duty</insert>...

# ON THE MYSTERIES.

...duty regarding the end of divine works: not because divine things do not act further, but because souls are admitted into the final stage of divine duties. <note>In the Neoplatonic hierarchy described here, souls are the "bottom" or "end" of the divine chain, serving as the bridge between the spiritual and material worlds.</note> Likewise, the soul can bring forth from itself such varied forms of living that, depending on how they fit, it can inhabit any specific region of the world. It can also meet with whomever it wishes, and return again into itself, and join itself both to the gods and to lower beings; it brings forth the divine principles <note>original: "rationes." These are the "logoi"—the rational blueprints or seeds of reality that the soul contains and expresses.</note> though in a lesser way. Although it is often joined to the gods through daemons and heroes, it can also join itself to the gods through certain means of its own that differ from theirs. Sometimes the soul reconciles itself to the divine through different harmonies of its essence and its actions than those which daemons use to connect to the higher powers. Even if the soul does not maintain a perfectly consistent way of life, it is often illuminated by the kind will of the Gods and rises above the daemons toward an **angelic life** <note>The Latin translator uses "angelica" (angelic) to describe the highest state of the soul—a life of pure intellect—distinguishing it from the "animalis" (animal) life of the physical body.</note> rather than an animal one. Although the soul seems to show all principles and every kind of form within itself, it is always defined by one specific thing—that is, one particular form. And meanwhile, based on previous causes, it coordinates itself now to some things and now to others, moving itself by its own power.

-># IAMBLICHUS<-

All the higher beings <note>original: "superi." In Neoplatonism, this refers to the entire hierarchy of spiritual entities residing above the material world.</note> come into view when invoked, but they appear in different forms and with different powers. The souls of the stars also move the sight in certain new ways. The visions of the **Gods** appear uniform and most simple, while those of **archangels** are somewhat less uniform or simple. Those of **angels** are even less so; those of **daemons** <note>These are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits that act as messengers or guardians.</note> are already varied; those of **principalities** <note>original: "principatuum." The visions of individual **souls**, of course, take on every kind of form. Since these higher beings are different in their natures and their actions, and appear to each person according to their own specific mode, they rightly appear in different ways to different observers. 

The **Gods** come into sight as entirely full of salvation; **archangels** are at once terrifying and gentle; **angels** are milder; **daemons** are to be feared; **heroes** are less to be revered; **principalities** are astonishing; **rulers** are harmful and hostile; and **souls** are similar to heroes, though lower in rank.

The images of the **Gods** appear utterly immutable in size, form, figure, and action. Those of **archangels** and **angels** are gradually less immutable, yet they remain close to the Gods. The images of **daemons** are indeed changeable in size and form—for they appear in one way at one time and another way at another, yet they are recognized as the same beings. Those of the **principalities** are immutable. Those of **heroes** are much like those of daemons. Those of the **rulers** appear multiformly...

### *On the Power of the Sacraments.*

**T**he proper observance of the precepts and divine works—which exceed all intelligence—along with the wonderful power of symbols and sacraments <note>original: "sacramentorum." Here used in the broad sense of sacred mysteries or ritual signs, not exclusively the Christian sacraments.</note> known only to the gods, grants us deific union. When we are occupied with sacred rites, we do not achieve the result through our intelligence regarding the sacrament; otherwise, the action of these rites would be merely intellectual and would originate from us. On the contrary: even when we do not understand them, these rites perform their own work, and the power of the gods to which they are referred recognizes its own ineffable images within them. This power is not stirred into action by our intellects. For universal causes are not moved by particular effects...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that the soul's union with God is achieved through the inherent power of sacred rituals (theurgy) rather than through human intellect or philosophy. ->*What prophecy is, and from where it comes.*<-

**P**rophecy <note>original: "Vaticinium." Into itself, I say—that is, into its **seminal and intellectual reasons** <note>original: "rationes seminales, & intellectuales." But if the soul soon unfolds the universal form of reasons and thoughts according to which it once lived, then it will bring back presages pertaining more to the universal condition of worldly things, under which it will also be able to perceive particular things everywhere. If, again, it is coupled to the very **minds of the gods** through such a universal form of its own, it will see moreover those things which belong to the higher world and those which belong to this one; likewise, through those divine minds as the primary causes, it will understand more absolutely. In this state, not only will thought be perfected, but *imagination* also will have pure images regarding both corporeal and divine things. 

But since the reasons of things to be generated are in the soul according to its power—both effective and cognitive—and since these reasons depend on the reasons which are in the gods, therefore the soul, when joined to these gods, awakens the reasons in itself...

### *Concerning divine inspiration, which occurs in the waking state.*

**P**orphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> touched upon two divine inspirations <note>original: "afflationes," literally "breathings-upon" or "inflations" of the soul.</note>: one, which is commonly said to happen in sleep; the other, which happens in the waking state, where those who are inspired and moved <note>original: "afflati, & perciti"</note> foretell the future, being so awake that they even use their senses. ### *Many miracles are performed by Prophets.*

**T**hat those inspired by the divine do not live a [merely] animal life <note>In this context, "animal life" (*animalis uita*) refers to the life of the soul as it governs the physical body and its senses, rather than "animal" in the modern sense of a beast.</note> at that time is evident, because many of them, when fire is brought near, are not burned, for the god breathing within them evidently repels the fire; or if they are burned, they do not feel it, nor do they perceive piercings, or scrapings, or any torments. There were generally three opinions concerning divine inspiration and prophecy: the first attributed its cause to the soul, the second to the body, and the third to the composite <note>The "composite" refers to the human being as a joined entity of both soul and body.</note>.

Iamblichus concedes these things, but he denies that these are the causes of divine inspiration: for they are human, partly natural and partly artificial, and they possess nothing divine in themselves.

This is what Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist who often sought rational or psychological explanations for religious phenomena, prompting Iamblichus's more "mystical" response.</note> seems to suspect when he says that some people are inspired when they hear flutes, or cymbals, or drums, while others are inspired by different melodies.

Various types of motions in the world correspond to the various orders of the gods—certain motions to certain gods. From these motions flow various melodies, which similarly agree through their own movements with specific gods who are the principles of those motions. These gods—since they are everywhere and impart their own essence especially to those things that belong to them—are especially present in the melodies that most agree with them. Insinuating <note>original: "insinuantes"; literally "winding their way into"</note> themselves through our spirits <note>In Neoplatonism, the "spirit" (spiritus) is a subtle intermediary between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note> as they are affected by those melodies, they occupy the person and soon fill them inwardly with their own essence and power.

The cause of this inspiration is not so much the human emotion <note>original: "passio"; here meaning a state of being acted upon or moved by external stimuli</note> excited by the music, but rather the music's own congruence with the god, to whom the god is naturally present. Things that come to the sight are too image-based and relate rather to intelligible things <term>intelligibilia; non-physical realities that can only be grasped by the intellect</term>. Things that come to the senses below hearing <note>Referring to touch, taste, and smell, which were considered more "base" or material senses</note> are too material. However, those things pertaining to hearing are "middle things" and agree with the soul; having been worked into the spirit along with motion, emotion, and meaning...

Neither water, nor air, nor any other physical thing provides prophecy <note>original: "vaticinium"</note>, but rather the sacred rites performed regarding these things; indeed, the purification of the mind along with the purification of the vehicle <term>vehicle: the "soul-vehicle" or ochema, an ethereal "body" that carries the soul and allows it to interact with both the divine and material worlds</term>, and the focusing of intent upon God, receives the divine power, which is present everywhere and always most ready.

Therefore, the various types of inspired people do not follow the natural variations found within us, but rather the different kinds of both the inspiring deities <note>original: "numinū afflantium"</note> and the modes by which we participate in the divine presence. Thus, when divinely inspired men behave differently—some remaining at rest, others being moved to excitement, others seeking out mountains and wilderness, and others behaving in various other ways—this does not proceed from differences in our natural causes, nor from locations, nor from the music they have recently heard or are hearing. Instead, it comes from the various properties of the gods by whom the inspired are ruled, and from the various modes of inspiration.

...prophecy <note>original: "vaticinium"; completing the sentence from the previous page</note> came: another was the **Delphic** oracle, where [the priestess], sitting at the mouth of the cave, would prophesy; a third was the **Branchidic** <note>The Oracle of Apollo at Didyma, managed by the Branchidae family</note>, where those inhaling vapor from the water would foretell the future. There was in **Colophon** <note>A Greek city in Ionia, home to the Oracle of Apollo at Clarus</note> a subterranean place in which there was a spring. The priest, therefore, would sacrifice on appointed nights and afterward taste the water. Finally, he would prophesy there, having become invisible to those present. It may seem to someone that the divine spirit passed through the water into the priest. However, this is not the case. For the divine does not pass through those things that participate in it according to physical distance or division, but rather it encompasses them from the outside, and thoroughly illuminates and fills the water with a certain power contributing to prophecy—namely, a purifying <note>original: "purgatoria"</note> power. 

So it is that when the priest drinks, the water itself purifies the **luminous spirit** <term>luminous spirit: the "augoeides" or radiant vehicle of the soul, believed by Neoplatonists to be the intermediary between the physical body and the higher intellect</term> implanted within us, and adjusts it to God; through this purification and adjustment, we are able to receive God. [Divine power] is present everywhere, suddenly [available] for those capable of participating in it, illuminating from the outside and filling all things, and running through all the elements. It does not leave any living creature <note>original: "animal," referring to any being possessed of a soul</note> or nature to which it does not impress something of itself according to that creature's capacity, contributing to a foretelling <term>præſagium: a sense of what is to come; a premonition or omen</term>. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a letter questioning the mechanisms of divine ritual; this book is Iamblichus’s point-by-point response</note>, besides the publicly celebrated prophecies <term>uaticinia: the act of foretelling or delivering a divine message</term>, mentions certain private ones—specifically, those who claim they will attract spirits <note>original: "ſpiritus"</note> for the purpose of prophecy through the use of certain symbols <term>characteres: magical signs, sigils, or inscribed marks believed to have ritual power</term>. 

Iamblichus <note>The Syrian philosopher and author of this text, who championed theurgy (divine work) over mere intellectual philosophy</note> rejects this practice. He argues that because these practitioners neglect all religion and holiness <note>original: "ſanctimoniam"</note> while trusting in symbols alone, they are unable to obtain the presence of any god or good deity <note>original: "numinis"</note> by which true prophecies are usually given. Instead, they are deceived; although they use symbols appropriate to the gods and possess an intention of the mind, they only bring back a certain imaginary apparition from the higher powers that is small and obscure. Furthermore, because they neglect holiness in the meantime, they fall under the power of evil demons <note>original: "malorum dæmonum"</note>, who lie and deceive. These demons pervert and confuse whatever small amount of signs or apparitions might actually come from the gods.

I speak of a purpose pre-signified and decreed from the beginning. Thus, birds often hurl themselves down, or dash themselves against objects, or otherwise kill themselves while contributing to the signaling; they do not do this of their own accord, but are drawn to it by divine influence. <page-num>74</page-num>

<header>IAMBLICHUS</header>

Signs are most easily made at the nod of the celestial gods, with the upper air <note>original: "aëre summo," referring to the ether or the highest part of the atmosphere closest to the heavens</note> there being ignited, which is very easy to guide and shape—especially by the gods—and into fire. Meanwhile, certain influences <note>original: "influxus," the celestial 'flow' of power</note> from the celestial bodies descend into this air, assisting in the creation and movement of such stars <note>referring here to "shooting stars" or meteorological phenomena used as omens</note> which are similar to the celestial ones in their light, power, and motion. 

The **World-Animal** <term>Mundanum animal: a central concept in ancient philosophy where the entire universe is viewed as a single, living, and interconnected organism</term> is so united with itself that its members sympathize <note>original: "compatiantur," from the Greek 'sympatheia,' meaning they react in harmony with one another</note> with each other and are moved together, even those parts that seem remote from each other, just as if they were close, like the limbs of a single animal. 

And this union and sympathy assists the gods in displaying signs to humans—first through the heavens, and then through the air. The gods do not act immediately <note>meaning "directly" or "without a gap"</note>, but through intermediate instruments—namely **daemons** <term>daemons: in this context, they are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans</term>, souls, natures, and all things depending on these. They create signs for humans by beginning from a single principle: and from there, they subsequently spread the motion descending from themselves wherever they wish. 

Therefore, without any personal entanglement or coordination with things that are born and perish <note>original: "generabilia," things in the material world subject to change and decay</note>, the gods rule such individual matters. And just as in their creative workmanship and providence, so too in the showing of signs: their intellect is not turned down toward our level; rather, while the divine mind remains within itself, it draws all signs and **prophecy** <note>original: "vaticinium"</note> back toward itself, recognizing that they all proceed from its own essence.

They do not bend themselves toward the subjects; rather, by their own stable state and most fully, they make all things like themselves. -># ON THE MYSTERIES<-

...to us everywhere proofs of things past, present, and future.

*No sacred work of any effectiveness takes place except through the power, or rather the presence, of some divine being.*

**I**n religion, no work of any marvelous power can be accomplished unless one of the higher beings is present there as an observer and fulfiller of the act. Therefore, it is not the soul, but divinity itself that is the cause of divine works. <meta>This page continues the philosophical inquiry into the nature of spirits and the soul, specifically addressing the impossibility of human or material forces creating higher spiritual entities.</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

Porphyry <note>The text refers to the philosopher Porphyry, who questioned the origins of spiritual beings in his letter to Anebo</note> denies that **demons** <note>original: "dæmones"; in this Neoplatonic context, these are intermediary spirits or "daemons," not necessarily evil entities</note> are generated or corrupted. For he denies that demons—who are superior to both bodies and the soul—can be generated by the soul from bodily forces. He denies that the actions of a particular soul, enclosed within a body, can result in essences that subsist by themselves outside of the soul. He denies that the forces of bodies, which are entirely devoted to matter, can be released from them to generate demons. Furthermore, he asks what power it is that releases material forces from matter and, in turn, fuses them into one to generate a demon; for it would seem that this power must itself be demonic, and thus the demon would exist even before it is generated. 

A soul cannot be generated from things lacking a soul or the power of prophecy—especially a prophetic soul. Something more excellent cannot be procreated from something inferior. No essence or substance can be constituted from the motions of the soul and bodily forces, which are themselves neither substances nor essences. Likewise, none of those things which are sown through generation possess anything greater than what is handed down to them by the principal generating cause. 

Therefore, since neither the body nor the soul possesses prophecy <note>original: "uaticinium"; the divine gift of foretelling or spiritual insight</note> by itself, the soul cannot procreate a prophesying demon from its own motions and from bodies. Perhaps someone will say that demons are not generated by us, but that they preside over living beings in an established order...

### *On Divine and Human Dreams*

**P**orphyry <note>A prominent Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who often sought rational or psychological explanations for spiritual phenomena.</note> says that the forewarnings of dreams come partly from within ourselves and partly from an external source. This is because we often study and perform various actions to "hunt down" <note>original: *aucupandum*, a metaphor derived from bird-catching or fowling</note> this foreknowledge, yet it is not granted; conversely, it is often given to those who are not even seeking it. For if the effect of dreaming arose from our own nature and human will, it would occur through our own foresight. Instead, it is sent by the gods according to their own will—namely, when and how they wish to demonstrate the future through a certain kindness. 

The Orphic hymn <note>Hymns attributed to the legendary poet Orpheus, used in ancient mystery religions.</note> declares the same thing. Iamblichus denies this, saying that passion is by its very nature unstable...

Finally, as much as divine things are distant from the lowest natural things, so much do their actions and effects differ from the effects of natural things. Thus, the **alienation** brought about **divinely** has nothing in common with that which occurs **humanly**. Therefore, when you think of the divine sort, you must completely separate from it all the defects and incidental qualities of the human sort. 

Furthermore, when you contemplate the **sacred sobriety** and **vigilance** received from the divine, do not compare it with human **sobriety**. And in both cases, remove from the mind whatever is in any way similar to any **imaginations** <note>original: *imaginationibus*; the mental images or visions presented to the mind's eye.</note> which the humors and similar causes stir up, when considering those **imaginations** applied by the divine. You should not think that the ambiguous human state—midway between a sober mind and one that is alienated <note>original: *alienatus*; here meaning a mind "outside itself" or in a trance-like state.</note>—is similar to the state of a sacred soul that looks upon God with a single gaze. Nor should you believe that the most certain insights into divine matters are similar to those imaginings stirred up by the art of sorcery <note>original: *arte uenefica*; literally "the poisonous art," referring here to deceptive magic or witchcraft.</note>. For the things we imagine while bewitched have no truth of action or essence beyond being mere phantoms <note>original: *imaginamenta*; mental images or illusions that lack substance.</note>. Indeed, the goal of that kind of magic is not to actually create anything, but merely to project these phantoms until they appear to be real.

One must not think that the divine prophet <note>original: *vates*; a divinely inspired seer or speaker of oracles.</note> happens upon the truth by chance, as the insane sometimes do; nor even through some natural susceptibility <note>original: *passio*; in ancient philosophy, this refers to being "acted upon" or affected by external physical forces.</note>, just as animals are often affected by certain parts and forces of the world that are beginning to bring about something in the future. These forces manifest in the air in some way before they reach the earth. By being affected in this way, animals sometimes sense coming earthquakes and storms—especially those animals that are either easily influenced or have acute senses. 

For foreknowledge arising either by chance or by such a natural impression is rare, disordered, discontinuous, and utterly obscure. Divine prophecy <term>vaticinium</term> <note>The gift of foretelling or the actual utterance of a prophet acting under divine influence.</note>, however, beholds the order of the universe with a continuous, firm, and connected reason. Even if we possess some innate faculty for perceiving the future, that faculty is not, by itself, true prophecy.

<meta>catchword: hæc (this/these)</meta>

<summary>Iamblichus distinguishes divine prophecy from the "phantoms" produced by sorcery and the natural instincts of animals, arguing that true prophecy is a stable, rational connection to the divine order rather than a random or physical occurrence.</summary>

<page-num>89</page-num>

<center>

### ON THE MYSTERIES

</center>

For this <note>referring to the natural instinct or susceptibility mentioned on the previous page</note> is not always truthful, but only occasionally; nor is it true in all matters, but only in some. True prophecy <note>original: *vaticinium*; the gift of divine prediction</note>, however, is truthful both always and in all things. Likewise, foreknowledge <note>term: <term>prænotio</term> — a technical term for "prior knowledge" gained through human effort or observation</note> achieved through technical art hunts for the future using signs that are not entirely reliable, because those signs do not always have the final event joined to them. 

But prophecy produced by divine providence beholds the effect directly from its causes with a gaze that is firm, present, and utterly continuous. It connects all things—even those that are changeable, temporal, and distant from one another—anticipating future events as if they were already present.

Someone might argue that the future can be predicted by combining four specific gifts: 
1. A person’s specific natural temperament.
2. A technical art applied to that nature.
3. The common sympathy <note>original: *compassio*; the Stoic concept that all parts of the universe are interconnected like a single living organism</note> of things for one another, as if they were parts of the same living creature.
4. That specific arrangement of bodies by which some things provide signs to others. 

But in truth, even when signs are clearly perceived through the meeting of these factors, such a perception only bears a slight resemblance to prophecy. While the universe contains traces of prophecy everywhere, they are not clear in every place. Just as the image of the "Good itself" <note>a Platonic reference to the highest principle of divinity</note> reflects God in all things, so too is there some trace of prophecy in all things. Yet, the single, divine, and unmixed form of prophecy must not be defined by these mere likenesses sent down into the realm of generation <note>original: *generationem*; the material world of birth, change, and decay</note>, and much less by the delusions of those who rave <margin>f 5</margin>...

<summary>Iamblichus distinguishes true divine prophecy from human "foreknowledge" and natural "sympathy," arguing that while the physical world contains traces of the divine, true prophecy is a certain and continuous gaze provided by providence.</summary>

...beginning <note>The text begins mid-word, likely completing "initium" (beginning) from the previous page</note>. For all these things are deceptive. Prophecy itself must be defined by a single principle, a single order, a single divine form, and one **intelligible** <term>intelligibilem</term> <note>In this context, "intelligible" refers to the realm of pure thought or divine ideas, which are more real than the physical world</note> and immutable truth. 

On the contrary, every changeable perception must be separated from this definition, as it is indefinite and in no way fitting for the gods and divine matters. When we perform some work that is natural to us, nature itself—which is the cause of such work—has certainly granted us the seeds and preparations for it from the start. However, no such preparations or seeds have been provided by nature (whether universal nature or human nature) for that prophecy which is above nature and human custom. 

For nature lacks intelligence <note>original: *intelligentia*; here meaning the higher faculty of divine reason</note> and is not the primary author of the things that happen, especially regarding the nature that resides within us. But prophecy is more than intellectual; it reaches the very causes of events and, in a single, sudden intuition, it embraces the order of the universe. An act of this kind is the unique property of **God**, who acts within us while we ourselves are, at that moment, free from our own personal activity. 

If any kind of "presage" <note>original: *præsagium*; a lower form of natural inkling or "gut feeling"</note> occurs to us, it is carried out either by natural instinct or by technical art. This can indeed have a certain preparation or aptitude within our human nature; but such a presage is very narrow and obscure, and it admits of "more or less" <note>meaning it varies in intensity and accuracy</note>. Divine prophecy, however...

For that which is produced by man is inferior to man; and that which is produced in this manner, like an idol <term>idolum</term> <note>original: *idolu̅*; here referring to a phantasm or a man-made simulacrum—an appearance rather than a divine reality.</note>, is a kind of shadow, appearing rather than truly existing, and as soon as it is made, it immediately vanishes. Instead, he produces worlds through intellects, delights <note>original: *voluptatibus*; in this Neoplatonic context, this refers to the divine joys or the inherent "satisfaction" of the divine mind's activity.</note>, and immaterial forms, and through the eternal soul—which is both above the world <term>super mundanam</term> and within the world <term>mundanam</term>. 

The maker of such idols is said to operate through the stars, yet he does not operate through the stars in the way that it might appear. For although there are innumerable powers in the celestial gods, the lowest of all is the natural power. Within this natural power of the celestial gods are principles <term>rationes</term>, both seminal <term>seminales</term> <note>original: *seminales*; generative principles that act like seeds to produce physical forms.</note>—that is, those which generate forms—and certain other immobile ones that precede the seminal principles in the same place—that is, the coordinative principles <term>coordinativae</term> of forms. Therefore, the authority of both these principles precedes the entirety of generation. 

Following these, there are qualities, powers, and motions in the celestial bodies, and from these come the dominant outpourings <term>defluxus</term> <note>The influences or "flux" that Neoplatonists believed flowed down from the stars to the earth.</note> which, under the guidance of the principles, govern the whole order <note>original: *exordi-* (the word is truncated at the end of the page); likely *exordinationi*, referring to the arrangement or ordering of the world.</note> of mundane things...

<summary>Iamblichus distinguishes between human "imitative" art, which creates fleeting shadows (idols), and divine "craftsman" art, which creates true essences through eternal principles. He explains that while stars influence the world, they do so through a hierarchy of natural, seminal, and coordinative powers ordained by God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s refutation of Porphyry’s doubts regarding theurgy. <page-num>96</page-num>

...possess nothing of divine power. There are no powers within physical materials that could serve as the "elements" or building blocks of demons <note>original: *daemones*; in Neoplatonism, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily "evil" spirits.</note>. Nor can these spirits be generated from particular physical bodies; on the contrary, it is by these spirits that physical bodies are generated and guarded. 

Furthermore, man cannot, by his own technical devices <note>original: *machinis*; referring here to the "machines" or artificial methods of the magician.</note>, procreate the very forms of the demons; rather, we ourselves are formed by the demons according to our physical bodies. One should not think that some multitude or composition arises from the union of elements that possesses a power proper to demons in itself. For the demon himself—simple, uniform, and existing within himself—assembles diverse elements into one and generates composite things from them. Whatever persistence or stability exists within those things is bestowed by the demon himself.

Therefore, it is not fitting to call these idols "demons." For the author of idols is one thing, and the demon—a great leader of demons—is quite another. The very substance <term>substantia</term> <note>The essential nature or "stuff" that makes something what it is.</note> of demons is different from the illusory phantasms <note>original: *phantasmata*; these are ghost-like images or visual tricks rather than substantial beings.</note> of idols. Concerning these matters, even you, **Porphyry**, admit that neither a god nor any demon is "dragged downward" <note>This refers to the "theurgic" belief—which Iamblichus is defending—that high spirits cannot be forced or coerced by human magic to descend to earth; they only appear out of their own grace.</note>. Therefore, this manufacturing of idols, since it is devoid of both god and demon, brings forth neither true prophecy <term>vaticinium</term> nor any sacred work.

**P**orphyry recalls the opinion of those who claim that all prophecies are poured into us by evil spirits <term>demons</term> <note>In the Platonic tradition, "demons" (daemones) are intermediary spirits. The gods grant true blessings to good people who have been purified through sacrifices. They dwell with these people and, through their association, drive far away all wickedness and passion <note>In this philosophical context, "passion" refers to being disturbed or influenced by external, material, or emotional forces.</note>. By their own splendor, they keep dark spirits away. For just as darkness vanishes before the sun, evil spirits flee when the light of the gods enters. They are no longer able to disturb the pious priest <note>original: *sacrificatorem*; one who performs the sacred rites.</note>, who has been freed from all wickedness, perversity, and passion. 

However, those who are harmful, and who insolently intrude upon sacred rites against the proper order and ritual, are surely unable to reach the gods because of the weakness of their actions and their lack of power. Instead, due to certain impurities <note>Ritual or moral pollutions that prevent a person from being spiritually "clean" enough to contact higher beings.</note>, they are both driven away by the gods and [delivered over] to evil demons...

When the profane handle matters against the prescribed rites, the outcome of the sacred ceremonies is ruined. For in place of the gods, other entities are celebrated, and in place of good spirits, evil ones creep in. Therefore, the errors of such people should not be mentioned when discussing legitimate sacred rites, nor should what happens to them be taken as a standard. 

Just as sacrilege is the opposite of divine worship, so those occupied by evil demons—who are the authors of excess and deceit—are the opposites of legitimate priests. From the true priests, every unjust spirit, depravity, and passion is far removed; instead, the presence of good divine powers <term>numina</term> <note>A Latin term for divine will or the presiding spirit of a deity.</note> is with them, and they are filled from above with truth by the divine fire <note>The "divine fire" represents the pure, elevating power of the gods that illuminates the priest's soul during a ritual.</note>. To these priests, evil spirits offer no hindrance...

Iamblichus distinguishes them in this way: The Gods indeed, and all those beings superior to our nature, grant things appropriate to worthy souls out of a fullness of goodness, a will for what is good, and a certain kindness. There are, moreover, certain middle classes of divinities, who are the <term>ephors</term> <note>original: "ephori". From the Greek "ephoroi," meaning guardians or overseers. There is, again, another class of spirits surrounding us—undiscriminating and unthinking—which has been allotted a single numerical power because of its distribution from the individual parts of the universe. For this reason, each one is devoted to only one single task. For just as a sword only divides and does nothing else, so among the spirits distributed in the world—due to that very divisible necessity of nature—this one only divides, while that one only collects the things that are being made and generated. Therefore, certain hidden spirits, each having been allotted a different power, [perform] only that single thing to which [they are assigned...]

...they carry out that for which they were ordained. If anyone, therefore, receiving those powers which contribute to the whole in their distributed order, should turn them elsewhere and accomplish something by a kind of transgression, the result of the act follows, and the harm belongs to the one using it wrongly. But let us return to the question. To answer the question: commands and forceful orders are directed toward spirits <note>original: "spiritus". In this context, these are irrational daemons or nature-spirits who lack the higher intellectual faculty of the gods.</note> that neither use their own reason nor possess a principle of judgment and discretion. Since our thought possesses a rational nature and the ability to discern how things are conditioned, and since it encompasses many powers of life within itself, it is accustomed to command spirits that do not use reason and are determined toward only one single action.

He invokes them, therefore, as superiors, because he attempts to draw those forces which contribute to the whole from the universal world surrounding us toward certain matters contained in particular and divided parts. On the other hand, he commands them as if they were inferiors, because our intellectual nature is more excellent than that which lacks intellect—even if the latter has a broader range of action throughout the world. 

Likewise, there is a double persona <note>original: "figura, siue prætexta". This refers to the ritual "mask" or role the priest assumes during a ceremony.</note> in the priest: one which is human, and another which is truly divine. This divine persona he puts on through the sacred rites <note>original: "sacramentis". Here, these are the theurgic rituals and mysteries of the Neoplatonists, rather than Christian sacraments.</note>, in which the divine power lies hidden, leading upward to the divinity...

<summary>Iamblichus explains that theurgists command irrational spirits because human intellect is naturally superior to unthinking force, even while they honor those spirits as part of the universal cosmic order. He also introduces the concept of the "divine persona" assumed by the priest during rituals.</summary>

Therefore, divine works which are fulfilled in sacred rites are not accomplished through the opposition of one thing to another (as things in the physical world are), nor are they summoned or transformed by the movement of the one calling or moving (as human affairs are). Instead, the whole is fulfilled by **identity, union, and consent**; and, once the discrepancy is removed...

**Porphyry** <note>A philosopher and student of Plotinus who wrote a skeptical letter questioning the practices of theurgy (ritual magic).</note> asks: why is it that the higher beings often command their followers to be just, yet sometimes, when entreated, they inflict injury?

If they should happen to be unjust, they are not gods, but wicked **demons** <term>dæmones: In Neoplatonism, these are intermediate spirits between gods and humans; unlike the modern "demon," they can be good, but the "wicked" ones mentioned here are prone to deception.</term>. This refers to the concept of the soul’s journey through many lifetimes or incarnations.</note>. And so, according to the merits acquired in a previous life, they often punish in a following one—whether they are asked to punish or not. 

Meanwhile, we—who see nothing beyond the present—think that adversities sometimes happen to us without merit; yet we often suffer in this life what we have already inflicted in another, and what we do now, we will one day suffer. Furthermore, many human sins are hidden from us, but they are not at all hidden from the gods. 

Likewise, we define **justice** as each person doing their own duty according to the current laws of the land. The gods, however, define it much more broadly, looking toward the whole order of the universe; and looking especially at that principle by which souls are led back to the gods, they execute their judgment from that basis. And so great a diversity exists between the divine judgment concerning right itself, and...
