...from the parts, a certain **manifold action** <note>original: "actio multiformis." This refers to the diverse ways divine power expresses itself as it moves down through the layers of reality.</note> descends into the individual particles. It descends most easily because of the **similarity of powers**: insofar as, clearly, the powers that follow correspond step-by-step to those that precede them—especially when the receiver is furthermore adapted to the actor. 

Therefore, due to the necessities of the body, certain **evils** and destructive things happen to specific particles from the "wholes" <note>The "wholes" refers to the entire cosmos or the major celestial bodies, which remain perfect even if their effects on small individuals seem harsh.</note>. These events are indeed beneficial to the wholes and in harmony with the **universe**, although they are meanwhile harmful to the parts. This occurs either because the parts cannot withstand the actions of the wholes, or because of the mixture occurring lower down, or the weakness natural to the lowest things, or because parts are not commensurate with other parts. 

Furthermore, beyond the body of the world itself, the **nature of the world** is capable of many things. For the concord of similar things and the discord of dissimilar things produce many effects. Moreover, the coming together of many things into the one "animal" of the whole <note>Platonic philosophy viewed the entire universe as a single, living "animal" or organism.</note>, and the powers flourishing in the world—however many and of what kind they may be—act one way in the wholes and another way in the parts. This is due to the very **weakness of the parts**, which is distributed and divided to the furthest extent. 

**Friendship** and **love** of the whole, as well as strife and similar things, are indeed active forces in the wholes themselves, but in the individual particles they are experienced as **passions** <note>original: "passiones." In this philosophical context, a "passion" is something "suffered" or received by a subject from an external force, rather than a feeling.</note>. Likewise, those things which are <term>Forms</term> <note>original: "species." In Neoplatonism, these are the eternal, divine Blueprints or Ideas.</note> and **pure reasons** <note>original: "rationes puræ." These are the *Logoi*, the rational principles that organize the material world.</note> in the **divine intellect**, in the [body] of the universe...

And the transmission itself, and the action descending from above, is moved through a certain **sympathy** <note>original: "compassione." Yet the transmission itself operates according to a single **harmony of the world**, so that even things which are most distant nevertheless cooperate. 

If someone, perceiving this, strives unjustly to lead certain parts or powerful forces of the whole into other parts, thereby causing harm, the universe is not the cause of such damage. Instead, it is the **human abuse** that transgresses the order of the universe, [the legitimate...] <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

### *Concerning Sacrifices: from where they derive their power, and what they provide.*

**I**t is asked by what logic sacrifices are both appropriate for the higher beings, benefit human beings, and what effect they have in the world. **Porphyry** <note>A Phoenician Neoplatonist and student of Plotinus, whose letter of doubts to the Egyptian priest Anebo prompted this book by Iamblichus.</note> says that not only the Prophets, but also the **interpreters** <term>hypophetas: from the Greek *hypophetēs*, these are secondary priests who interpret or deliver oracular messages received from the gods through a primary medium</term>—that is, all priests who deliver a prophecy received from others—must abstain from animal meat, lest the gods be contaminated by the vapors exhaling from it. Yet, the common saying is contrary to this opinion: namely, that the gods are greatly [attracted] by the **smell of burning meat**...

<page-num>111</page-num>

...to be soothed as if by bait, and thus captured. **Iamblichus** condemns both ideas: namely, that the gods are either defiled by the **smell of meat** <note>original: "nidoribus carnium." This refers to the heavy, greasy smoke produced by burning animal fat in ancient sacrifices, which critics often claimed was "food" for the gods.</note>, or that they are ensnared and lured by it. The **World Soul** <term>Anima mundi: the conscious, animating principle that permeates the entire universe in Neoplatonic philosophy</term> and the celestial beings do not receive passions from the bodies they inhabit, nor are they distracted from their higher contemplations by them, simply because they are present to those bodies. **Particular souls** <note>meaning individual human or animal souls</note>, however, suffer both: they are affected by the body's passions and distracted by its needs. One would wander far from the truth by attributing similar defects to the superior souls. For the condition of universal beings and particular beings—or of causes and their effects—is not at all equal.

To eat the bodies of creatures that were once joined to a soul undoubtedly brings a burden and a stain upon us; it creates a **downward inclination** <note>original: "proclivitatem," a tendency for the soul to sink toward material things rather than rising toward the divine</note> in the soul, through which it melts away and succumbs to pleasures, and it produces many other diseases in the soul. However, the vapor exhaling from animals and the **sacred fumigation** <note>the ritual burning of incense or sacrificial offerings</note> rightly performed does nothing to harm the gods, nor the worldly or universal causes. For the vapor does not contain or order the higher beings toward itself; rather, the vapor is contained by them, and it is coordinated with the universe and the gods alike. Therefore, by the command of those higher powers, the ritual can be harmoniously fitted to them. Religious men, therefore, **abstain from animal meat** <note>Iamblichus explains that vegetarianism is for the benefit of the human worshiper's purity, not because the gods find meat "gross."</note>; yet they do not do so because the gods could be defiled by the vapors of animals. For the power of the gods—long before any material thing can even touch it—itself also...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that while eating meat "stains" human souls, the ritual smoke of sacrifice does not affect the pure, impassive nature of the gods. He distinguishes between the vulnerability of individual human souls and the untouchable nature of the World Soul and divine beings.</summary>

<keywords>Iamblichus, World Soul, animal sacrifice, ritual purity, vegetarianism, Neoplatonism, divine impassivity, vapors</keywords>

...it disperses them without touch <note>original: "sine tactu." This implies the divine power acts upon matter through its mere presence or higher nature, without needing physical contact.</note>. Not only does it destroy and eliminate these bodily things without needing to be near them—doing so even before they can approach it—but even the celestial bodies themselves do not receive any material element into their being. They do not admit anything foreign, nor do they lose anything that is their own. Furthermore, the vapors of earthly things, having traveled scarcely five stadia <note>original: "quinque stadia." A stadium was an ancient measurement of roughly 600 feet; five stadia is approximately half a mile, which was thought to be the limit of the dense atmosphere.</note>, flow back down again; they neither infect nor nourish that immaterial and revolving body [the heavens]. 

This celestial body possesses no potential for change within itself; it contains nothing contrary to itself, nor is it carried from a center or toward a center <note>referring to linear motion—up and down—which Aristotelian physics assigned to the four heavy earthly elements</note>. Instead, it must either remain at rest or revolve in a circle. Therefore, the bodies below the Moon <term>Sublunary: the region of the universe between the Earth and the Moon, which in ancient science was the only place where change, decay, and death could occur</term>, since they are composed of clashing powers and motions and are subject to change, are carried entirely upward or downward. They have nothing in common with the heaven—neither in their nature, nor their power, nor their action. 

Consequently, no vapor from these bodies, nor anything else from them, ever reaches the heaven, from which they are entirely separated. Rightly, then, the heavens receive no change born of things subject to generation <term>Generation: the cycle of birth, growth, and decay characteristic of the material world</term>. Can the nature of the gods then be defiled by vapors of this kind—a nature which repels material vapors with (so to speak) a single blow? Such things are therefore not harmful to the beings above, but to us. For these divisible and material things, being related to us, have something in common with similar things in...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that the celestial realm is physically and metaphysically separated from the earthly (sublunary) world, meaning that sacrificial vapors cannot reach or affect the gods.</summary>

### What is the rationale for sacrifices, and what is their utility?

**P**orphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a critical "Letter to Anebo" questioning the logic of Egyptian and Chaldean rituals.</note> thinks that sacrifices are offered to the gods for this reason: so that we may honor them with gifts of this kind, just as we are often accustomed to honor our superiors; and also, so that we might return thanks for the good things received from the divine, rendering good things in return for good. Iamblichus <note>The author, Iamblichus, is here referred to in the third person by the translator/editor of this edition, though the text represents his response to Porphyry.</note> says that this kind of reasoning is derived from common human custom toward other men, and that it does not suit the nature of the gods, which exceeds human habits beyond all measure. 

Moreover, such modes and explanations of sacrifices do not at all demonstrate the greatest efficacy of sacrifices—an efficacy, I say, without which we are not liberated from plague, famine, or scarcity, nor do we obtain timely rains; indeed, even that efficacy through which we achieve the purification and perfection of souls, and liberation from this <term>Province of generation: The material world of flux, birth, and decay (the sublunary realm) where souls are trapped in a cycle of rebirth.</term>. Therefore, anyone following your assignment of reasons will not much approve of these modes, as if you had assigned a cause worthy of their effects. And, if by chance he does approve, he will certainly accept them only as secondary...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that Porphyry’s view of sacrifice as a simple exchange of gifts or thanks is too human-centered and fails to explain the true theurgic power of ritual to purify the soul and provide relief from natural disasters.</summary>
<keywords>sacrifice, Porphyry, Iamblichus, purification, perfection of the soul, province of generation, theurgy, ritual efficacy</keywords>

We seek, therefore, the reason why sacrifices possess the power to produce results, and from what source they are joined to the gods, who are the primary causes and principles of those things that are brought to pass. 

Someone might say that because the world is one living being <note>This refers to the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul, a central Platonic idea that the universe is a single, interconnected living organism.</note>, and possesses one and the same life everywhere, it is the very communion of similar forces—or even the distance between dissimilar ones—or certainly a certain fitness of the agent to the patient <note>The "agent" is the thing that acts, and the "patient" is the thing being acted upon.</note> that moves similar things in the same way. This occurs while life spreads according to a single sympathy <note>original: *compassionem*. In this philosophical context, it does not mean "pity," but *sympathia*—the hidden natural bond that allows one part of the universe to affect another instantly.</note> even from the most remote point to the most remote, as if these were also close at hand. 

For among these things as well, the communion of life is an equal distribution of this kind; he who says this indeed speaks the truth, and it is a point that necessarily follows regarding sacrifices. However, the true method of sacrifices is not demonstrated in this way. For the very essence of the gods is placed neither in nature nor in natural necessities, through which obligation they might be co-excited by natural passions <note>In ancient philosophy, "passions" refers to "passive states" or the capacity to be affected/changed by an external force, rather than just emotions.</note> or moved by powers extended through the whole of nature. Instead, the divine essence is defined according to itself, outside of these things. It has nothing in common with them, whether in essence, power, or in action and passion alike.

<summary>Iamblichus argues that while "cosmic sympathy" exists within the living universe, it is not the true explanation for why sacrifices work, because the gods exist beyond the reach of natural laws and cannot be "forced" or "affected" by earthly actions.</summary>

This general reasoning regarding sacrifices is, I believe, sufficient for the ingenious, who are able—following this general rule—to sagaciously investigate what is specific to each individual sacrifice. Nevertheless, showing indulgence to those of slower wit, we shall add certain specific points to these, bringing clearer matters into the open. 

The best starting point for these matters is that which explains the context of sacrifices, which is consequently annexed to the order of the gods. We posit that some gods are indeed **material**, while others are **immaterial**. Material gods are those who encompass matter within themselves and adorn it; whereas the Immaterial gods are those entirely and deeply segregated from matter. 

Therefore, according to the <term>priestly art|original: "sacerdotiam artem." This refers to theurgy, the practical ritual methods used to communicate with or ascend toward the divine.</term>, it is fitting to begin sacrifices with the material gods, for the ascent to the immaterial gods is not otherwise open to us. These material gods have a certain communion with matter, insofar as they preside over it and hover over it. These same gods also rule over the processes that occur within matter, such as division, <term>striking percussion|original: "percussioni repercutienti," likely referring to the physical interactions and "clashing" of elements in the material world.</term> change, generation, decay, and all material bodies. 

If anyone, therefore, wishes to worship these gods properly, they must certainly offer worship according to the gods' nature and rank; I mean, to material gods one must offer material worship. For in this way, we shall be led, as whole beings through whole things, into a proper intimacy with all of them, [by] kinship... <note>The text breaks here; "kinship" (cognatio) will be completed on the following page.</note>

Therefore, there are two species of sacrifices: the purest sacrifices belong to men who are exceedingly purified—which indeed rarely happens to a single person, or to a very few, as **Heraclitus** <note>Heraclitus of Ephesus (c. 500 BCE) often remarked that most men are blind to the truth of the universe, and only the rare "best" men seek eternal glory over mortal things.</note> says. But material sacrifices, and those which involve change, are suitable for beings still occupied with the body. 

Therefore, for **cities** <note>Iamblichus is addressing the religious life of the community (the "polis"). While a rare philosopher might achieve purely spiritual prayer, the general public requires tangible rituals to maintain their connection to the divine.</note> not yet purified from the **lot of birth** <note>original: "genitali sorte", referring to the fate of being born into a physical body.</note> and from bodily companionship, unless you provide sacrifices of this kind, you will stray equally from both immaterial and material goods. The former they are not able to receive, and to the latter, they do not offer what is proper and fitting. 

In addition to these points, everyone ought to provide **care for their essence** <term>care for their essence|original: "essentiae curam". This refers to the duty of a soul to maintain its specific place in the cosmic hierarchy through appropriate action.</term> according to what they are, and not according to what they are not. One should not, therefore, violate this proper measure and nature of the worshiper. I judge that a **constitution** <term>constitution|original: "complexio". This refers to the specific blend of physical and spiritual traits that make up an individual's nature.</term> which is properly fitted between the men who perform the worship and the powers being worshiped will choose a mode of cult suitable to itself. For a constitution of this kind, when it is immaterially tempered, chooses the immaterial; for it is clearly joined by purely **incorporeal powers** <note>Divine beings or forces that have no physical weight or substance.</note> to those things which are purely incorporeal...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that there are two types of sacrifice: purely spiritual ones for the rare elite and material ones for those still tied to physical existence. He maintains that worship must match the worshiper's nature, or else they will fail to receive divine benefits.</summary>

Only they, therefore, know what constitutes the most perfect fullness of worship, and how much our goal is frustrated if even a few things are omitted. Just as in a musical harmony, if one string is broken, the whole suddenly becomes dissonant; so too if one **divine power** <note>original: "numine"; a deity or divine presence</note> is passed over, the rite lacks its communal nature, and religion itself does not achieve its desired end. For everywhere, the more that appropriateness and intimacy are perfected, the more perfect are the goods that descend to us from that source.

Nor are these things merely human inventions, nor did they gain authority through human customs; rather, God himself, rightly invoked during the sacred rites, is the author of such laws. Around him, many gods and **angels** revolve, and under him, throughout whatever nations exist on earth, some **divinity** <term>numen</term> <note>a divine power or presence presiding over a specific domain</note> has obtained a **prefecture** <note>original: "præfecturam"; a designated area of spiritual governance or oversight, similar to a Roman administrative district</note> and a common province. From that same source, a specific divinity is assigned to each individual temple.

In other cases, following the same pattern according to their own kind, a perfected being has obtained a related prefecture. Since, therefore, we conduct sacrifices under the supervising divinities and authors of the sacred rites, we must revere the laws of divine holiness and the legitimate sacrifices. We should, for this reason, place our hope in these rites, because under the leadership...

### On the sacrifices of animals.

**P**orphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a student of Plotinus who questioned the more ritualistic aspects of Neoplatonism defended here by Iamblichus</note> is in doubt as to why, by the law of sacred rites, he who is to behold divine things must not touch a dead body at that time; and yet, through the bodies of dead animals, the invocations and attainments of divine things are frequently performed.

He then introduces Porphyry's critique regarding the apparent contradiction of using dead animals in holy rites.</summary>

Iamblichus explains it in this way: the priest <note>original: "uates"; literally a seer or prophet, here referring to the ritual authority</note> commands the observer of divine things not to touch a lifeless body that has not been consecrated; however, they do permit touching that which is being consecrated. Furthermore, they forbid even looking upon human bodies which the soul has already departed. For a certain trace, image, or demonstration of divine life is extinguished in the human body through death.

However, no religious law forbids touching the dead bodies of other animals, since even in life they did not share in a more divine nature <note>The author argues that human bodies are uniquely "divine" while alive, making their corpses uniquely "impure" once that divinity leaves</note>. Moreover, insofar as we rise toward the **immaterial gods**, it is beneficial not to have touched such a body; but insofar as we strive to approach the **material gods** <note>In Neoplatonism, material gods are those who govern the physical world and elements</note>, it will frequently be beneficial to touch them. For we are accustomed to call upon gods of this kind through animals—specifically those gods who preside over such animals, and especially those who govern them most closely and through a kind of kindred condition.

Likewise, for humans who are confined within matter, bodies deprived of life bring a certain stain <note>original: "maculam"; ritual impurity or "miasma"</note>—namely, the non-living to the living, the filthy to the pure, and the deprived to the one who possesses a state of being. And the dead brings a stain to one who still has the potential for dying, because of a certain common relationship between them. But to a **demon** <term>daemon</term> <note>original: "daemoni"; in this Neoplatonic context, a "daimon" is a non-physical intermediary spirit between gods and humans, not an evil entity</note> who is entirely incorporeal and incapable of suffering, such bodies do no harm.

### *Concerning Divination through Animals.*

**W**hen divination is carried out through the bodies of sacred animals, such as hawks <note>original: "asturum"; specifically the goshawk, which in the Neoplatonic tradition was often associated with the sun and divine vision</note>, it must not be thought that the gods themselves approach these things—that is, that the universal providers of the cosmos descend to a divided, particular, material, and proportional care for individual animals. Rather, it is the daemons <term>daemons: in this context, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits that act as messengers and administrators between the high gods and the physical world</term>, and these indeed being greatly divided into many ranks, and distributed individually to specific species of animals, who have been allotted the immediate care and governance of those animals. 

For these spirits have obtained a leadership that is not entirely self-sufficient or free from matter. Therefore, they are naturally suited to make use of instruments of this kind. To this end, therefore, so that we may obtain such divination from these daemons through animals, it is necessary to prepare for them a certain seat <note>original: "sedem"; a spiritual "receptacle" or "station" where the spirit can manifest</note> through which they can be observed among men and interact with us. This seat must be incorporeal <note>not having a physical body</note>, so that the incorporeal daemons may be present to us through it. 

This seat will therefore be the soul of such animals, now released from the body. For insofar as this soul is itself in a way separated from the physical body, it is compatible with the daemons; yet it is also compatible with us because of a certain kinship of life. Thus, acting as a medium, it serves the presiding daemon by suggesting a prophecy to man...

But the soul, in using these kinds of prophecies, does not only hear or receive the prophecy, but also contributes not a little from itself toward its execution in practical works. For the soul is moved, and cooperates, and simultaneously foresees through a certain sympathetic necessity <note>original: "compatientem necessitatem"; this refers to the Neoplatonic concept of "cosmic sympathy," where all parts of the universe are interconnected like strings on a lyre</note>. 

But this kind of prophecy is very far removed from the divine and true kind, and it deals with small and fleeting matters. These are things situated in "divided nature" <note>the physical realm where things are separate and individual, as opposed to the unified divine realm</note>, and whatever things are currently being swept along in the realm of "generation" <note>the world of birth, change, and decay</note>. These things exhibit motions from within themselves to those who are capable of receiving them, and they inflict various passions <term>passions: in this philosophical context, "passions" are not emotions, but "affections"—the state of being acted upon or changed by an external force</term> upon those things which are naturally inclined toward sympathy. Therefore, a foreknowledge of this kind arises through this shared sympathy.

However, a perfect foreknowledge cannot occur through being "acted upon" <gloss>passionem</gloss> in this way. For that which is unmixed <note>original: "immundæ"; likely a printer's error for "immixtum" (unmixed) or "immaculatum" (pure), as the context contrasts it with the "material" and "dark"</note>, immutable, and pure is the most accustomed to grasping the future. But that which has dealings with what is material, "passible" <note>subject to being affected or changed by outside influences</note>, and dark is instead overwhelmed by ignorance. Therefore, we judge this artificial "machine" <note>original: "machinam"; used here to mean a contrived or technical method rather than a literal device</note> of foretelling to be neither worthy of the name of legitimate prophecy, nor should it be taken seriously, nor should the one using it be believed as if he were a speaker of truth.

### How petitioners used threats against the spirits.

**P**orphyry relates that priests were accustomed to using certain violent threats against the higher beings <term>superos: the celestial gods or higher powers</term>, saying things like: "Unless you do this," or conversely, "if you do a certain thing, I will shatter the heavens," or "I will expose the secrets of Isis," or "I will divulge the hidden mystery in the abyss," or "I will stop the *baris*" <note>original: "barim"; a baris was a sacred barge or boat used in Egyptian religious processions</note>, or "I will scatter the limbs of Osiris to Typhon" <note>Typhon is the Greek name for Set, the Egyptian god of chaos who murdered Osiris and scattered his body; the threat is to repeat this primordial trauma</note>, and other similar things. 

Iamblichus replies that those who invoke these curses do not actually direct these kinds of threats toward the Sun or the Moon, or other celestial bodies, as Porphyry believes. Rather, he explains that there is a certain category of powers in the world that is highly fragmented, lacking in discernment, and unthinking. This class of spirits receives reason <note>original: "rationem, siue sermonem"; here meaning a logical command or a formal speech</note> from another and obeys it, but possesses no intelligence of its own; it cannot distinguish truth from falsehood, nor the possible from the impossible. Therefore, when this class of spirits is provoked by threats, it is immediately stirred and dazed <gloss>stupet</gloss>, because it is naturally agitated by forceful words, and it leads or pulls other things along through a certain dull and unstable imagination <term>phantasia: in this context, the capacity of a spirit to be moved by mental images or sensory impressions rather than intellect</term>. 

Furthermore, the priest often commands and threatens these worldly spirits not by any human virtue, but by the divine power of the "ineffable sacraments" <note>original: "sacramentorum ineffabilium"; referring to the secret, holy rites of theurgy that were believed to carry the authority of the gods themselves</note>. # CONCERNING THE MYSTERIES. #

The Chaldean priests <note>The Chaldeans were ancient Mesopotamian sages whom Neoplatonists like Iamblichus regarded as the primary masters of theurgy, often held in higher esteem for their "pure" approach compared to the Egyptians.</note>, among whom the speech directed to the gods alone is judged and decreed to be pure, never use threats. The Egyptians, however, who mix discourses regarding <term>daemons: intermediary spirits that rank below gods but above humans; they are not necessarily "evil" in this philosophical context</term> with divine sacraments, sometimes turn to such threats.

->*An explanation of the symbols of Egyptian theology.*<-

**I**mitating the nature of the universe itself and the craftsmanship of the gods, the Egyptians also display certain images of mystical and hidden notions by creating symbols; just as nature expresses hidden <term>principles: original "rationes" (Greek: logoi), the divine blueprints that give shape to the physical world</term> in visible forms as if through symbols, and the gods explain the truth of the <term>ideas: the eternal, divine archetypes or "thought-forms" of the Creator</term> through manifest images. Therefore, since they <gloss>per</gloss>ceive that all superior beings delight in being represented by the likeness of inferior things, and furthermore desire to be filled with goodness from those superior beings—insofar as they are able to imitate them—they rightly offer a mode of action suited to the higher powers to the best of their ability. They do this when they introduce hidden mysteries through manifest symbols. In interpreting these, set aside the mere words and receive the underlying meaning. Therefore, when they name "mud" in the sacred rites, as they often do, understand this to represent the body of the world and <term>matter: the raw, chaotic substrate of the physical universe</term>, as well as the generative power inserted into it and, as it were, stirred up alongside it.

Since this is the case, God himself is the cause of generation and of all the natural forces inherent in the elements; as such, he transcends all these things, being himself immaterial, indivisible, motionless, and unbegotten <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "unbegotten" means existing eternally without having been created by another</note>, existing entirely from himself and within himself. In the lotus, all parts are round, both the fruit and the leaves; this represents the circular motion of the <term>Mind: the divine Intellect (Greek: *Nous*), which moves in perfect circles of thought</term>, always remaining the same and acting in the same manner. God himself, therefore, stands even above this activity, remaining within himself, surpassing such a dominion as one who is holy, venerable, and contained within himself...

Furthermore, even if we were able to translate the specific qualities of these meanings through another language, they still do not preserve the same <term>power: the inherent spiritual efficacy or "potency" of the sound</term> once they have been changed.

They also recognize a vital power, both that which resides in the heavens and that which exists above the heavens. Likewise, they place a pure intellect above the world, and one indivisible intellect throughout the whole world, and another that is distributed through all the celestial circles. Now, they are not accustomed to contemplate these things through mere speech and naked reason; rather, they additionally advise and teach that our nature must advance toward higher, more universal, and superior things—beyond the reach of **fate**—toward God himself and the **Craftsman** of the world.

This is done so that the soul carries no matter with it, nor anything else except for the observance of the **opportune time** <note>original: "opportuni temporis," referring to the concept of *kairos* or the specific astrological/ritual timing required for spiritual success</note>. They teach that we attain this through **sacred works** <note>original: "sacrorum opera," referring to theurgy, or rituals designed to invoke divine presence</note>, which they simultaneously bring into effect. **Mercury** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage to whom these teachings were attributed</note> himself handed down this path to us. However, the prophet **Bitis** <note>A priest-prophet often associated with Hermetic and alchemical lore</note> interpreted it for **King Ammon**, having found it in the **inner sanctuaries** <note>original: "adytis," the most sacred and restricted parts of a temple</note> of the temple in the city of **Sais** <note>original: "Sayn," an ancient Egyptian capital famous for the Temple of Neith and its library of sacred texts</note> in Egypt. Inscribed in **sacred letters** <note>Hieroglyphs</note>, he also provided us with the name of God which pervades the entire universe. There are many other ranks and orders concerning these same subjects.

Therefore, you do not seem to me to be correct in reducing all the teachings of the Egyptians to **natural causes** alone. For among them, there are...

### *On free will, and how*
### *we are released from fate.*

**A**fter this, Porphyry says that many of the Egyptians have also subjected our very **free will** <note>original: "arbitrium," the power of choice or judgment</note> to the motion of the stars. Therefore, the soul descending into us from these worlds follows the circuits of those worlds as well. But that soul which comes from the intelligible exists in a mental, spiritual way and rises above the **cycle of generation** <term>cycle of generation: the physical world of birth, change, and decay governed by time and the stars</term>. And through this higher soul, we are both released from **fate** and ascend to the intelligible gods; and we possess a religion that tends toward eternal things. Therefore, it must not be thought (as you were doubting) that all things are bound by the unbreakable chains of necessity, which they call fate. For the soul has a principle within itself, by which it may join itself to the intelligible, and indeed depart from those things which are born. ### *On the judgments of astrologers, and the daemon.*

**P**orphyry says that if anyone could know the **birth-chart** <term>birth-chart: "figura nativitatis," the specific alignment of stars at the moment of birth</term> and find the ruler of that chart, they would discover their own daemon, and through it, they would be released from the fate of their birth. But he adds that it is impossible to know that chart or to find this spirit; he claims the rules of astronomy and astrology are incomprehensible and uncertain, citing **Chaeremon** <note>Chaeremon of Alexandria: a 1st-century philosopher and Egyptian priest who wrote on astrology and the stars</note> as a witness.

Iamblichus, however, says the daemon is neither known nor granted by that chart or its daemonic influence. Otherwise, it would not release us from the fate of our birth. Instead, it is granted from a more ancient and higher principle—namely, from the superior gods—at the very moment the soul first inclines toward the world of the senses, even before conception. Furthermore, we are released from fate not so much through the daemon, but through the worship of a higher divinity. 

Not only do those statements by Porphyry contradict themselves, but they also depart from the truth. For the daemon is not assigned to each person solely by the specific chart of their generation; this origin is more ancient. Furthermore, if the daemon were recognized from this chart alone, the person who knew their **natal spirit** <term>natal spirit: "genesicum," the spirit specifically tied to the astrological moment of birth</term> would not necessarily be happy for that reason...

It is better, however, to employ a conjecture of this sort: namely, that the body, soul, and intellect are all governed by the same single **daemon** <note>original: "dæmone." In Neoplatonism, the personal daemon is a singular protective spirit assigned to a person at birth.</note>. 

Therefore, do not divide them such that there is one daemon for the body, another for the soul, and another for the intellect. For it is absurd to think that while the **living creature** <note>original: "animal." Referring here to the "animated being"—the unified human composite of body and soul.</note> is one, the divinity set over that creature is multiform. Indeed, those who hold the leadership are everywhere simpler than those who are subject to them <note>This reflects the Neoplatonic principle that the higher a being is in the cosmic hierarchy, the more unified and "simple" it is, while lower levels are more complex and divided.</note>. Furthermore, it is even more absurd if many ruling spirits were like parts of a daemon—not merged into one, but separated from each other. You would also introduce a conflict among them, as if some of the ruling daemons were good, and others were evil. Yet evil spirits never hold such a command, nor are they ever distributed with equal authority or in equal number in opposition to the good.

After this, you suspect that the personal daemon is simply a certain part of the soul—specifically the intellect—and that a man is <term>eudaimon</term> <note>original: εὐδαίμονα. A Greek word literally meaning "having a good daemon," commonly translated as "happy" or "fortunate."</note>, that is, happy, if he possesses a wise intellect. But if this were so, there would no longer be any order of being more excellent than man set over man. Instead, among the divided parts of the soul, the higher part would merely rule the lower.

<summary>Iamblichus argues that a single daemon governs the entire human person—body, soul, and mind—rather than multiple spirits for each part. He also rejects the idea that the "daemon" is merely the human intellect, insisting it is a superior, external divinity.</summary>

For the division of things into various species and the **otherness of matter** <note>original: "materiæq; alteritas." ### *On Happiness.*

**Y**ou suspect, perhaps, that some other way to **happiness** <term>happiness: "beatitudo" in Latin, referring to the ultimate state of human flourishing or "blessedness" achieved through union with the divine.</term> lies hidden besides divine worship, and you ask what that might specifically be. But indeed, if the essence and perfection of all goods are contained in the gods, and the primary power and first principle of all goods is found there, then deservedly only we priests—and those who have similarly dedicated themselves to the higher powers and have legitimately attained **union** <note>original: "unionem." In Neoplatonic theurgy, this is "henosis," the mystical union with the One or the divine.</note> with them—studiously pursue the principle and end of all goods. In this state, certainly, the contemplation of truth is present, as is the consummation of **intellectual science** <note>original: "intellectualis scientiæ." This refers to "noetic" knowledge, or direct intuitive understanding, rather than discursive reasoning.</note>. And along with the knowledge of the gods, there follows a conversion toward ourselves and a recognition of our own nature. You suspect in vain that perhaps the religious man depends on human opinions and favors. For what leisure can there be for a soul dedicated to the gods to listen to human praises?

### *Commentaries on the First*
### *Alcibiades of Plato.*

**T**HE beginning of the Platonic dialogues, and the chief and most firm principle of all philosophy, is considered to be the knowledge of our own nature. <note>original: "naturæ nostrę cognitionem." This refers to the famous Delphic maxim "Know Thyself," which Neoplatonists believed was the essential starting point for any spiritual or intellectual journey.</note> For once this is rightly known, we will be able to more perfectly understand the good that is suited to us, as well as the evil that is at odds with us. Indeed, it is so ordained by nature that just as the essences of things differ among themselves, so too do the proper perfections <term>perfections: "perfectiones," referring to the state of a thing when it has fully realized its natural purpose or highest potential.</term> of those things. Therefore, so that we may find what the perfection of our nature is and how it may be acquired—for we ought first and foremost to recognize our own essence <term>essence: "essentiam," the fundamental nature or "whatness" of a being that makes it what it is.</term>, which is indeed the subject proposed in the *Alcibiades* and is the goal of all Plato's teaching—when we consider the essences of things, we must investigate whether the essence of a thing is among the number of those which are indivisible <note>original: "indiuiduæ." In Neoplatonic thought, indivisible things are purely spiritual and eternal, whereas "divisible" things are material and spread out in space.</note>, or of the kind which are divided around bodies, or of those which are placed in the middle. Likewise, whether the essence is eternal, or through all ti-

# PROCLUS

...time existing, or whether it comes to be in some part of time. Again, we must ask whether it is simple and existing before any composition, or whether it is indeed composite, but joined by indissoluble bonds—or whether it can, in turn, be resolved at some time into those parts from which it is composed. For if we consider each thing in this way, we will then be able to more easily judge what its particular "good" is. 

For it is established that for an entirely indivisible essence <term>essence: "essentia," the fundamental nature or "whatness" of a being.</term>, its good is eternal; however, the good of a divisible essence is involved in time and motion. Finally, the perfection of the middle substance <note>In Neoplatonic thought, the "middle substance" usually refers to the Soul, which stands between the eternal realm of Intellect and the temporal realm of Matter.</note> is weighed according to its own measures. For such a perfection indeed requires time, but it is a "primary time," which can be appropriately measured in the circuits of the body. 

We are indeed ignorant of ourselves, because we are occupied by generative oblivion <note>original: "oblivione genesica." This refers to the Platonic idea that the soul forgets its divine origin and true knowledge when it is "generated" into a physical body.</note> and struck by the disturbance of the life of rational forms. Meanwhile, we think we know many things of which we are actually ignorant, because we have the inner principles <note>original: "rationes rerum." These are the innate blueprints or concepts that Neoplatonists believed were "hard-wired" into the human soul from birth.</note> of things innate to our essence. 

There are three species of conversion <term>conversion: "conversio," the act of a being "turning" its attention or energy in a specific direction.</term>. For whatever is converted either:
1. Turns toward something inferior to itself, while it falls from its own perfection; 
2. Or it rises toward the better because of the vigor of its own life and its natural action; 
3. Or it is reflected back toward itself because of a cognition that is kindred to itself, holding the middle ground.

Therefore, gods love gods: the elder ones love the lesser by the gift of **providence**, while the lesser in turn love the greater by a certain duty of **conversion** <note>original: "conversionis." Indeed, to perfect lower things and provide for inferiors belongs to souls also, insofar as they are souls. For this very reason they descend: for the sake of providing for things that are born and die, and for the care of mortals. Yet, to provide in such a way as one provides for the governed—without being mixed with them, nor affected as if bound to them, nor receiving any stain from them—is the unique property of the gods and of good **daemons** <note>original: "dæmonum." These are intermediary spirits that act as messengers and guides between the divine realm and the human world.</note>. Whenever this happens to human souls, it happens through divine or daemonic generosity.

In daemons, however, Love exists through their very essence. Finally, in souls, it exists through the effect of illumination. 

And indeed, this threefold order appears similar to the triple power of the intellect. A third kind is infused by this into souls, which is surely the perfection of the souls themselves. **Timaeus** <note>The narrator of Plato’s dialogue *Timaeus*, which discusses the creation of the universe.</note> himself indicates these three things regarding the intellect. *He refutes two opinions: the first stating that there are no other daemons except our souls released from the more solid body; the second, that of Amelius, who thinks daemons are certain wandering gods.*

**T**herefore, we will not accept those who say that <term>daemons</term> <note>In this Neoplatonic context, daemons are not evil spirits, but "middle beings" that bridge the gap between the perfect gods and the material world.</note> are our souls, having already finished this life and moved into another. For it is not fitting to equate a daemon defined by a certain temporary state <note>original: "per habitudinem quandam." In Neoplatonic thought, this is the vital "middle rank" that holds the universe together.</note> for all worldly things from a life that changes itself in so many ways. For the daemonic guardianship itself always stands in the same manner, preserving the whole universe. But the soul does not keep its order in this way, as <term>Socrates</term> <note>The famous Greek philosopher and primary speaker in Plato's dialogues.</note> says in the <term>Republic</term> <note>Plato's influential work on justice, the state, and the soul.</note>: for at different times, the soul chooses different lives. Nor, again, will we approve of those who believe that some of the gods are daemons, as if they were wandering gods, as <term>Amelius</term> <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> thinks. Instead, we shall follow <term>Plato</term> himself, who calls the gods the masters of the universe while placing the flocks of daemons under the gods' command; and we will everywhere uphold the reasoning of <term>Diotima</term> <note>The priestess and philosopher from Plato's *Symposium* who explains the nature of Love as a mediating daemon.</note>, who assigns to daemons a middle rank between gods and mortals.

**S**ince, therefore, <term>daemons</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, daemons are not "demons" in the modern sense, but essential "middle beings" that bridge the gap between the perfect, unchanging gods and the changing, material world.</note> are established in the middle, as we have said, the first and highest among them are the **divine daemons**. These frequently appear as gods themselves because of their excellent similarity to the gods. Indeed, in every order, the first rank bears the form of the order above it. For <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus." In this philosophy, Intellect (or *Nous*) is the second great principle of reality, proceeding from "The One" and acting as the source of all forms and logic.</note> proceeds from itself as if it were a god, and the most ancient of souls exists as purely intellectual; therefore, the highest genus of daemons, being closest to the gods, is uniform and divine.

The second group after these are the daemons already endowed with an **intellectual property**. They preside over ascents and descents <note>These refer to the "ascent" of the soul toward the divine and its "descent" into a physical body.</note> and generally declare and hand down the operations of the gods to all things.

The third group are the daemons who distribute the operations of **divine souls** into the things that follow. They fulfill the bond for those who look upward, acting as the flow from the gods to those souls.

The fourth group transmit the effective powers of **universal natures** into the realm of <term>generation</term> <note>original: "generabilia." This refers to the physical world where things are born, change, and die.</note>; they inspire life, order, and rational principles into particular natures, and oversee the entire production of mortal beings.

The fifth group are, in a certain way, **corporeal** <note>Meaning they are closely tied to the element of matter or the physical bodies they govern.</note>, and they bind the extremities of bodies together. For in what way will eternal bodies meet with perishable ones? In what way will causes meet with their effects, unless bound together by such a middle-link? For a nature of this kind [middle...]

For if the daemon was assigned to that same person when they were alive, whom it also presents for judgment after death, then surely it was assigned to the human being specifically, and not just the living body. Furthermore, beginning from above and commanding, it governs our entire constitution.

In the first place, to say that daemons are merely parts of human souls is the view of those who admire human life far too much. Such people do not accept the hierarchy of **Socrates** in the *Republic* <note>Plato’s famous work on justice and the soul.</note>, where he arranges the **heroic** race and the human race only after the gods and daemons. He even rebukes the poets for introducing heroes who are no better than ordinary men, but are instead enslaved to similar passions. 

Therefore, since Socrates rebukes such things, he would be very far from the opinion that places daemons—who are superior to heroes—among the parts and powers of the [human] soul. For it would follow from these views that things which are better by their very **essence** <term>essentia (essence/fundamental nature)</term> would be brought inside simply to complete things that are inferior. Furthermore, such a view would imply that various changes in a person’s lifestyle would result in a change of their daemon. For a greedy man is often changed into one seeking an ambitious life; and the ambitious man may change into a state of living by **right opinion**; and that person, in turn, into a state endowed with **knowledge** <term>scientia (knowledge/certainty)</term>. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the nature of the soul and its spiritual guardians. This page specifically references Plato's "Timaeus" and "Phaedrus" to explain the hierarchy of Essence, Power, and Action.</meta>

...soul's <note>Completing the word *animae* from the previous page</note> essence is not easy for everyone. Therefore, **Timaeus** <note>The main speaker in Plato’s *Timaeus*, who describes the mathematical and philosophical structure of the universe</note> alone declared its entire essence. For what its nature is altogether is divine and requires a long exposition to be explained, as **Socrates** says in the ***Phaedrus*** <note>One of Plato’s dialogues dealing with the soul, beauty, and rhetoric</note>. However, it is easy to explain the powers of the spirits <note>original: *numinum*</note>; for we perceive those very powers from the actions of which the forces themselves are the immediate mothers. For **power** <term>potentia (the capacity for activity that flows from a thing's fundamental nature)</term> is the middle ground between action and essence, being produced by the essence while in turn producing the action.

Furthermore, power itself has the closest familiarity with spirits <note>original: *daemonibus*</note>. For everywhere, power—just like a spirit—occupies the middle position. In **intelligible** <term>intelligibilibus (referring to the highest realm of pure being, beyond human thought)</term> matters, it joins the Father and the Intellect. For power exists simultaneously with the Father, while the Intellect exists from the Father. But in **intellectual** <term>intellectualibus (the realm of mind and divine thought)</term> matters, it couples actions with essences: for action is the offspring of power, while essence gives birth to powers from within itself.

Therefore, spirits <note>original: *numina*; here referring to the intermediary beings between humans and the ultimate gods</note>, as intermediaries between us and the gods, are properly designated by the name of "power," since they occupy the middle position everywhere. For true **essence** and true **being** <note>original: *esse*</note> belong to the gods. But power, duly serving the gods, has its place in the spirits. Finally, **action** and the resulting **effect**, having moved outward through their power, are found within us.

## *Knowledge of future contingencies is certain and necessary among the higher beings.*

**D**ivine **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who sought to reconcile Platonic philosophy with religious ritual and theurgy</note>, and that leader of ours <note>Likely referring to Proclus, mentioned on the previous page, who was a major authority for the translator</note>, thus inquire and resolve the matter: How is it not absurd to determine the differences between types of knowledge based on the nature of the things being known, rather than the other way around—namely, to categorize the things being known according to the differences of the knowers? 

This is so that whatever is eternal and divine by its very essence may know all things in an eternal and divine way; what is human may know in a human way; what is indeed **indivisible** <term>individuum (that which cannot be divided or separated into parts)</term> knows in an indivisible way, or rather, it anticipates things that are divisible; what is eternal knows even temporal things in a way that is above time; and what is rational knows even irrational things in a rational way. 

From these points, therefore, it is clear that the gods and **spirits** <note>original: *daemones*; in this context, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spiritual beings between gods and humans</note> know indefinite things in a definite way, and unstable things in a stable and firm manner. Do we not see that many things unknown to those beings below us are meanwhile well-known to us? For irrational creatures are unable to grasp the nature of the universal itself. We, however, are able to gather it. 

Why then do we wonder any further that the things which we only guess at with ambiguous and fallible knowledge, the higher beings comprehend with certainty? For our weakness is not the judge of their power; just as the irrational creature below us does not possess the judgment of our reason.

For this reason, a common and unchanging opinion defines happiness as self-sufficiency. For those for whom it is fitting to fare well, it is also fitting to have what is sufficient.

# ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

[...time] is the opportunity for any action, bringing as it does the good and the end both to those who act and to the results. Wherefore the **Pythagoreans** also named the **first cause**—from which the good is present to all things—**Opportunity** <note>original: "opportunitatem" — translating the Greek "Kairos," the perfect or "ripe" moment for action</note> itself; for it grants to all things that they might be perfect. 

By just such a timely occasion, **Socrates**, relying on his <term>daemon</term> <note>original: "dæmonem" — the famous "divine sign" or inner voice that Socrates claimed guided his actions and timing</note>, approached **Alcibiades** <note>A prominent Athenian statesman and student of Socrates; their relationship is a central theme in Platonic dialogues</note>. He arrived intending to say certain things to him, precisely at the moment when Alcibiades was also thinking of going to him to ask those same things. 

For all things are joined together in this way, and thus a shared communion of goods is completed everywhere for all things, specifically while the perfective causes are most ready to bestow their gifts. Those things destined to receive, however, awaken toward participation, and those causes again extend their perfective power; <margin>-</margin> the former [the recipients] have received the power of aptitude from nature. 

For <term>power</term> <note>original: "potentia"</note> is twofold: one indeed belongs to the <term>agent</term> <note>original: "agentis" — the being or force that performs an action</note>, the other to the <term>patient</term> <note>original: "patientis" — the person or thing that receives the action</note>. The former is the mother of action, while the latter is the vessel for <term>perfection</term> <note>original: "perfectionis" — in this context, the state of being fully realized or completed</note>. 

And yet it is necessary both that the one who will produce the effect be overflowing in itself and so ready for action that even if no recipient were present, it would nevertheless be perfect in itself and moved of its own accord toward giving; and also that what is to be acted upon should long for participation and [prepare] itself...

...that these two things precede these participations: both the **perfective power** of the giver and the **complete aptitude** of the receiver; and that the perfection of the donor concurs with the preparation of the recipient. Together with such a meeting, the **efficient cause** <note>original: "efficientem causam" — the active force that brings about a change or effect</note> is carried over to the recipient according to its essence.

Furthermore, such a meeting is not fortuitous, nor is an ordered result usually obtained from unorganized and uncoordinated things—just like things that flow together by chance. Instead, it is necessary that such a **harmony** <note>original: "conspirationem" — literally a "breathing together" or cosmic sympathy where different parts of the universe act in concert</note> occurs in some cases through nature, and in others through the **intellect** <note>original: "intellectum" — the higher, divine mind</note>.

Likewise, in some places it arises from a certain **daemonic cause**, and in others rather from a divine one. Indeed, it was under this condition that **Socrates** met with **Alcibiades** <note>Alcibiades was a brilliant but volatile Athenian statesman; his relationship with the philosopher Socrates is a famous example of how a teacher tries to guide a soul toward virtue</note> at the opportune moment for the same purpose. The cause of this opportune meeting was the **good daemon** <note>original: "bonus daemon" — referring to the "daimonion," the divine inner voice or guiding spirit that Socrates claimed directed his actions</note>, who determined the opportunity for Socrates to meet him.

For opportunity itself, starting from above from divine beginnings, proceeds down to the furthest ends. One kind of opportunity is determined by the gods; another is daemonic; another pertains to **fate**; and another is **fortuitous** <note>original: "fortuita" — happening by chance or luck</note>. For Fortune, as it is said, and Opportunity govern all human affairs.

**A** Our souls <note>original: "Animæ" — the OCR "Nimæ" is a transcription error for "Animæ"</note> wander here among the images of those things which they had seen in the first place <note>Referring to the "first realm" or the world of divine Forms before the soul's descent into a body</note>, and they are more deeply moved by those images whose archetypes <note>original: "exemplaria" — the eternal, perfect patterns of which earthly things are mere shadows</note> they had contemplated more attentively in that higher world. For different souls are attuned to different spectacles; therefore, some dwell upon certain images and others upon different ones, for they love the likenesses of the things they inspected there.

Truly, whichever souls were followers <note>original: "pedissequæ" — attendants or handmaidens; here, souls following in the train of a god</note> of great **Jupiter** <note>In Platonic philosophy, Jupiter (Zeus) represents the supreme Demiurge or the ruling intellect of the universe</note> and lived in his company—as he holds the leading rank among the **twelve princes of the universe** <note>The twelve Olympian deities who lead the celestial processions in Plato's "Phaedrus"</note>—these souls, having journeyed even to this world, surely desire a commanding form of life according to the nature of their own god. 

And yet, they are ignorant of what is truly imperial; instead, they pursue a mere appearance of leadership among these worldly images. And if they should find wise teachers, such an inclination leads them toward salvation through a certain return to the celestial realms; but if they linger too long among these images, they decline into **tyranny**. 

Hence **Socrates** says in the *Republic* <note>Plato, "Republic", Book X, 617d–620d, the Myth of Er</note> that souls recently arrived from the heavens most often choose commanding lives. For since a short time ago they traveled in the company of the celestial gods and beheld their powers dominating all things, they themselves also long for a life similar to theirs, ruling over others. And very many indeed abuse such a desire...

->*Higher beings hold with certain judgment those things which*<-

**Y**ou shall receive from this a wonderful principle: that those things which are more excellent <note>referring to higher spiritual or divine principles</note> uniformly and everywhere anticipate those that are inferior; but truly, the inferior are not equal to the power of the superior. Likewise, the knowledge of higher beings firmly encompasses within itself the actions of inferior ones. However, the knowledge of inferior beings can never fully encompass the entire action of the superior. That which is superior receives nothing into itself from the inferior, just as the heavens receive no earthly passion from change; nor does the immovable cause <note>The "unmoved mover" or the primary divine source of motion</note> admit anything worldly from the motion of worldly things; nor do eternal things entirely admit anything temporal into themselves from the actions of others. Finally, while these [higher powers] know all things through necessity, they do not undergo change even in the act of knowing that which is contingent <term>contingens (contingent)</term> <note>Something that is not guaranteed to happen; the result of free will or chance as opposed to destiny</note>.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary, shifting from the nature of divine knowledge to the dialectic method used in Plato’s "Alcibiades I." It uses the character of Alcibiades to illustrate how the soul’s journey of learning mirrors its cosmic descent into the body and its ascent back to the divine.</meta>

<page-num>228</page-num>

# PROCLUS

**I**f Alcibiades is unable to assign a time in which he thought he was ignorant of those things about which he now consults, then certainly he never sought them out, nor did he ever learn them from teachers. Because if he neither sought them out nor received them from others, then surely he neither learned nor discovered them; if he neither learned nor discovered them, then he rightfully does not know them. And if he does not know them, he is not a good judge in matters where he cannot point to a specific time when he realized his own ignorance.

You see indeed how, if a dispute is conducted in this manner, we proceed sometimes by <term>composition</term> <note>original: "compositio" — the process of building up complex ideas from simpler ones, or the soul's descent into the complexity of the material world</note> and sometimes by <term>resolution</term> <note>original: "resolutio" — also known as analysis; the process of breaking down complex things into their simple origins, or the soul's ascent back to the divine unity</note>. We speak by affirmative composition, but by negative resolution.

This process of composition and resolution perfectly suits the nature of the soul. Indeed, the soul slips from more perfect things toward the inferior through the composition of reasons and the adding on of certain "foreign garments" <note>This refers to the Neoplatonic idea that the soul acquires "veils" or "garments" (lower faculties or subtle bodies) as it descends from the divine realm into the physical body</note>, until it is imprisoned in this thick and solid bond <note>A common Platonic metaphor for the physical body</note>. Conversely, the soul rises back to the heights through resolution and the expulsion of those things that disagree with its own nature, until, escaping "naked" — as the sacred words <note>original: "sacra eloquia" — Proclus often uses this phrase to refer to the Chaldean Oracles or other divinely inspired texts</note> relate — it is joined with the <term>Forms</term> <note>original: "speciebus" — the eternal, perfect archetypes or "species" that exist independently of matter</note> that are entirely separated from matter. Therefore, argumentation that proceeds through affirmatives descends from more perfect things to the more imperfect; but that which proceeds through negatives does the reverse <note>By stripping away what is "not" true to find the simple, divine essence</note>.

<summary>Proclus explains the dialectic methods of composition and resolution, likening the soul's intellectual journey to its cosmic descent into a physical body and its eventual ascent back to the immaterial Forms.</summary>

**T**he Good itself, as if existing in itself above intellectual nature—if it is right to say so—descends all the way to the final things, illuminating everything, and preserving, and adorning them, and meanwhile turning them back toward itself: First, indeed, it is present to those things that truly exist <note>In Platonic philosophy, "truly existing things" refers to the eternal Forms or Ideas, rather than physical objects</note>; second, to divine souls; third, to the <term>divinities</term> <note>original: "numinibus" — these are the "daemons" or tutelary spirits mentioned in the title, acting as intermediaries between gods and men</note> presiding over the human race; fourth, to our own souls, and then to animals, plants, and all bodies. For this reason, the divine Good itself has inserted a longing for itself in all things, so that through this longing it might be able to impart its gifts to us.

### *The soul becomes like the mind through acquired knowledge; through double ignorance, it becomes like matter.*

**T**he soul, through knowledge itself, turns out to be like the intellect <term>intellectus</term> <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "Intellect" or "Mind" refers to a higher realm of pure, eternal truths above the human soul.</note> by grasping the knowable object in its actual state, just as the intellect grasps the intelligible. However, through double ignorance, it becomes like matter. For just as matter seems to possess all things, while in truth it possesses nothing, so too does one suffering from double ignorance seem to himself to possess what he does not have. Consequently, there are two kinds of knowledge for souls. One is indistinct, existing through a simple and naked understanding; the other is articulated, master of its knowledge, and free from ambiguity.

They join every body everywhere with similar measures and carry out every motion everywhere with musical measures. Therefore, the musical disposition within us is a gift from the Muses, though it is the most distant reflection of them. For the artistic and contemplative dispositions within us have gods as their presiding guides and derive their origin from them.

->*He who is ignorant of the final cause is ignorant of every cause.*<-

Since the end is the first, foremost, and most powerful of causes—for it is for the sake of this that the active causes act and the things being made are brought into being—for this reason, <term>Timaeus</term> <note>The speaker in Plato's "Timaeus" who explains the mathematical and divine construction of the universe.</note> judges that such a cause is the best for wise men to grasp. In the <term>Sophist</term> <note>A dialogue by Plato that analyzes definitions and the nature of the soul.</note>, Plato teaches that there is a twofold corruption of the soul: one is ignorance occurring within the rational mind, and the other is the discord of the irrational part against the rational. These are the rational principles or "blueprints" that the Soul uses to organize the physical world.</note>, various proportions, and many bonds. Likewise, you will see certain "wholes" and "parts," the circles of the soul, and a multiform variety of powers.

Furthermore, you will see the perfection of souls—which is not eternal in the sense of being fixed, nor consisting of all its parts at once, but is unfolded through time and engaged in <term>discursive reasoning</term> <note>original: "discursionibus." But after you have viewed the multitude belonging to souls, bring yourself to the **Intellect** and the intellectual realms, so that you may possess the unity of things. There indeed...

...to correct. For it is not right to believe that things which have no true reality are the primary causes of the knowledge existing within the soul. For the very essence of the soul is full of these things. However, they remain hidden because of **the forgetfulness of birth** <note>original: "oblivione genesica." Everyone, therefore, must begin with the knowledge of oneself. ### *Whoever knows something, they entirely agree regarding it.*

**I**t is necessary for those who know something to be in concord regarding it. Of this concord, the first cause is the determined nature of things itself; the second is that the judicial faculties of cognition are the same in everyone; the third is that in first principles, the intellect is united to itself. And therefore, whatever exists is capable of intelligence and a participant in union. Science <note>original: "Scientia." For it is a union of differing things. It is necessary, therefore, that participants in the same science agree with one another.

This is indeed consistent with the nature of the self-moving soul. This saying certainly also confirms that **learning is recollection** <term>reminiscence (reminiscentia): the Platonic doctrine that the soul already possesses all knowledge and that learning is the process of "remembering" these innate truths</term>; for the fact that those answering say everything from within themselves is the greatest sign of recollection—namely, that souls bring forth reasons and discourses from themselves, and only need someone to awaken them. # PROCLUS

...are inscribed, and the writer himself is within. Yet not all are able to read these inscriptions, or even to recognize that they have been written; for indeed, because of the **oblivion of birth** <note>original: "genesicam oblivionem." This refers to the Platonic belief that the soul forgets its divine knowledge when it enters the material world of "becoming" or "generation."</note>, the eye of the soul is surrounded by filth, and through that very forgetfulness, they have fallen into the passions. Therefore, the only work necessary is to remove that which stands in the way. Knowledge cast into us from the outside is not necessary, for souls have within themselves the **gates of truth** <note>A metaphor for the soul's innate capacity to access universal truths without external instruction.</note>, but they are closed by earthly and material forms.

If, therefore, someone demonstrates these matters with the greatest diligence, the souls—though stirred by an external source—produce the known answers from within themselves. By this very fact, they declare that famous Platonic saying to be true: that the soul knows all things, and needs only someone to stimulate it from the outside in order to provide an answer.

Furthermore, the fact that someone purifies himself while being educated is the work of a **daemonic power** <note>original: "daemonicæ potestatis." In Neoplatonism, a "daemon" is a guardian spirit or intermediary being that guides the soul, not an evil entity.</note>. For these guiding spirits do not act upon us from the outside, but as if from the **stern of a ship** <note>original: "ex puppi." A common ancient metaphor for the soul's governing part directing the "vessel" of the human being.</note>, they direct and govern us from within. Nor do they purge us as if we were mere bodies that had received a nature capable of being moved only from the outside; rather, they care for us as beings who are **self-moving** <term>self-moving (mobiles ex se ipsis): a technical term in Platonic philosophy (Greek: "autokineton") describing the soul's unique nature as the source of its own motion and agency.</term>. For in this way, they both provide what is good and purge the passions. Therefore, **Socrates** <note>The philosopher Socrates, who used the "Socratic method" of questioning to lead students to discover the truth for themselves.</note>, acting in the role of a good guardian spirit, shows that the youth is refuted not so much by another person as by himself.

# ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

### *Why the evil and ignorant man is at odds with himself and others; and why the good man is in agreement, and those with knowledge are in harmony with one another.*

<insert>National Library of Rome, Vittorio Emanuele</insert>

It happens, and rightly so, that many experience frequent discord within themselves: for they take in some things from the senses, others again from the imagination; some frequently from opinion, several from anger, and many from desire. For such passions are not stirred up in men solely by opinions, as the <term>Stoics</term> <note>The Stoics were a school of ancient Greek philosophers who taught that emotions are essentially errors in judgment or "opinions" about what is good or bad.</note> claim, but on the contrary, because of certain passions and impulses, they often change their opinions, frequently moving from the best views to the worst. Therefore, since these people receive various motions within themselves from many principles and powers—and inferior ones at that—they naturally possess a soul that is at odds and in discord.

However, those endowed with knowledge receive their entire cognition from a single, higher principle. For the intellect <note>original: "intellectus." In Neoplatonic thought, this refers to the higher mind or 'Nous,' which perceives universal truths directly rather than through step-by-step reasoning.</note> provides them with their principles. Indeed, all true judgments are the daughters of the intellect. Since, therefore, they all proceed from such a principle of simplicity, they are all rightly in harmony with one another.

*Those who believe that man is composed of soul and body consequently separate what is useful from what is just; but those who believe that man is the soul itself join them together.*

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s discourse on the nature of man. While the previous page discussed the psychological conflict within the ignorant man versus the harmony of the wise, this page transitions into a specific philosophical debate: the relationship between justice and utility, and how our definition of "human" dictates our ethics.</meta>

<page-num>258</page-num>

-> ## PROCLUS <-

**W**hether the just and the useful are the same thing is a matter on which others certainly disagree. But the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of Plato, who argued that being a good person is always in one's own best interest.</note> judge them to be the same. Indeed, the <term>Epicureans</term> <note>Followers of Epicurus, who believed the goal of life was pleasure and the absence of pain.</note> and certain of the <term>Stoics</term>—who place our ultimate goal in living according to nature—as well as the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for teaching while walking (peripatountes) in the Lyceum.</note>, who define our "good" through the fulfillment of necessary physical needs, cannot easily confirm that the just and the useful are one and the same. This is similarly true for whoever claims that man is merely an "animated body," or a composite of body and soul. For such a person will flee from wounds and death, even if it requires acting unjustly, so that the "animal" <note>original: "animal." In Latin, this refers generally to any "living being" endowed with a soul (anima).</note> may be preserved; since the good of any animal is to exist in a state according to its physical nature and to be preserved in that state. In this case, therefore, what is "useful" for survival clashes with what is "just."

But those who place that goal within the soul itself, requiring nothing of the body, and who believe that man is actually the soul using the body as a tool—these people certainly judge that the just and the useful are the same. For they place both [justice and utility] in the soul, and they understand that the "passions" <note>In ancient philosophy, 'passions' are things that happen to you or that you suffer, like physical pain or external damage.</note> of the instruments <note>original: "instrumentorum." This refers to the physical body as the "tool" of the soul.</note> are entirely separate from the users themselves. The argument proving that the just is useful proceeds as follows: Everything just is beautiful; <note>original: "pulchrum." This term captures the Greek concept of *kalon*, which means both "beautiful" and "morally noble."</note> everything beautiful is good; therefore, everything just is good. And since the good and the useful are the same thing, it follows that everything just is useful.

*The soul draws into itself the form of the thing to which it adheres; likewise concerning the vehicles <note>In Neoplatonic thought, the "vehicle" (ochema) is a subtle, celestial body or "carrier" that the soul inhabits as it descends from the divine realm to the physical world.</note> of divine souls and of our own.*

<meta>catchword: Souls,</meta>

<summary>Proclus explores the philosophical debate on whether justice and utility are identical, arguing that if man is defined as a soul using a body, then being just is always beneficial.</summary>

**S**ouls also take on the **forms** <note>original: "species."
