### How these two differ: namely, "in
### itself" and "as itself."

**E**xpressions of this kind—namely, <term>in itself</term> <note>Latin: *secundum seipsum*. Referring to a property belonging to a subject's own nature.</note> and <term>as itself</term> <note>Latin: *qua ipsum*. A more restrictive logical term meaning a property belongs to a subject precisely because of what that subject is, and nothing else.</note>—are distinguished even in the works of Aristotle. For that which belongs to something **in itself** might not belong to it primarily. However, that which belongs to something **as itself**, in addition to belonging "in itself," also belongs to it primarily and is exactly equal to it.

Therefore, if the Beautiful is the cause of <term>proportion</term> <note>Latin: *commensuratio*. The harmonious arrangement of parts; a key concept in ancient aesthetics.</note> in the soul—and for this very reason is called "beautiful"—and if it brings it about that the better part of the soul dominates the worse, and perfects us, and purges the soul's deformity: by this very reasoning, it is **the Good**. It is not so by <term>accident</term> <note>Latin: *per accidens*. A property that happens to be true but is not part of the thing's essential definition.</note>, but for the very reason that it is beautiful. For if, insofar as it is beautiful, it is proportionate, it is also good. For the Good is the measure; certainly, insofar as it is beautiful, it exists also as the good. 

Similarly, the ugly, <margin>The nature of evil</margin> insofar as it is ugly, is evil. For insofar as it is ugly, it is formless, indeterminate, and uncomposed; and by this very reasoning, it is evil. Therefore, insofar as it is ugly, it is surely evil. Thus, the same thing is both always beautiful and good; and conversely, it is equally ugly and evil. Keep this rule in mind here, which Aristotle also used hereafter: if any two things are <term>convertible</term> <note>Latin: *convertuntur*. In logic, two terms are convertible if they imply one another (e.g., if every human is a rational animal, and every rational animal is a human).</note>, then in turn their op- <note>The text cuts off here and continues on the next page with "posita" (opposites).</note>

# PROCLUS ON SACRIFICE AND MAGIC,
### *Translated by Marsilio Ficino of Florence.*

**J**ust as lovers proceed gradually by reason from that beauty which appears to the senses toward divine beauty: so also the ancient priests, when they considered in natural things a certain kinship, and the <term>sympathy</term> <note>Latin: *compassionem*. In ancient philosophy, this refers to a hidden "resonance" or "co-suffering" between distant parts of the universe, like a string on a lute vibrating when a corresponding string is plucked.</note> of some things for others, and of manifest things for hidden powers, and found all things in all things, they established their sacred science. The ancients, contemplating these things, employed some celestial and some earthly things, from which they drew down divine powers into a lower place because of a certain similarity. Indeed, similarity itself is a sufficient cause for binding individual things to one another. 

For if someone heats **hemp** <note>original: *canabim*</note>, or **papyrus** <note>original: *papyrum*</note>, and then brings it near a lamp, even if it does not touch it, they will see the hemp suddenly ignited, although it has not touched the fire, and the ignition descends from above to the lower parts. # P O R P H Y R Y
## ON THE OCCASIONS,

->*<-

### On the nature of corporeal and incorporeal things.

**E**VERY body is in a place. But none of those things which are <term>incorporeal</term> <note>original: *incorporea*; refers to things that have no physical substance, such as the soul, the mind, or mathematical truths.</note> by their own nature, or any such thing, is in a place. Things which are incorporeal by nature—by the very fact that they are superior to every body and every place—are everywhere; not indeed by being stretched out across a distance, but in a certain <term>indivisible</term> <note>original: *indiuidua*; in this context, it means the spirit does not have "parts" spread out over space, but is present in its entirety at every point.</note> condition. Things which are incorporeal by nature are not present to bodies in a spatial way; rather, they are present to them whenever they wish, by turning and inclining toward them, insofar as they naturally turn and incline toward them. Yet, since they are not present to bodies by a spatial condition, they are present to them by a certain <term>disposition</term> <note>original: *habitudo*; a technical term describing a relationship or "leaning" of the soul toward the body without the soul becoming part of the physical world.</note>. Things which are incorporeal by nature are certainly not present to bodies through substance or through essence. For they are not mixed with bodies, but—

<summary>Porphyry begins by defining the difference between physical bodies, which occupy space, and incorporeal realities like the soul, which exist everywhere simultaneously through their relationship to the material world rather than by being "inside" it.</summary>

### On the nature, binding, and release of the soul.

**T**he Soul is indeed a certain middle-ground between <term>indivisible essence</term> <note>original: *essentiam indiuiduam*; refers to pure spiritual reality, like the Intellect, which cannot be broken into parts.</note> and the essence that is divisible among bodies. The <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: *Intellectus*; in Neoplatonism, this is the realm of pure thought and eternal truths, higher than the individual soul.</note>, however, is an essence that is solely indivisible. But qualities and material forms are divisible according to the nature of bodies. Not everything that acts upon another does so through physical proximity and touch; indeed, even those things that do something through approaching and touching as an <term>accident</term> <note>original: *secundum accidens*; a philosophical term for something that happens to a thing but is not part of its essential, internal nature.</note> do not [necessarily] make use of proximity in their own essence. The soul is bound to the body by a certain turning toward the <term>passions</term> <note>original: *passiones*; here meaning physical sensations, emotions, and the "suffering" of bodily needs.</note> originating from the body. And conversely, it is released insofar as it experiences nothing from the body. What nature has bound, nature itself also releases. Again, what the soul has joined together, the soul also sets apart. Nature, for its part, binds the body within the soul; the soul, however, binds itself within the body. For this reason, nature separates the body from the soul <note>This refers to physical death.</note>, but the soul separates itself from the body <note>This refers to "philosophical death" or the ascetic practice of detaching one's mind from physical desires.</note>.

<vocab>Soul, essence, intellect, nature, binding, release, Porphyry, body</vocab>

<summary>Porphyry defines the soul as a bridge between the indivisible spiritual realm and the divisible physical world. He explains that while nature binds the body to the soul, it is the soul's own desires and "turning" that bind it to the body, implying that spiritual liberation is a self-directed process.</summary>

->*All things are in all things in a certain way,*<-
->*according to the condition of those things in which they exist.*<-

**W**e do not understand "all things in all things" to be the same in every case, but rather the <term>essence</term> <note>original: *essentia*; the fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing.</note> of each thing relates to all others in its own specific way: in the intellect, things exist intellectually; in the soul, however, they exist rationally; in plants, they exist <term>seminally</term> <note>original: *seminariè*; referring to the "seed-like" formative principles that govern growth.</note>; in bodies, they exist <term>imaginatively</term> <note>original: *imaginariè*; meaning as images or reflections of the true reality.</note>; and in that which is above all these (the One or the First Principle), they exist in a way that is <term>super-intellectual</term> and <term>super-essential</term> <note>original: *supereſſentiali*; a term used to describe reality that is beyond the category of "being" or "existence" as we understand it.</note>.

->*In the highest things there is unity with power;*<-
->*in the lowest, there is a multitude with weakness.*<-

**W**hen <term>incorporeal substances</term> <note>original: *Incorporeæ ſubſtantiæ*; realities without physical bodies, such as minds or souls.</note> descend, they are indeed divided and multiplied into individual parts through a lack of power. But when they ascend, they gather themselves and return into a single unity through an abundance of power.

### On the types of life.

**N**ot only among physical bodies is there an <term>equivocal</term> <note>original: *æquiuoca*; a term used when the same word is applied to different things with different meanings.</note> condition, but life itself is also spoken of in many ways. For the life of a plant is one thing, and that of an animal is another. Again, the life of an intellectual essence is one thing, the life of a higher nature another, that of the soul another, and that of the intellect another. For even those higher things live, even if none of the things that come into being through them are granted a life similar to their own.

It also defines 'life' as a multi-layered concept that changes as one moves from plants to the divine intellect.</summary>

*Of those things that generate, some turn toward their offspring, while others do not at all.*

**E**verything that generates by its own <term>essence</term> <note>original: *essentia*; the fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing.</note> generates something inferior to itself. Furthermore, everything generated turns back toward its <term>generator</term> <note>original: *genitorem*; the source or cause from which a thing arises.</note> by nature. Of those things that generate, however, some in no way turn toward the things they have generated; others are partly inclined toward them and partly not; and finally, others are only turned toward their offspring and do not, in the meantime, reflect back upon themselves.

*Sensation, imagination, memory, and intelligence.*

**M**emory is not some kind of preservation of imaginations, but is the bringing forward of the conceptions and problems that have been meditated upon <note>original Greek: *ἀλλὰ τῶν μελετηθέντων προβαλέσθαι ἐννοίας, προβλήματα*</note>; rather, it is to bring forth into active expression the very propositions or productions of those things which the soul has recently contemplated. The <term>soul</term> <note>original: *anima*; the life-principle that mediates between the pure intellect and the physical body.</note> indeed possesses the <term>formative principles</term> <note>original: *rationes*; referring to the "logoi" or rational blueprints of all things held within the soul.</note> of all things. It acts according to these principles, whether it is provoked to such an exercise by something external, or whether it turns itself inward toward its own principles. When it is provoked by something else, it employs the senses to introduce external things; but when it enters into itself, it reaches the <term>intellects</term> <note>original: *intelligentias*; refers here to the higher intuitive grasp of truths.</note>. Therefore, neither are the senses outside of the imagination, nor, as one might say, are the intellects, insofar as they belong to the soul—

->*The Soul is immortal.*<-

**T**he soul is an <term>unextended essence</term> <note>original: *essentia inextensa*; a substance that does not occupy physical space or possess physical dimensions.</note>, immaterial and **immortal**; possessing life from within itself and likewise possessing its own being.

->*The passive experience of the soul and the body is far different.*<-

**I**t is one thing for bodies to be acted upon, and another for incorporeal things. For the **passive experience** of bodies occurs alongside <term>transformation</term> <note>original: *transmutatione*; a physical change in state, such as turning from cold to hot.</note>. The passive experience of the soul, however, is a certain accommodation and an attraction toward the thing itself; it is a certain action, in no way similar to the heating or cooling of physical bodies. Therefore, if the passive experience of bodies occurs through physical transformation, it must be said that all <term>incorporeal</term> <note>original: *incorporea*; things that lack a physical body or material substance, such as minds or mathematical truths.</note> things are free from such experience. For those things that are actually separated from matter and bodies remain the same; but those that approach matter and bodies are not themselves passive—rather, it is the things in which they appear that suffer the experience. For when an animal senses, the soul indeed similarly...

<summary>Porphyry defines the soul as an unextended, immortal essence and distinguishes between physical "passion" (change in bodies) and the soul's "passion" (which is actually a form of activity).</summary>

### On the differences of incorporeal things.

**T**he very name "**incorporeal things**" <note>original: *incorporeorum*; things that do not have physical bodies, such as thoughts, souls, or mathematical truths.</note> is not applied according to a shared commonality of one and the same genus—in the way that "bodies" are named—but according to a bare **privation** <note>original: *priuationem*; a definition based on what is missing (the lack of a body) rather than what is present.</note> of bodies. For this reason, nothing prevents some among them from being **substances** <note>original: *essentia*; the core being or reality of a thing.</note>, while others are not substances; and again, some being prior to bodies, while others exist together with bodies; likewise, some are separated from bodies, and others not separated. Furthermore, some are **self-subsistent** <note>original: *secundum se subsistentia*; having an independent existence that does not rely on anything else to be real.</note>, while others are dependent on other things for their existence. Finally, some are identical to their own actions and **self-moving lives**, while others [are distinct from their] lives and...

<summary>Porphyry uses the metaphor of a musician and a lyre to argue that the soul is the active mover of the body, and then explains that "incorporeal" is a broad category defined by what it lacks (physicality) rather than a single shared nature.</summary>

### *The properties assigned to prime matter* <note>original: *Passiones materiæ primæ*; In ancient philosophy, "prime matter" is the most basic, formless "stuff" of the universe before it is given shape or qualities.</note>
->*similarly described by Plotinus.*<- <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism and Porphyry’s teacher.</note>

**T**he properties of **matter** <term>materia; the fundamental underlying substance that has no form of its own</term> according to the ancients are these incorporeal things. For matter is diverse from physical bodies; furthermore, it is devoid of life, possessing neither intellect, nor soul, nor anything that lives by its own power. Likewise, it is formless, changeable, infinite, and powerless. For this reason, it is not "being," but truly **non-being** <note>original: *uerum non ens*; Plotinus argued that matter is "non-being" because it lacks any defining characteristics or reality until form is applied to it.</note>, a fleeting appearance of an image. Since that which exists primarily as a mass is itself powerless. Likewise, it is a longing for substance, standing yet without stability. Furthermore, it is always appearing within itself as now small, now large, now less, now more, now deficient, now exceeding; it is something that is always becoming, but never remains, yet it is not able to escape; for it is the total lack of all being. Wherefore, whatever it promises, it lies: and even if it appears large, it suddenly turns out small; for it is like a kind of mockery <note>original: *ludus*; a game, play, or illusion.</note> escaping into non-being. For its flight does not happen in space, but occurs as it falls away from being; for this reason, the images that are within it are held within a further, worse image. Just as in a mirror, that which is elsewhere...

is situated, it appears elsewhere, and the mirror itself seems to be full, yet it holds nothing, while it seems to hold everything. <note>Porphyry is using the "mirror" metaphor popular in Neoplatonism: just as a mirror reflects images without being changed by them, matter reflects the "Forms" of the universe without being altered in its own fundamental nature.</note>

->*What suffers, and what does not.*<-

**A**ll **passions** <term>passiones; in this philosophical context, "passion" refers to being "acted upon" or undergoing a change or affection, rather than a modern emotion</term> are centered around that which is also subject to **destruction** <term>interitus; the process of perishing or ceasing to exist</term>. For the path toward destruction is the admission of a change, and it is the nature of a thing to perish if it is also its nature to suffer such change. However, no **incorporeal** <note>original: *incorporeum*; referring to things without physical bodies, such as the soul or the intellect.</note> thing perishes. Instead, certain things among them either simply are, or are not. For this reason, none of them "suffer": for that which undergoes change ought not to remain as it is, but must be of such a nature that it can be altered, specifically by the qualities of those things which enter into it and thus inflict a "passion." For alteration does not happen to a thing's inner essence from just any source; therefore, **matter** <note>Prime matter, the most basic "stuff" of the universe.</note> does not suffer change. In its own nature, matter is devoid of quality, nor do the **forms** <note>The ideal blueprints or shapes that give matter its identity.</note> that are within it—which enter and exit in turn—affect it. Rather, "passion" occurs within the **composite** <term>compositum; a physical object made of both matter and form joined together</term>, and the being of a single entity consists in this composition; for this composite seems to persist in its existence despite the contrary forces and qualities of the things entering it and bringing about change. For this reason, those things whose life is derived from external sources, and not from themselves, can naturally "suffer" both living and not living <note>Meaning physical bodies can be alive or dead because their life is "added" to them.</note>. But those things whose very existence consists in life are necessarily devoid of passion...

<summary>Porphyry explains that while physical "composite" objects can be changed or destroyed, incorporeal things and prime matter itself do not "suffer" or change because they lack the qualities necessary for such alteration. He uses the metaphor of a mirror to show how matter reflects forms without being influenced by them.</summary>

### *Every incorporeal life, however it may be changed, remains immortal.*

### *Non-being is either superior to being, as is God, or inferior, along with matter.*

**W**hat is called "non-being" is either something we devise ourselves when we are occasionally separated from Being itself, or something we understand through higher intellect while we possess Being. Therefore, if we are separated from Being, we do not understand that "non-being" which is above Being itself, but we instead conceive of non-being as a false passion <note>original: "passionem"; here referring to a state of being acted upon or a distorted perception, rather than emotion.</note> occurring to one who wanders outside of themselves. For just as any person—insofar as they exist, which is to say truly and by their own self—can be led back to that non-being which is superior to Being <note>Referring to the "One" or the Absolute, which is "beyond being."</note>, so too by wandering away from Being and from their own self, they are then led toward that non-being which is the downfall and ruin of Being itself <note>Referring to "matter" or "privation," the lowest level of reality which lacks true existence.</note>.

### *Incorporeal substance is wherever it wishes to be.*

**T**he nature of a body is no obstacle to that which is incorporeal by its own nature, so that it may be wherever and in whatever manner it chooses. For just as that which is devoid of mass <note>original: "mollis" (likely a typo for "molis"); referring to "bulk" or "extension." Incorporeal things lack the physical dimensions of matter.</note> is incomprehensible to a body, and nothing of it pertains to the body, so too that which is distended as mass does not become an obstacle for an incorporeal thing; it is, as it were, non-existent to it.

lies. For that which is incorporeal does not run about here and there according to local conditions as it wishes. For place exists together with mass <note>original: "mole"; referring to physical matter or bulk.</note>. Nor, on the other hand, is it confined by the limits of bodies. For whatever lies in mass in any way can be squeezed into a narrow space and undergo change through local conditions. But that which is entirely removed from mass and magnitude cannot be contained by those things which are in mass, and it remains free from local motion. Therefore, it is found there, wherever it is disposed, by a certain specific disposition; meanwhile, it exists at once both everywhere and nowhere in terms of place. For this reason, by a certain specific affection <note>original: "affectione"; in this context, a state of being or a relation rather than an emotion.</note>, it is grasped either above the heavens or in some part of the world. However, when it is held in some part of the world, it is not indeed seen with the eyes, but its presence is made manifest to men through its works.

### *Universal causes do not turn toward their effects, but they turn the effects toward themselves.*

**N**one of the substances which are universal and perfect turn toward their own offspring <note>original: "genituram"; referring to the lower things they have generated or brought into being.</note>. Instead, all perfect substances are brought back to their producers, and this indeed continues down to the cosmic body <note>original: "corpus mundanum"; the physical universe seen as a single, complete organism.</note>. Since this body is perfect, it is brought back to the soul—I mean the intellectual soul, and for that reason it revolves in a circle. But the soul of the world is raised toward the Intellect <note>original: "intellectum"; the Divine Mind or Nous in Neoplatonic thought.</note>. The Intellect, moreover, is raised toward the Principle <note>original: "principium"; referring to "The One," the ultimate source of all existence.</note>. And so all things arrive at this very point, starting from the furthest extremes, as far as the capacity of each allows; they arrive, I say...

Wherefore, a perfection that is second to the first principles provides support, keeping those same things turned toward what came before. But a defect turns even the prior things toward the posterior, and causes these very things to love the lower things, meanwhile diverting from the higher.

### *How God, Intellect, and Soul are everywhere in different ways.*

**G**od is everywhere, because Intellect is nowhere <note>In Neoplatonic thought, "nowhere" means not being confined to a physical location. ->*The soul sleeps in this body.*<-

**W**e command abstinence from animals <note>original: "Abstinere animalibus"; this refers specifically to the practice of vegetarianism as a spiritual discipline.</note>, not indeed for all people, but certainly for those who intend to contemplate divine things. Such a person is one who truly notices the <term>poisonous spells</term> <note>original: "veneficia"; Porphyry views the sensory attractions of the physical body as a kind of sorcery or drug that dulls the mind.</note> of this dwelling in which we live here below. Moreover, he recognizes that part of himself which is by its very nature perpetually awake, and he perceives the sleep by which he is oppressed here in the world of the senses. To such a person, we shall surely deliver a method of education and nourishment that is consistent with the nature of this place and suitable for the knowledge of his own self.

->*True happiness is not the knowledge of divine things,*<-
->*but a divine life.*<-

**F**or us, blessed contemplation is not merely an accumulation of words or a multitude of academic disciplines, as someone might perhaps have thought. For contemplation is not constructed in that way, nor does it increase according to the quantity of arguments and words...

...receives an increase from words <note>original: "uerborum"; this completes the word begun on the previous page.</note>. Indeed, it is not simply that any discipline fills a person with the happiness of contemplation; nor do even those doctrines concerning things that are true ever achieve this, unless there is also present a life transformed into the very nature of divine things.

Truly, the goal of contemplation is <term>Being</term> <note>original: "ens"; in Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to the ultimate, unchanging reality.</note> itself, and the attainment of truth. Therefore, the goal is to live by the Intellect. For this reason, if happiness itself consisted in a heap of words and arguments, it would be possible for men who despise education and specific duties to attain the blessed end.

But since it is necessary to change this life for another, purifying the soul through words, reasons, and works—come then, tell me: what sort of discourses and what sort of works might best instruct us? Is it not...

### *On the descent and ascent of the soul.*

**I**t is necessary for us—if we are to fly back to those things which are truly our own—to completely cast aside these things which we have taken on from our mortal nature. We must also shed the inclination toward these things, for it is through this leaning that our descent <note>In Neoplatonic thought, the "descent" is the process of the soul leaving the divine realm to inhabit a physical body.</note> occurred. Moreover, we must remember that blessed and eternal substance; and, while we strive to ascend to the <term>incorporeal</term> <note>original: "incorporeum"; things that have no physical body or material form, such as the soul or the divine.</note>, we should meditate especially on two things: first, by what means we may shed this material and fleeting existence, and second, by what path we may best return. We must travel back by a path that is the opposite of the one by which we descended to these physical circumstances. 

For we were, and still are, <term>intellectual essences</term> <note>original: "intellectuales essentiæ"; the core of our being that belongs to the realm of pure thought rather than the physical world.</note>, pure from all sense-perception and living free from irrational nature. However, we have been joined to the <term>sensible</term> nature <note>original: "naturæ sensibili"; the world of things that can be seen, heard, and touched.</note>, partly through the soul’s inability to maintain its eternal connection to our <term>intelligible</term> <note>original: "intelligibile"; the realm of reality that can only be perceived by the mind, not the eyes.</note> nature, and partly through a power that pulls us down toward lower things. For all those powers that operate through the senses and the body only begin to flourish and take effect when the mind persists <note>original: "perseuerat"; the text breaks here at "per-", but the catchword "seuer" indicates the word is completed on the next page.</note> least in the intelligible realm itself...

<summary>Porphyry describes the soul's need to reverse its descent into the material world by casting off physical attachments and returning to its original state of pure, intellectual existence.</summary>

->*On the release of the soul.*<-

**T**he ancient sages diligently avoided all things that could fasten the soul to the body. Thus, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, known for their strict lifestyle and belief in the transmigration of souls.</note> and similar wise men partly withdrew themselves into solitude, and partly lived as a group within temples and sacred groves, so that all the turmoil of the crowd would be moved far away from them. Plato, however, chose to inhabit the **Academy** <note>The school founded by Plato in Athens.</note>, a field that was not only solitary and removed from the city, but also (as it is said) unhealthy. Others truly did not even spare their own eyes, so that they might preserve an intimate contemplation that was perpetual and interrupted by nothing. The philosopher, indeed, will not thrust the soul from the body by violence. For if he uses force, nonetheless...

[The body] is tempered like an instrument to the powers of the soul. One clearly understands how much **passion** <term>passion</term> <note>original: "passio"; in Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to a state where the soul is "acted upon" or disturbed by physical sensations rather than being an active agent of reason.</note> is ready to sound—whether you will it or not—whenever the body is struck by external things and that striking reaches the level of perception. Furthermore, the eating of meat does not contribute to health at all, but rather hinders health. For health is maintained by the same means through which it is recovered. It is recovered through a very sparse diet and by abstaining from meat; therefore, health is also preserved by this. 

Even if abstinence from animals contributes less to the **strength of Milo** <note>Milo of Croton was a famous 6th-century BCE wrestler known for his legendary strength and for supposedly eating massive amounts of meat. He should not give himself over to outward actions or to **incontinence** <term>incontinence</term> <note>original: "incontinentia"; the inability to control one's physical appetites or impulses.</note>. It is certainly fitting to preserve health, though not [the health] of death indeed...

For much vigor overflows to the body from that state, as the experience of our friends has proven. Indeed, it has gone so far that they simultaneously drove out the most bitter pains of the joints—in both the feet and the hands—which for eight whole years had compelled them to be carried by another. ### *On the types of good and evil demons.*

**T**here remains the multitude of invisible beings, whom Plato called "undifferentiated demons" <note>original: "dæmones indistinctos"; in Platonic thought, "demons" are not necessarily evil but are spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans.</note>. Of these, some have indeed been given names by men and have received honors equal to the gods and other forms of worship among various individuals. Others, though appearing in many forms, are not named, but instead receive a name and worship in a somewhat secret manner from certain people in various villages or cities. The remaining multitude is thus commonly called by the general name of **demons** <term>dæmonum: spirits occupying the air between the earth and the moon, acting as intermediaries between the divine and the mortal.</term>. Indeed, there is a fixed belief among all people of this kind: that these beings will certainly harm the human race if they become angry because they are neglected or do not receive their lawful worship; and conversely, that they will benefit those men who have won them over through vows, supplications, sacrifices, and the other rituals that follow. Since, therefore, this common opinion regarding demons is confused and carries much slander against them, it is necessary to distinguish their nature through reason...

...and the common crowds, hearing ideas similar to their own opinions from celebrated writers, are even more firmly convinced of these views regarding the gods. For the art of **poetry** has further stirred the suspicions of such men. This is because poetry uses a style of speech that is designed to stun and enchant—it is heavily adapted to a kind of magical attraction <note>original: "attractū quasi magicum"; the author suggests that the beauty of poetic language can bypass reason like a spell.</note>. It easily possesses the power to soothe and lure the mind, and therefore leads us to believe in things that are entirely impossible. 

But surely we must hold to a firm belief: that which is good never causes harm, and that which is evil never provides true benefit. For, as **Plato** says <note>referring to Republic 335d, where Plato argues that it is not the property of the good to harm.</note>, it is not the nature of heat to make things cold, but rather the nature of its opposite. In the same way, it is not the nature of a just person to cause harm. 

Divinity itself <note>term: divinity <gloss>original: "diuinitas." Here referring to the highest divine nature or the gods themselves.</gloss></term> is, by its very nature, the most just of all things; otherwise, nothing would truly be divine. Therefore, must we not distinguish this [harmful] power from that of the **beneficent spirits**? For a nature that is prone to harm is naturally the complete opposite of one that is beneficent. Two such opposite qualities can never naturally exist within the same being.

Therefore, while spirits of that [malicious] kind harm our mortal nature in many ways, and sometimes in great matters, the **good spirits** <note>term: good spirits <gloss>original: "boni dæmones." Instead, they signal the dangers threatening us from the evil ones whenever they are able. They do this sometimes by showing us truths in **dreams**, sometimes through minds that are divinely inspired, and through many other...

### *It is a sin to kill animals.*

It is unjust to slaughter animals, since they are not entirely foreign to us. ...and [Nature] made the **sentient animal** <note>original: "animal sensuale." In this context, it refers to any living being endowed with senses.</note>, not indeed so that it might simply feel and be acted upon, but so that it might perceive what things were advantageous for it and what were disadvantageous, and follow the former while fleeing the latter. Therefore, the senses bring the knowledge of both to individual animals. 

But those actions which follow after sensation—namely, the pursuit and grasping of useful things and the avoidance of harmful ones—must be thought to belong only to those possessing a certain **reasoning** <term>ratiocinationem: the process of logical thought or calculation.</term>, judgment, and memory. Although **Strato the Naturalist** <note>original: "Strato physicus." Strato of Lampsacus was a Greek philosopher and head of the Peripatetic school who argued that all sensation involves a degree of mental activity.</note> says that sense-perception does nothing without intelligence—since we often do not perceive things right before our eyes when our minds are intently focused on something else—nevertheless, let it be granted that the senses do not require the mind for their basic function. Yet, when sense-perception, in its operation, turns toward what is its own and what is foreign, and makes a distinction between these two, fleeing the one and following the other, and sagaciously finds the means of following and escaping, we can conclude that reason is present. These things are indeed characteristic of reason, and they are present in all animals—that is, in those capable of **self-movement** <term>progressiuis: literally "progressive" or "advancing" animals; those capable of navigating through space.</term>.

...[to harm] no one, he surely is most happy, and most like to God, who so prepares himself that he needs as little as possible from others, and harms as little as possible. This man, therefore, will feed only on the **fruits of the earth**, so that he may not harm men, nor harm animals; and as much as possible, he will even spare plants and herbs. For the ancients themselves lamented even this: that we stand in need of the fruits of trees <note>Porphyry is referring to the "Golden Age" trope in Greek philosophy, where original humans lived without even harvesting from nature.</note>. 

Moreover, the cause of this neediness is **birth** <term>generatio: specifically, the soul's entry into the physical world of change and "becoming."</term>, and because in this very state of want—having been established through birth—we are now further removed from **abundance** <note>original: "copia." In Neoplatonic thought, "abundance" or "plenitude" refers to the fullness of the divine realm.</note>. For want seeks its safety from external things. He, therefore, who needs more external things is more closely joined with want, and is separated further from God. For he who is like God possesses true abundance through this very likeness. 

But the wealthy man, truly enjoying riches, inflicts injury on no one. Indeed, as long as he inflicts injury, even though he might possess all the money in the world and occupy the whole earth, he must be considered poor, since he is a companion of **want** <note>original: "inopia." Here, Porphyry argues that greed and the desire to consume others (animals or humans) is a sign of spiritual poverty, not wealth.</note>. 

Wherefore the unjust man is profane, and polluted with every wickedness. This vice was brought upon us by a certain **ruin of the soul** as it descends into **matter** <term>materia: the physical, tangible world, which Neoplatonists viewed as the source of limitation and evil for the soul.</term>, departing from the Good. All things, therefore, are trifles, insofar as one falls away from the first principle. The soul is in need of everything as long as it does not look up toward **fullness** <note>original: "plenitudinem." A reference to the Pleroma or the complete, divine reality.</note> itself. But it yields...

...to that part which is immortal in its own nature, insofar as he does not truly know himself. But he who, having already become **like God**, is content with the smallest amount of food, enjoys that prosperity of the **Golden Age** <note>The "Golden Age" (aureum seculum) was a mythical era in Greek and Roman thought when humans lived in peace, and the earth provided all they needed without labor or slaughter.</note>.

->*A certain reason is present even in animals.*<-

**R**eason is indeed naturally present. However, right and perfect reason arises from meditation and instruction. Therefore, a certain participation in the **rational faculty** <term>rationalis facultas: the ability to process information and make choices, which Porphyry argues is not exclusive to humans.</term> belongs to all animals. Yet, one cannot find even a human who has fully attained perfect rectitude and wisdom. And just as there is a difference between one type of sight and another, or one type of flight and another—for **hawks** do not see in the same way as **cicadas**, nor do **eagles** fly in the same way as **partridges**—so too not every rational being shares equally in sharp-wittedness and cunning.

...was judged to be golden. He adds that they killed no animal. They certainly proved that nothing is better for health than to gather as little excess as possible. Thus, they did not wish to consume nourishment stronger than nature, but rather that by which nature might be stronger. The ancient priests of the Egyptians, devoted to the study of wisdom—about whom Chaeremon the Stoic <note>Chaeremon of Alexandria (1st century CE) was a scholar and priest who wrote about Egyptian religion and hieroglyphics; his works are mostly lost except for fragments preserved by Porphyry.</note> treats most diligently—also mostly abstained from animals. Furthermore, they venerated many things as divine, some of which they said were suited to different gods, just as for the **Sun** they designated the hawk, the scarab beetle, the ram, and the crocodile. For they understood that the soul of every animal is **rational** <term>rationalis: Porphyry argues that animals possess a degree of reason, though perhaps different in scale or expression than humans.</term> once it has been separated from the body, and is capable of foretelling the future, divining for us, and accomplishing all things which a human can also do when released from the body. Therefore, they did not honor animals without reason, and they restrained themselves from them as much as possible.

### *The sober life of the Essenes.*

**H**e then relates from the history of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus was a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian. Porphyry uses his descriptions of Jewish sects to provide "barbarian" (non-Greek) examples of philosophical living.</note> the life of the **Essenes** <note>original: "Essæorum." The Essenes were a Jewish sect known for their communal property, asceticism, and strict adherence to purity laws.</note>, a religious and philosophical people among the Jews. He notes that they held all things in common and, above all, cultivated mutual charity, abstinence, and patience, always intent upon divine worship.

...and they were so brave in spirit that they preferred to be killed rather than to deny God. And even in the midst of their very tortures, they were accustomed to laugh openly. For this reason, while being tortured, they would release their souls joyfully, as if they were about to receive them again. For this opinion is firmly held among them, he says, that souls are immortal, and that descending from the thinnest ether, they are attached to bodies, drawn to them by a natural force and instinct—or *rhume* <note>original Greek: ῥύμη, meaning a rushing force or momentum</note>. But after they have departed from the prison of the body, they rejoice as if now free from a long servitude, and they raise themselves through the heights. They used to abstain both from many animals and from all types of lack of self-control altogether. Finally, because of this life—which was most temperate, most studious of truth, and most devoted to God—many among them would foretell future events, and for that reason, they were called **Prophets**.

# PORPHYRY

...exhibited. These Samaneans <note>derived from the Sanskrit 'Sramana', referring to non-Brahminical Indian ascetics like Buddhists or Jains</note> bore the time of this life as if it were a certain necessary servitude ministering to nature, and they did so unwillingly; they strove to release their souls from the body. Therefore, their kinsmen considered them blessed in their death, and they wept for those who remained behind as if they were unhappy.

->*Sobriety and contemplation join the mind to God.*<-

**T**he <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>meaning "naked philosophers," a Greek name for Indian ascetics known for their extreme renunciation of clothing and food</note>, besides their other temperance and holiness, abstained from animal flesh. Indeed, a holiness that abstains from mortal things contains within it the potential for eternal life. However, a fattened body forces the soul to go hungry as it falls away from a happy life; it increases the mortal part of our being, thereby expelling and hindering the eternal life intended for us. It also contaminates the soul, namely by rendering it corporeal <note>weighted down by the needs and desires of the physical body</note> and turning it aside toward that which is different from its divine nature. The magnet stone, however, draws iron that approaches it as if by a certain soul of its own. In this way, iron—which is by nature extremely heavy—becomes light and is elevated by the spirit of the magnet as it draws itself toward the stone. If anyone, therefore, should emerge suspended toward God (who is the incorporeal and intellectual <note>original: 'intellectualem', referring to the 'Nous' or Divine Mind in Neoplatonic philosophy</note> being), he rightly ought not to nour- <note>The page ends mid-word, likely 'nutrire' (to nourish)</note>

<header>ON ANCIENT ABSTINENCE</header>
<meta>The catchword "EX" from the previous page suggests the beginning of "extra" (outside), which led into the discussion of seeking external nourishment.</meta>

...to seek nourishment, by which the body is fattened—an act that blocks the path to the mind. Instead, the philosopher will reduce the body to the smallest and most absolutely necessary sustenance. He himself will be nourished by divinity, joined more naturally to God than iron is to a magnet. Indeed, if we did not even require the smallest amount of food, we would be as much happier as we would be more immortal. But as it stands, living in this mortal state, we secretly make ourselves (so to speak) even more mortal whenever we enlarge the body. As Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle in the Peripatetic school</note> says, this occurs through <term>indwelling</term> <note>original Greek: ἐνοίκησιν (enoinēsis); the concept of the soul "taking up residence" in the body</note>, which is to say the soul contracts a deep intimacy by living too familiarly with the body, and moreover, it eventually devotes its whole self to it. But would that we had been able to live life entirely without food and drink! Then, by restraining the physical waste of the body, we might immediately be joined with the highest things, in which God, being who He is, truly exists as God.

But why do we cry out and lament these things in vain to men who are so blinded? They constantly cherish their own misfortune, yet they hate first themselves and their true Father <note>referring to the divine source or Creator from which the soul originates</note>. Furthermore, they even hate those who warn and encourage them to eventually wake up from their drunkenness <note>a common philosophical metaphor for the state of being distracted by worldly desires and bodily needs</note>. Democrates <note>likely a reference to the philosopher Democritus, whose ethical maxims were frequently cited by Porphyry</note> says that to live imprudently, intemperately, and impiously is not so much to live "badly" as it is to be a long time in dying.

<summary>Porphyry argues that minimizing food intake allows the soul to detach from the body and unite with the divine, whereas indulgence "corporealizes" the soul and traps it in a state of living death.</summary>

# FROM MICHAEL
## PSELLUS ON 
### DEMONS,

->*Translated by Marsilius Ficinus.*<-

<note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078) was a renowned Byzantine polymath. This Latin translation by Marsilius Ficinus, a central figure of the Italian Renaissance, helped introduce Psellus’s demonology to Western Europe.</note>

The nature of demons is not without a body; rather, it possesses a body and is active around physical bodies, as our venerable fathers <note>the early Christian theologians and Church Fathers</note> have also judged. There are even those who assert that demons have appeared to them in person with their own bodies. Furthermore, Basil <note>Saint Basil the Great (c. 330–379), a highly influential Greek bishop and theologian</note>, that divine observer of hidden mysteries, attributed bodies not only to demons but even to pure angels, describing them as certain thin, airy, and pure spirits. He brings forth David <note>traditionally regarded as the author of the Psalms</note> as a witness, saying: *Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flaming fire* <note>original: "Qui facit angelos eius spiritus, ac ministros eius flammeos"; a citation of Psalm 104:4</note>. And this is indeed necessary; for it is required, as the divine Paul <note>the Apostle Paul, specifically in Hebrews 1:14</note> asserts, that the ministering spirits who are sent forth must have a body by which they move, take their stand, and appear openly. For they knew that these ministries could not be fulfilled in any other way than through some kind of body. If you should read anywhere in Scripture that they are called <term>incorporeal</term> <note>original: *incorporeos*; literally "without body"</note>, I respond that our writers and others are accustomed to calling only the thicker, heavier bodies "corporeal."

<summary>This page introduces Michael Psellus's argument that demons and angels are not purely immaterial but possess subtle, airy bodies. It supports this claim by citing Saint Basil and biblical passages from David and Paul, explaining that "incorporeal" in scripture merely distinguishes these spirits from dense, heavy matter.</summary>

# PSELLUS ON DEMONS.

...to name. Indeed, thin bodies, which escape both sight and touch, are frequently nicknamed "incorporeal" <note>bodiless</note>. However, the body belonging to angels is not the same as that related to demons. For the angelic body, pouring out certain rays of light, cannot be endured by the eyes of others, vanishing entirely from them; but whether the demonic body was ever like that, I cannot say. It seems, however, to have been so at one time, since Isaiah names the angel who fell "Lucifer" <note>original: "luciferum"; literally "the light-bringer," referring to the Morning Star</note>; but now it exists otherwise—obscure and dark—and if it presents itself to our eyes, stripped of its former light, it appears to us as something troublesome.

The angelic body is indeed entirely free of matter, for which reason it penetrates and passes through every solid thing; it is even less subject to physical alterations <note>the capacity to be affected or changed by external forces</note> than a ray of the sun. For earthly obstacles and opaque objects block a ray of the sun as it proceeds through transparent and translucent bodies, or as it enters them, to such an extent that it undergoes refraction—seeing as it has a kinship with the material world <note>original: "malum"; in the Neoplatonic tradition used here, "evil" was often equated with "matter" or the lack of divine light</note>. But nothing of this sort blocks the angelic body, as it suffers no opposition from anything; certainly, it does not match any of these material things in its order or its nature. Demonic bodies, however, although they are invisible due to their thinness, are nevertheless material...

...bodies are in some way subject to sensation and suffering <note>original: "passioni"; here meaning the capacity to be acted upon or to feel pain</note>, especially those that inhabit underground places. For these are so dense that they are subject to touch; they feel pain when struck, and they can be burned when brought near fire—to such an extent that some of them even leave behind ashes. History records that this actually happened among the Tuscans <note>The people of Etruria in Italy, known in antiquity for their expertise in religious rituals and divination</note>. I am not recounting these things as if they were a poetic fable, nor am I bringing forth monsters in the manner of the Cretans or Phoenicians <note>a reference to the ancient reputation of these cultures for telling tall tales or "myth-making"</note>. Rather, I affirm these things because I am persuaded by the words of the Savior himself, which teach that demons are tormented by fire. This is possible only because they are corporeal <note>original: "corporei"; meaning they possess a physical body or substance</note> and are thus able to suffer. For how could they suffer if they were bodiless? That which is incorporeal cannot even be imagined to suffer at the hands of a physical body.

### ON DEMONS ###

...man who, if anyone else had advanced in the cult of demons and had observed the apparitions of demons, he previously used to despise and detest these things as vain and false. But then he sang a palinode <note>original: "palinodiam cecinit"; a formal retraction or "singing a different tune" after a change of heart</note>, and adhered to the true dogmas and to ours. This man revealed many wonderful and demonic things to us. To me, occasionally asking whether demons were capable of suffering, he said, "Extremely so, to the point that some demons cast seed and are born into certain tiny animals."

Then I said, "It is incredible that demons have excrement and genital organs."

"They do indeed have organs," he said, "but not like ours. However, some kind of excrement does emanate from them."

Then he added, "Believe me."

But I said, "They are in grave danger if they are nourished in our manner."

"They are indeed nourished," said Marcus, "some by inspiration <note>original: "inspiratione"; referring to the drawing in of air or spirituous vapors</note>, just as the spirit thrives in the arteries and nerves. But not all of them experience this; only the kinds of demons closest to matter <note>referring to the theory that demons have bodies of varying density, with "material" demons being the most base and physical</note>, and the kind of demons that hate the light: the aquatic and the subterranean." I asked these things: "Are there, O Marcus, many kinds of demons?" 

"Many," he said, "and diverse, both according to their forms and according to their bodies, so much so that the air which is above us, and that which is around us, is full of demons. The earth and sea are also full, as are hidden and deep places." 

"If it is not a bother," I said, "enumerate them."

For the aquatic, the subterranean, and also the light-shunning types are exceedingly wicked and destructive. Then Marcus, noticing my doubt, said: "No demon is male or female by its own nature. For such <term>passions</term> <note>original: *passiones*; in the philosophical sense, these are "undergoings" or characteristics that belong to physical, "composite" bodies made of flesh and bone.</note> belong only to composite beings. The bodies of demons, however, are **simple**; they are easy to lead and bend, and naturally suited to take on any configuration.

But there is this difference: clouds are driven into various shapes by external winds, whereas demons, by their own purpose and as they themselves wish, vary the forms of their bodies. At one moment, they contract their mass into a smaller shape; at another, they extend themselves into a longer one."

# ON DEMONS.

Just as it seems to happen with **worms** <note>original: *lumbricis*; the author uses the flexibility of worms as a biological analogy for the "soft" or "yielding" substance of spirits.</note> on account of their better substance and being very easy to guide: not only does a difference in size occur in them, but they also vary in multiform shapes and colors; for the body of a demon is prepared by nature for both. For by the same reason that its nature is easily yielding, it is thus transformed into various species of shapes. Indeed, because it is <term>aerial</term> <note>original: *aëreum*; meaning composed of air rather than solid flesh, which allows for transparency and change.</note>, it takes on different colors just like the air. But while air is colored from the outside <note>such as by the setting sun or reflections.</note>, the body of a demon receives the appearance of colors from the internal action of its <term>imagination</term> <note>original: *phantasiæ*; in this context, it refers to the power of the mind to project an internal image onto the spirit's physical form.</note>. Just as our cheeks turn pale when we are terrified, but redden when we are affected by shame, as the soul is affected in this or that way. It must be thought of demons in the same way, with such <term>passions</term> <note>original: *passiones*; here meaning physical reactions or "undergoings" triggered by internal emotional states.</note> being transferred into the body by the same logic. For these beings also transfer the types of colors from within into their own bodies; wherefore each one of the demons, having chosen its own shape, transforms its body, bringing out a certain appearance of color to the very edge of the body, and thus it appears as a man, and soon after it encounters one as a woman, or roars in the manner of a lion, leaps like a leopard, barks like a dog, and sometimes transforms itself into the shape of a wineskin or a vessel: and while it changes all such forms in turn, it [possesses] none of them [permanently]...

...and recognizes its owners. **Gnats**, however, and **mice**, and similar creatures, possess a narrower and more indistinct power; they do not recognize the hole from which they emerged, nor the place to which they have traveled, nor where a thing ought to be brought. Instead, they possess only a single <term>imagination</term> <note>In this context, *imaginatio* refers to the internal mental faculty of forming images, which in demons is the mechanism by which they physically alter their appearance.</note>, namely that of food. 

In this same way, the many and diverse kinds of **demons** <note>original: *dæmonum*</note> differ among themselves. Indeed, among these, the **fiery** and **aerial** demons possess an imaginative power that is quite varied, distinct, and discrete, capable of taking on whatever imaginable form they might choose. For they shape themselves according to this very image. 

By contrast, the **light-shunning** <note>original: *lucifugum*; literally "fleeing the light," referring to subterranean or deep-earth spirits who avoid the sun.</note> genus of demons is quite different. This was Ficino’s influential idea that a single, true theology existed in antiquity, passed down through a chain of "enlightened" pagan thinkers before being perfected in Christianity.</note>. Aglaophemus was initiated into the sacred rites of **Orpheus**; Pythagoras succeeded Aglaophemus in theology; Philolaus followed Pythagoras, and was the teacher of our divine Plato. 

Thus, one school of ancient theology, consistent with itself in all its parts, was forged from these six theologians in a certain wonderful order, taking its beginnings from Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes.</note> and reaching its total completion in the divine Plato. Moreover, Mercury wrote a great many books pertaining to the knowledge of divine things, in which—O immortal God!—what secret mysteries, what astounding oracles are revealed! He speaks not only as a philosopher, but frequently as a prophet, and he sings of things to come. He foresaw the ruin of the old religion <note>Meaning the pagan Egyptian religion.</note>, the birth of the new faith, the advent of Christ, the future judgment, the resurrection of the age, the glory of the blessed, and the punishment of sinners. Because of this, it happened that **Aurelius Augustine** <note>St. Augustine (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Church Fathers, who discussed Hermes in "The City of God."</note> doubted whether he knew these things by skill in the stars, or...

<meta>The text cuts off here with the catchword "reuel" (from the Latin "reuelatione," meaning revelation), which will begin the next page's discussion on how Hermes received his knowledge.</meta>

[Egyp]tian letters, and being likewise skilled in the Greek language, he communicated the mysteries of the Egyptians to the Greeks by translating them. The purpose of this work is to discourse upon the power and wisdom of God. Since the operations of these are twofold—the first remaining within the very nature of God, while the second is extended to external things—the former conceives the first and eternal world, while the latter brings forth the second and temporal world.<note>Ficino is describing the Neoplatonic and Hermetic view of two realities: the "Intelligible World" (the eternal blueprint in the Divine Mind) and the "Sensible World" (the physical, time-bound universe we inhabit).</note> He discusses most seriously both of these operations and both worlds: what the power of God is, what His wisdom is, by what order they conceive inwardly, and by what progression they bring forth outwardly.

Furthermore, he discusses how those things which have been produced relate to one another, in what ways they agree or differ, and finally, in what manner they look back toward their author. The order of the volume is such that we distinguish it into fourteen dialogues: the first parts of the dialogue are given to **Pimander**;<note>Also known as Poimandres, representing the "Divine Mind" or the "Shepherd of Men" who reveals the truth to Hermes.</note> the second parts are held by **Trismegistus**; the third by **Aesculapius**;<note>Asclepius, named after the Greek god of healing, is depicted here as a disciple of Hermes.</note> and the fourth place is occupied by **Tatius**.<note>Tat, the son and student of Hermes Trismegistus in the Hermetic dialogues.</note> 

Mercury, therefore, intends to instruct Aesculapius and Tatius in divine matters. One who has not learned cannot teach divine things, and we cannot discover by human ingenuity those things which are above nature. Therefore, there is a need for divine light, so that we may look upon the sun itself by the light of the sun.<note>A classic Platonic metaphor: just as we need the sun’s light to see the sun, we need God’s illumination to understand God.</note> But the divine light...

When I was contemplating the nature of things, and raising the sharp edge of my mind toward the heights, with the senses of my body already lulled to sleep—as usually happens to those who are heavy with sleep due to fullness or exhaustion—suddenly it seemed to me that I perceived someone of immense physical magnitude, who, calling me by name, shouted in this manner: "What is it, O <term>Mercury</term><note>original: "Mercuri"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, whom the Renaissance scholars identified with the Roman god Mercury.</note>, that you desire both to hear and to see? What is it that you wish to learn and to understand?" Then I said, "Who then are you?" "I am," he said, "<term>Pimander</term><note>The "Divine Mind" or "Shepherd of Men." In this text, he acts as the revealing deity who grants Hermes secret knowledge of the cosmos.</note>, the Mind of the divine power; see what you desire, and I truly shall be present with you everywhere." "I desire," I said, "to learn the nature of things and to know God." To this he replied: "Embrace me with your mind, and I shall instruct you in all things that you have wished for." When he had said these things, he changed his form, and suddenly revealed all things. For I perceived

What else is it for God to have cried out with a holy word: *"Sprout, grow, and propagate all seeds and my works,"* than that **Mosaic** command: *"Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the earth"*? <note>A direct comparison between the command in the *Poimandres* and Genesis 1:28.</note> 

Soon **Mercury** <note>Hermes Trismegistus.</note> instructs us where the path to the **Mind** <note>original: "mens"; in Hermetic philosophy, the *Mens* is the divine part of the human soul that allows for communion with God.</note> lies open, and what evil error finally leads us away from it. He explains to whom the Mind is present as a bountiful giver of goods, and from whom it is likewise absent. He further shows how, just as we slip and degenerate by certain steps from an intellectual and immortal nature down to perishable things, so too by certain opposite steps we are restored and reintegrated into that prior state of a purified mind. 

**Moses**, by divine appointment, became the leader of the Hebrew flock; **Mercury** became the leader of the Egyptian flock. Now, through holy instruction, he feeds his flock while living an **active life**; then, praising the Father of all things with hymns and thanksgivings, he rises into the light and the **life of contemplation**. This is the summary of the *Pimander*.

### The General Discourse of Mercury to Aesculapius. II.

**G**od and divinity itself—I speak now not of that which is begotten <note>Created or brought into existence.</note>, but of that which is unbegotten <note>original: "ingenitum"; that which has always existed and has no cause.</note>. If, therefore, it is a divine thing, it is essence; but if it is God, it is even above essence. However, this is to be understood in this way: the primary **intelligible** <note>Perceivable by the intellect or "Mind" rather than the physical senses.</note> God exists not for himself, but for us. For that which is intelligible falls under the perception of the one who understands through the senses. Thus, God is not at all "intelligible" to himself; for he is not some other thing existing apart from that which he understands, such that he would be understood by himself. Yet he is something different from us, and for that reason, he is understood by us. But if the **Word** <note>original: "logos"; the divine reason or creative order.</note> is intelligible, then he is not God. If he is as God, then certainly not as the Word, lest the Word be spoken of as something distinct. Furthermore, everything that is moved is moved not in a thing that is itself in motion, but in something stable. That which moves the object also remains constant, for it is impossible for the mover to be agitated at the same time as the object it moves.

<term>AESCULAPIUS.</term> In what way then, Trismegistus, are the things in the world changed along with those things that move? For you used to say that the **wandering spheres** <note>The planets.</note> are moved by the **fixed sphere** <note>original: "aplane sphæra"; the outermost celestial sphere containing the fixed stars, which was believed to drive the motion of the inner planets.</note>.

<term>TRISMEGISTUS.</term> That is not motion, O Aesculapius, but resistance. For they do not travel in the same direction, but in a contrary manner. This opposition, however, contains a stable reverberation of motion. For the repercussion of the station <note>The "station" or "standing still" refers to the point where a planet appears to stop before changing direction; Hermes argues this stability is what allows for the ordered movement of the universe.</note>...

<summary>In this dialogue, Hermes explains the nature of God as existing beyond "essence" and explores the physics of the cosmos, arguing that all motion requires a stable, unmoving foundation.</summary>

For do you think the **Bears** <note>original: "arctos"; the constellations Ursa Major and Ursa Minor (the Great and Little Dipper).</note>, which you know never rise nor set, but perpetually circle the same point, do not move, or rather that they stand still?

**AESCULAPIUS.** They move, O Trismegistus.

**TRIS.** By what motion, Aesculapius?

**AESCULAPIUS.** By a motion that runs forever around the same point.

**TRIS.** But truly, that circulation is both the same and around the same point: it is a motion held in place by stability. For the "around the same" prevents the motion from wandering, while that which is above it remains fixed. Thus, the contrary agitation is firm, perpetually stabilized by that very opposition. I will place an example before your eyes from the living things on earth: just as when a man swims (while the water is surely flowing), the counter-thrust of his hands and feet together makes the man stay in place, so that he is not swept away with the water or submerged in it.

**AESCULAPIUS.** You have brought forward a very clear example, O Trismegistus.

**TRIS.** Whatever is moved in a state of stability, therefore, is moved by that stability. Therefore, the **motion of every living creature** <note>original: "motus animalis"; the "soul-driven" motion that animates a physical body.</note> that consists of matter is by no means caused by those things which are outside the world. ## B

You are mistaken, O Aesculapius. Those things which are vast and most full of all things, you consider to be empty.

**AESCULAPIUS.** How can that be, O Trismegistus?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** Air is indeed a <term>body</term> <note>original: "corpus"; in Hermetic philosophy, air and spirit are considered "subtle bodies" that occupy space, meaning a vacuum cannot exist.</note>; that body penetrates all other things and, running through them, fills everything. For a body is of such a kind that it is not composed of material parts. Thus it happens that whatever things you call "empty" are actually full of air. Therefore, those things ought to be called hollow rather than empty; for they both exist and are full of air and <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus"; here referring to the "pneuma" or life-force that permeates the cosmos.</note>.

**AESCULAPIUS.** This reasoning is invincible and beyond doubt, Trismegistus: air is a body. This body flows through all else and, by flowing in, fills all things. What then shall we say the "Place" is in which everything is moved?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** It is <term>incorporeal</term> <note>original: "incorporeum"; something that lacks physical mass or dimensions, serving as the container for the material universe.</note>, O Aesculapius.

**AESCULAPIUS.** But what is the Incorporeal?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** It is <term>Mind</term> <note>original: "Mens"</note> and <term>Reason</term> <note>original: "ratio"</note> embracing itself, free from every bodily mass, a stranger to error, <term>impassible</term> <note>original: "impassibilis"; meaning it cannot be affected, changed, or made to suffer by external forces.</note>, intangible, standing by itself, purifying and preserving all things: whose rays are the Good, the Truth, the primordial Light, and the first form of souls.

**AESCULAPIUS.** What then is God?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** He is none of these things, yet He is the cause of them all; a certain presence within the whole and a presence within each individual thing, nor does He allow anything not to exist. All things are procreated from those things which are. Out of nothing, however, nothing comes. For those things which do not exist at all have no nature...

**AESCULAPIUS.** What then? Do you say that God exists only at certain times? <note>Aesculapius is asking if God is subject to time or temporary existence.</note>

**TRISMEGISTUS.** God is certainly not <term>Mind</term> <note>original: "mens"; in Hermetic philosophy, Mind is a created faculty, and God is the source or "Father" of that faculty rather than the faculty itself.</note>. But rather, He is the cause by which Mind exists; nor is He <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus"; the vital breath or pneuma that animates the world.</note>, but the cause through which Spirit exists; nor is He Light, but the cause through which Light exists. For this reason, it is necessary to worship God with those two names which belong to Him alone, and which are entirely unsuitable for any other. Indeed, among those who are called gods (aside from Him), whether they be <term>demons</term> <note>original: "daemones"; here referring to intermediary spirits or lesser divine beings, not necessarily "evil" spirits in the modern sense.</note> or men, none can be so good as the one God. For He Himself is the Good itself, and nothing else besides the Good. All other things are separate from the very nature of the Good. The Body and the Soul have no place within them that can contain the Good. For goodness is as vast as the existence of all things—both <term>corporeal</term> <note>having a physical body</note> and <term>incorporeal</term> <note>lacking a physical body, such as thoughts or spirits</note>, both <term>sensible</term> <note>perceived by the physical senses</note> and <term>intelligible</term> <note>perceived only by the intellect or mind</note>. That is the Good; that is God. Therefore, beware that you never call anything else "good," for this would be a profane error. ### COMMENTARIES.

*The second section discusses how God is intelligible in a rational way only to man; and from the center, the pole, the location, and the forms of things, he hunts for God himself* <note>original: "uenatur ipsum deum"; a metaphorical expression for the intellectual pursuit or seeking of the divine through the study of the physical cosmos.</note> *around whom, in whom, and by whom all things are moved—stable, immovable, and continually remaining always the same to Himself—and that nothing in the world can be empty. This clearly* <note>original catchword: "innuit"; suggests or hints.</note>

### COMMENTARY

*The third part recounts again how, from the depths of formless matter illuminated by forms acting as holy splendors, all things proceeded to their birth in their own order, and how the blessed minds of the heavens fulfill the task committed to them by the highest Father.* *And it teaches that man was born for a twin duty: namely, for the contemplation of eternal things, and for the judgment of good and evil, and for the governance of human affairs through both the invention of various arts and through wisdom.* *To man, indeed, the heavens, the earth, the herbs, the sprouts, and the whole harmony of the world and the most beautiful order of things, most abundantly supply the material for contemplation and for lifting himself up toward the divine.* *For nature is like a single book full of divinity and a mirror of divine things <note>The "Book of Nature" is a theological concept suggesting that God can be understood by studying the natural world as if it were a secondary scripture.</note>.* *Thus far the Sacred Sermon.* *I warn, however, that this third dialogue must be read cautiously; for the pagans <note>original: "gentiles"; refers to non-Christian or polytheistic philosophers.</note> explain it in a purely pagan manner, and they make it...*

# PIMANDER.

The choice, which is honorable to the one choosing, not only makes the man who chooses divine <note>original: "deum reddidit"; literally "renders him a god," reflecting the Hermetic belief in the deification of the soul through knowledge</note>, but also demonstrates his piety toward God to others. God is certainly free from the blame for the evils that come from us; for we are the ones who prefer evil things to good things. You see, O son, that we must transcend the heavenly bodies, leave behind the choirs of spirits <term>Daemones: in Hermetic philosophy, these are intermediary spirits or celestial intelligences that govern the lower world, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense</term>, and rise above the orbits of the stars and their motions, so that we may reach toward the one and only God.

For the Good is an insuperable thing, infinite in its bound—having no beginning in itself, yet having a beginning for us in our human knowledge <term>Gnosis: a deep, experiential knowledge of the divine</term>. Such knowledge, however, is not the start of the Good itself, but it provides the starting point for us to know it. Let us therefore embrace this First Principle <note>original: "Principium"; the source or origin of all things</note>. For once this is known, we shall travel through all things with the greatest speed. It is difficult, however, for one who is leaving behind familiar and present things to cross over to higher...

A beginning, however, is not a beginning of the principle itself, but of something else. The Monad, therefore, as the principle, contains every number while being contained by none, and it generates every number while being generated by no number. 

Whatever is generated is surely imperfect, divisible, increasing, and decreasing. But to that which is perfect, none of these things happen. Indeed, that which grows, grows by the power of the Monad. But it fades away through its own weakness when it can no longer contain the Monad. 

Let this <term>image of God: original "imago dei"; the conceptual representation of the divine essence</term> be described for you, O <term>Tat: the son and disciple of Hermes Trismegistus in the Hermetic dialogues</term>, according to my ability. If you consider it diligently and come to know it with your internal eyes, believe me, my son, you will find the way of ascent to the heights. Moreover, the image itself will lead you; for the vision has a certain power, and it seizes those who burn with the desire to behold it...

## COMMENTARY.

The fourth discourse encourages us to take hold of wisdom, which is the open <term>Mixing Bowl: original "crater"; a metaphor for a vessel of divine essence or mind into which souls are "dipped" to receive enlightenment</term> of the divine Mind. Any soul that immerses itself in this bowl becomes a participant in higher knowledge and looks upward toward the Mind. But truly, in order to lift herself up to it, the soul must transcend the heavens and go beyond the orbit of the stars and their movements, leaving the choirs of the blessed far below. 

Then she strives toward the one and only God—the insurmountable and boundlessly infinite Good. When she gazes upon this, she looks down on all material bodies and considers the life we live here as mere misery, focused solely on the desire for the incorporeal Good. Yet no one is able to immerse themselves in this divine bowl who does not hate their own body <note>In Hermetic thought, "hating the body" refers to rejecting material desires that distract from spiritual growth</note>, and who has not loved God himself rather than their own self. One must neglect mortal things and cling to divine things alone, stay with them alone, meditate on them alone, and burn with passion for them. Presently, through the analogy of unity and numbers, this discourse raises us to contemplate the true <term>Monad: the singular, indivisible source of all existence</term> and the true numbers of nature. This is "The Mixing Bowl."
