He places all other things before your eyes, but He Himself remains a secret, as one who enjoys eternal life. Indeed, <term>phantasia: the power of imagination or the realm of appearances</term> deals only with things that are created, in which nothing exists except the process of being born. 

But that unique Being is uncreated, and incomprehensible to the imagination. Since all things become clear through Him, He shines back through all things and in all things. He appears especially to those to whom He wishes to communicate knowledge. You, therefore, O my son <term>Tat: the son and disciple of Hermes Trismegistus, representing the initiate seeking wisdom</term>, must first with pious prayers beseech the Lord and Father—the Unique One, the One, and the source from whom the "one" comes—that you may be worthy of His mercy. 

In this way, you will finally be able to perceive so great a God, if even a single ray of His light shines kindly upon your intelligence. For only the hidden power of <term>intellection: the capacity for direct spiritual or mental understanding, as opposed to sensory perception</term> perceives things that are hidden. Therefore, if you look with the eyes of the mind, O Tat, He will—believe me—be revealed to you. God, being entirely free from envy, shines everywhere through every single particle of the world, and makes Himself so well-known that you may not only understand Him, but even (so to speak) with your very hands...

...manifest. <note>The text begins mid-word, completing the thought from the previous page: that God is not more "manifest" than his works.</note> He is hidden, yet again he is the most manifest of all. Shall I sing of those things you have created, or rather of those you have not created? Shall I sing of those things which you have perhaps brought into the light out of the darkness, or of those which still lie hidden, tucked away in your **secret bosom** <note>original: "arcano sinu"; a poetic reference to the unmanifest state of potential before creation</note>? 

Through what, finally, shall I dedicate my hymns to you? ### COMMENTARY

*The fifth book teaches that God is equally hidden and yet shines through every single particle of the world. All things which present themselves to us are His images, so that the wonderful and most beautiful order of things clearly declares the Ordainer; and individual things, circumscribed by their own certain limits, declare a Lord and Author, whom the Sun—the king and prince of the stars—obeys and serves, whom he fears and whom he respects. In short, the entire structure of the universe declares its Craftsman. Presently, it brings forth a more confident judgment concerning the divine internal generation: that it is the essence of God to conceive and to make all things, so that it would be impossible for God to exist unless He were always acting upon all things. For the divine <term>Logos</term> <note>original: "logos"; the Greek term for Word, Reason, or the rational principle that governs and creates the universe</note> is so much "all things" that He is "nothing of all things," in whom the corporeal and incorporeal being, and nothingness itself, harmonize and coincide. Finally, <term>Mercury</term> <note>The Latin name for Hermes Trismegistus</note> finishes and ends the dialogue in songs of divine praise.*

**T**he Good <note>original: "Bonum"; in Hermetic philosophy, "The Good" is not just a moral quality but the very essence of God’s life-giving nature</note>, O Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of healing, here addressed as a student of Hermes</note>, is found in nothing else except in the one God; indeed, the Good is always God Himself. Therefore, the essence <term>essentia</term> <note>The fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</note> of all motion and knowledge must be God. Nothing is deprived of this essence; it possesses within itself a stable action, lacking in nothing, providing an infinite and superabundant supply. This is the one principle of all things, extending good and pouring forth good. 

Whenever I name the "Good," understand it as that which is all good and which is always good. This belongs to the one God alone. For He is not in need of anything, such that He might become evil by desiring to acquire it; nor can any loss ever occur to Him, such that He would be afflicted by pain after a loss. For He is greater than any portion of evil, nor is there anything stronger than Him by which He could be conquered. No injury can fall upon Him, by which He might be provoked or harassed into a fit of anger <note>original: "excandescat"; literally to catch fire or glow with heat, used here for the heat of rage</note>. 

Nothing escapes His yoke, whereby He might feel indignant or angry through contempt, nor is there anything wiser than He, which might strike Him with envy <note>original: "aemulationem"; the Latin implies a sense of rivalry or jealous competition</note>. Therefore, since these things do not happen to Him, nothing remains of His nature except the Good itself. Just as none of those things which are evil exist in this essence, so also the Good is found in nothing else. For in all other individual things, other qualities are present, both in the small and in the great, and even in

...[except in His own nature,] which relates to those things according to the One; and also in the greatest living being <note>original: "animali maximo"; the Hermetic tradition views the entire universe or Cosmos as a single, living entity</note> of all and the most powerful, which certainly fills all things born with <term>passions</term> <note>original: "passionibus"; here "passion" refers to the philosophical concept of being acted upon or undergoing change, rather than just emotion</note>. For generation <note>The process of being born, created, or coming into existence</note> is a certain kind of passion. Where there is passion, there is in no way the Good; where the Good is, no passion is ever placed. Where there is day, there is in no way night; where there is night, there is not even day. For this reason, the Good cannot exist in the process of generation. It remains, therefore, only in that which is <term>unbegotten</term> <note>original: "ingenitũ"; that which was never created and has no beginning, i.e., God</note>. 

However, just as matter is granted a participation in all things, so also the world is "good" through its participation in the Good. I say "good" insofar as it also produces all things; in that specific part, the world is good, but in all other respects it is not good. For it is subject to change <note>original: "passibilis"; literally "capable of suffering change"</note> and is in motion, and is moreover the cause of all passions. In man, furthermore, "good" is defined by comparison to evil. Indeed, that which is not excessively evil, or is even the "lesser evil," we call "good" among men. Thus it happens that our "good" is nothing other than the smallest portion of evil. 

From this it also follows that a good of this kind cannot be separated from evil. For this human good is tainted by the mixture of evils. Once it is infected, it no longer remains a further good; and if it does not remain, it is turned into evil. Therefore, the Good itself exists in God alone. For this reason, O Aesculapius, only the *name* of "good" exists in man; the nature of the Good does not exist in him at all. For it is not...

## COMMENTARY.

*Sextus <note>Likely referring to a commentator or authority cited by the editor to explain the Hermetic text</note> maintains this: that in God alone is found the Good and the nature of the Good—that is, Goodness itself—as well as the nature of Beauty, Power, and Wisdom. In the world, however, there is only the name of the "good," and he convicts men who are blinded by their errors. He warns us to shrink from vices and teaches the path that leads us to Goodness itself and Beauty itself: namely, piety joined with knowledge <note>original: "cognitio"; in this tradition, this refers to 'Gnosis' or direct spiritual realization of divine truths</note>. Ignorant mortals, wandering from the path of piety, can never reach this. So says Sextus.*

### That the greatest evil for men is to be ignorant of God. VII.

**W**hither are you rushing, drunken mortals, you who have drunk deep of the unmixed wine of ignorance? Since you cannot bear it, vomit it out! Live soberly; look with the eyes of the mind. If not all of you can do this, at least let those who are able do so. The plague of ignorance subverts the whole earth and corrupts the soul enclosed within the chains of the body, nor does it allow her to take up the path of salvation. Do not permit yourselves to be submerged in the lake of corruption and death. Breathe now, breathe! Return to the fountain of life, and seek him who will lead you into the sanctuary <note>original: "adytum"; the innermost, most sacred part of a temple, where the deity's presence was felt</note> of truth...

...return to your senses! There, you will find a bright light mixed with no darkness; there, no one raves with drunkenness, but all are sober and watchful, and with the eyes of the mind <note>original: "mentis oculis"; in Hermetic thought, the 'eye of the mind' is the faculty of spiritual perception that sees beyond physical appearances.</note>, they gaze more sharply upon Him who wishes to be seen. He is perceived neither by the ears, nor discerned by the eyes, nor brought forth by speech: the mind alone beholds Him, the mind alone proclaims Him. 

But first, it is necessary to strip off the garment <note>original: "ueſtem"; a metaphor for the physical body, which was seen by some ancient philosophers as a restrictive covering for the soul.</note> you carry around: the clothing of ignorance, the foundation of wickedness, the chain of corruption, the dark veil, living death, a sentient corpse, a walking tomb, and finally, a thief in your own house. This garment is a flatterer who hates you; while it hates, it envies. Of such a kind is this hostile shadow in which you are wrapped. 

It drags you down toward itself, lest by chance, beholding the beauty of truth and the Good that is so near, you might come to hate its depravity—or lest you might eventually perceive the snares it constantly plots against you. This body dulls and blunts the edge of your inner senses; thick matter <note>original: "materia"; refers to the heavy, physical substance of the world which "suffocates" the spiritual light of the soul.</note> suffocates the mind, intoxicating it with abominable and loathsome pleasure, so that you might never hear or see those things which by right ought to be heard and, above all else, gazed upon.

### COMMENTARIES.

*The eighth [chapter] teaches primarily that the celestial bodies constantly preserve one and the same tenor <note>original: "tenorem"; meaning a continuous course or steady condition.</note>, which they first received from their father. It also teaches that death and destruction first appear among earthly living bodies, but that the very name of "death" and the "destruction" of bodies is empty. This is because the bodies themselves are changed, but they do not perish. Rather, immortal matter exchanges the qualities themselves—which are the idols and images of the Ideas <note>This refers to the Platonic concept that physical things are just "shadows" or "images" of perfect, eternal "Ideas" or "Forms."</note>—with which God had wished to adorn it. And man is an immortal living being <term>animal</term> <note>From the Latin "anima" (soul); here meaning a being possessed of a soul.</note>, yet dissoluble <note>original: "dissolubile"; meaning the physical form can be broken down even if the essence is immortal.</note>, the bond and the knot of all nature, being partly corporeal and partly incorporeal. He was born in the likeness of the world and capable of a higher mind, so that he might comprehend the sensible world and, through his mind, rise toward the highest Mind in happy contemplation. This concludes the eighth.*

od. And like a skilled farmer, whatever has grown too large, he prunes away, so that at fixed intervals of time, it may flourish again. Nor is there anything to which the world <term>mundus</term> <note>original: "mundus"; the Latin term for the world, often implying a clean or ordered system.</note> itself does not provide life. Bodies, however, are made from matter in diverse ways: some of these consist of earth, some of water, others of air, and very many of fire; yet all are certainly composite. Some, however, are more dense, while others are simpler. Some are heavy, others are light. The speed of the world's motion, through its very variety, brings about the generation of qualities. For the frequent breathing <term>spiratio</term> <note>original: "spiratio"; refers to a cosmic respiration or "spirit" that animates physical matter.</note> provides quality to bodies along with an abundance of life. 

God, therefore, is the father of the Cosmos <term>Cosmi</term>, that is, of the world. But the Cosmos is the father of those things which are in the cosmos; and the Cosmos is indeed the son of God. Those things which are in the cosmos remain under the dominion of the cosmos, and it is rightly called the "Cosmos"; for indeed it "adorns" <note>original Greek: "κοσμει̃" (kosmei); the author notes that the word "Cosmos" comes from the Greek word for "to adorn" or "to order."</note>—that is, it beautifies—all things through the variety of their generation, as well as by the unceasing and eternal operation of life’s necessity, the speed of the elements, their mixing, and the order of those things brought into being. 

Therefore, the cosmos itself—that is, the "adornment"—is named both by necessity and by merit. It is the sense-perception and intellection of all living things, which flow into them from external things, inspired by that which contains them. Moreover, whatever the Cosmos receives from itself...

### COMMENTARY.

*The ninth lesson instructs men, who, although they all use understanding, nevertheless conceive material things from the seeds of <term>demons</term> <note>original: "dæmonum spermatibus"; in this context, "demons" refers to intermediary spirits or supernatural influences, often viewed in Hermeticism as the source of earthly impulses and passions.</note>—whose presence no part of the world is without—and being pregnant, they finally bring forth adulteries, lustful acts, murders, parricides, and every kind of crime. Yet essential and spiritual men conceive every ornament of the virtues with God as the sower, and they bring forth every good duty of virtue. For the seeds of God are few, yet they are indeed great, beautiful, and good, and far superior to the innumerable multitude of vices. However, those who follow these seeds neither please the common crowd, nor does the crowd please them; they are ultimately thought to be insane and they draw ridicule, because the earth is the seat and province of wickedness. Yet the world was formed by that law, so that receiving all seeds from God, it might become an <term>instrument</term> <note>original: "organum"; a tool or vessel through which the divine works.</note> worthy of divinity, and all things in the marvelous beauty of fair order would proceed toward their birth. In which order they persevere, and finally attain their end; which would certainly happen, unless the enemy [coming...]*

## The Key of Hermes Trismegistus to Tat. X.

**I** dedicated yesterday’s discourse to you, O Asclepius; wherefore it is right to dedicate today’s to Tat, and it is all the more worthwhile because the present discussion will be a sort of concise summary <note>original: "compendiaria... summa"</note> of everything we have said to him before. God, and the Father, and the Good, O Tat, have the same nature, or rather the same activity <note>original: "actum"; in this philosophical context, "act" or "activity" refers to the outward expression of a thing's inner essence.</note>. For that is the name for growth and <term>divinity</term> <note>original: "divinationis"; here meaning the process of becoming divine or the quality of the divine.</note>, which concerns both the mutable and the immutable—that is, the human and the divine. Each of these He wills to exist. But elsewhere His activity (as we have shown in other places) concerns things divine and human, which must indeed be understood in this. The will of this activity is His essence: to wish for all things to have their being <note>original: "subsistere".</note>. What is God, and the Father, and the Good, if not the very "being" <note>original: "esse".</note> of all these things that do not yet exist? Because He receives nothing, He wills all things to be. I do not say, O Tat, that He *makes* all things; for a maker, if failing over a long period of time, is unworthy of the name. If He were merely a maker, He might sometimes act and sometimes cease, being deficient in both quantity and quality; sometimes arranging things of a certain kind and size, and at other times their opposites. But God is both Father and the Good, by the very fact that He is all things. Therefore, He can command such things for Himself. For He wills this to be, and it is. And He is truly Himself in the highest degree, for all other things exist because of Him. Indeed, it is the property of the Good, O Tat, to make itself known. That is the Good, O Tat.

The world is the first living being; Man is the second living being after the world, but the first among all other living creatures. Indeed, whatever gift of the soul is granted to others, Man also possesses. He is judged to be not only "not good," but even evil, insofar as he is mortal. For the world is also "not good" because it is in motion; yet it is not "evil," because it is immortal.

And so, by the power of these two—namely, man and the world—individual things are governed. Finally, all things are subjected to the One.

### COMMENTARY

*The tenth book constantly asserts that God is absolutely all things, which individual things contract through <term>participation</term> <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "participation" refers to the way finite things derive their being and qualities from a higher, divine source.</note>. Nevertheless, it asserts that God is the Father, and good by the very fact that He Himself is all things. Soon after, he discusses the rapture of the soul in silence, where what is discerned by the eyes of the mind is neither lawful to reveal, nor is the freedom to reveal it granted. As for what he adds regarding the <term>transformation of animals</term> <note>original: "animalium transformatione" - a reference to metempsychosis or the soul moving into different forms.</note>, the following discourse of the same Hermes declares that it is not a literal fiction of words, but an allegory of fiction that should be followed, when he says: "For another..."*

<meta>catchword: For</meta>

<summary>Hermes describes the extraordinary power of human nature, famously defining man as a "mortal god" who can span the distance between earth and heaven. The commentary clarifies that God is the totality of all things and warns that the soul's highest visions are inexpressible and its transformations allegorical.</summary>

# PIMANDER

likewise [master] this art: be higher than all loftiness, deeper than any depth. Gather within yourself all the sensations of your experiences: of fire, water, the dry, and the moist. Be present at once in all parts of the world—in heaven, on earth, and in the sea. Live through every age; dwell beyond the shell <note>original: "utrem," literally a leather bottle or wineskin, used here as a metaphor for the physical body as a temporary container for the soul.</note> of your little body, and believe that nothing perishes through death. Comprehend all these things at once—places, times, masses, qualities, and quantities—and in this way you will be able to understand God.

On the contrary, if you sink your soul into the body and cast it down, prostrating yourself in the mire <note>original: "coenum," meaning mud or filth, often used in Neo-Platonic texts to describe the degradation of the soul when it focuses solely on material things.</note> with these words: "I know nothing, nor am I even able to know; I dread the vast depths of the sea; I cannot fly into heaven; I do not know what I am now, and I do not know what I shall be hereafter"—what have you to do with God? For you, being wicked and a slave to a foul body, cannot perceive that which is Beautiful and Good. Indeed, the ultimate depravity is to fail to recognize God.

But to be confident and to hope that one might eventually find the Good is a divine path, leading to the Good by a straight route. It is easy and accessible; it will meet you everywhere as you go—whether you are walking or sailing, speaking by day or night, or even while you are silent. For there is nothing in the nature of things that does not bear within itself some image of divinity. <term>TRIS.</term> <note>TRIS: Short for Hermes Trismegistus, the seeker and student in this dialogue.</note> Is God not invisible?

->MERCURIUS TRISM.<-

...[is He] God? **MIND.** Speak more reverently, Trismegistus: for who is more brilliant than He? He fashioned all things for this very reason, so that you might perceive Him through each individual thing. This is the goodness of God, this is His power: that He shines through all things. There is nothing—even among incorporeal things—that is invisible. The mind itself is seen through the act of understanding <term>intellectio|the mental perception or intellectual "sight" of the soul</term>, while God is perceived through His works <note>original: "operatione," referring to the divine activity or the manifestation of God's power in the physical creation</note>. Let these things be explained to you thus far, Trismegistus; all the rest you shall now search out for yourself, and you will not be deceived by a false image of the truth.

### COMMENTARY.

*The eleventh treatise concerning the Mind, full of divine discourse, declares that eternity depends on God, the world depends on eternity, time depends on the world, and change <term>transmutationem|the constant shifting and flux of the material world</term> depends on time; and from change depend both death and life. It demonstrates most gracefully—using both logical reasons and analogies—that no power, whether divine, human, or of the beings in the heavens or the underworld, is comparable to the insurmountable power of God. He is the One, who, since He cannot be idle, is always making all things. You may rightly understand this as being said regarding the eternal generation of the Word <note>original: "verbi generatione," a phrase used by Renaissance commentators to link the Hermetic "Logos" with the Christian concept of Christ as the eternal Word of God</note>: for he says that it was necessary for the divine work to be present so that those things might exist which are being made, which were made, and which shall be made in the future. This is life, this is beauty, this is goodness, and finally, this is God, and the life of all...*

<summary>This page concludes a dialogue on the visibility of God through His creation and begins a scholarly commentary on the hierarchy of existence, linking God to eternity, time, and life.</summary>

->## HERMES TRISMEGISTUS <-

...of irrational creatures (as I believe) are passions: therefore, the mind is a certain <term>passion</term><gloss>In this philosophical context, "passion" (passio) does not just mean strong emotion, but the state of being acted upon or "affected" by an external force.</gloss>, for in this way it is shaped by passions. 

**TRISMEGISTUS.** Excellent, my good son! How nobly you inquire; it is only right that I answer you. All incorporeal things that exist within bodies are <term>passible</term><gloss>Capable of being affected, changed, or moved by something else; the opposite of being "impassible" or unchangeable.</gloss>—indeed, they are properly called passions. Every bodily movement, even within the bodies themselves, is moved by the mind; and movement is a form of passion. 

Therefore, both that which is moved and that which moves are affected: the latter as the ruler, the former as the subject. But when the mind is separated from the body, it is liberated from these passions. Yet truly, my son, nothing anywhere is entirely "impassible," for all things are capable of being affected. 

However, "passion" and "the passible" differ most in this: that one acts, while the other is acted upon. Bodies, by their own nature, also act; for they are either immobile or they are moved. Whichever of these occurs, it is a passion. But incorporeal things are always <term>operating</term><gloss>From the Latin "operari," meaning to work, act, or produce an effect.</gloss>, and for that reason they are passible. 

Do not let these names trouble you. For "operation" and "passion" are the same thing; nevertheless, there is no harm in using a more honorable term <note>original: "uocabulo tamé magis honorando." Hermes suggests that while "being acted upon" and "acting" are philosophically linked, we prefer to call the Mind's work "operation" to reflect its higher status.</note>. 

**TAT.** You have given a very clear explanation of these things, O father. 

**TRISMEGISTUS.** Consider this further, my son: that God himself has bestowed these two gifts—<term>Speech</term><gloss>In Latin "sermo," translating the Greek "logos," which implies both spoken word and the rational principle behind it.</gloss> and **Mind**—upon man alone of all the living creatures. These indeed...

And it is no less ridiculous than to call that body sterile; for calling it "immobile" signifies nothing else than something sterile.

Consider this whole matter generally, O son: everything that is in the world is moved either by increasing or decreasing. But that which is moved also lives; yet individual living things do not [have] the same...

-># HERMES TRISMEGISTUS<-

...is necessary to be. For at the same time, the whole universe, as it exists, is indeed entirely immobile, yet its parts are mobile in every direction. Nevertheless, nothing is subject to corruption <note>original Latin: *corruptioni*. In this context, it refers to total annihilation or the permanent ceasing to exist.</note>, but certain false names disturb men. For birth is not the creation of life, but the unfolding of a hidden life; nor is change death, but rather a concealment. Since these things are so, all things are immortal. 

The matter of life is spirit, and the mind <note>original: *mens*, or *Nous* in the Greek source. This refers to the divine intellect.</note> is the matter of the soul. From the mind flows everything that lives. Therefore, every living thing, through the mind, remains immortal. 

But of all things, man is most immortal, for he receives God and is conformed to the divine essence. For to him alone, out of every kind of living thing, God himself comes: by night through dreams, and by day more frequently through portents, by which he foretells all future things to him—through birds <note>The practice of augury, or reading the flight of birds.</note>, through intestines <note>The practice of haruspicy, or inspecting the internal organs of sacrificed animals.</note>, through spirit, and through the Sibyl <note>A legendary prophetess of antiquity who spoke with divine inspiration.</note>. Because of these things, it is truly said that man knows:

->*What is, what has been, and what is soon to come.*<-

Moreover, I would wish you to observe this first of all, my son: that each of the other kinds of living things inhabits its own province of the world—the aquatic ones in the water, the terrestrial ones on the earth, and the winged ones in the air. Man, however, makes use of them all: the earth, water, air, and fire. He looks up to the heaven and reaches it with his perception; God...

<summary>Hermes explains that "death" is merely the concealment of life rather than its destruction, asserting that all things are immortal. He highlights man's unique status as a being who communicates with God through various forms of divination and who, unlike other animals, masters all four elements.</summary>

### COMMENTARY.

*The twelfth section concerning the lower mind—which is an image of the primary mind, or a certain footprint of it—proceeding after the precise definition of the primary mind, associates it with individual souls. However, in irrational beings, this "mind" is merely nature, whereas in humans it is reason. Those men who are deprived of the benefit of reason are snatched away in the manner of wild beasts by a certain flaming impulse toward the fulfillment of their desires. They set no limit to their lust, nor do they find an end to their evils and passions; they suffer by fate and divine decree, and they give*

<summary>Hermes concludes that God is the "All" through which everything exists, defining true worship as the avoidance of evil, followed by a commentary on the difference between animal instinct and human reason.</summary>

### COMMENTARY

The thirteenth book <note>original: *Tertiusdecimus*. This refers to Book XIII of the *Corpus Hermeticum*, often called "The Secret Sermon on the Mountain."</note> concerns the secret mystery of rebirth, before which no one was saved; the author of this rebirth is the Son of God <note>original: *dei filius homo*. You, O Christian, read the rest; for if you have been reformed by a new rebirth in God through the Son of God, and have driven away ignorance, sadness, desire, injustice, luxury, deception, envy, fraud, anger, rashness, and malice—those twelve horrible avengers of darkness—then rejoice with your whole mind. Having attained the ten opposing powers through the piety of God <note>In Hermetic thought, the twelve "vices" or avengers are replaced by ten "virtues" or divine powers during the process of rebirth.</note>, remember to give thanks to God the Reformer with all the vigor of your mind. Burn entirely with His love; having become entirely spirit and reborn of the spirit, sing a hymn of piety and maintain the purity of your rebirth. Thus, having turned yourself completely toward God the Parent and His Son, the author of rebirth, you will have gathered this fruit from this thirteenth book—or at least your mind will be stirred by its own goodness toward such pious contemplation.

**S**ince my son Tatius <note>original: *Tatius*. Usually referred to as Tat in Hermetic literature, he is the son and disciple of Hermes.</note> (while you were absent) wished to learn the nature of all things, and since he himself did not want me to delay—being younger and having only recently approached the knowledge of each matter—I was compelled to speak at great length so that his insight might be easy and unhindered. Therefore, I have judged it worthwhile to select the more important points from many and now summarize the preceding discussion for you. For I am permitted to run through certain mysteries with you, as you are one skilled in the nature of things.

Everything that is perceived by the senses has been made, and is made daily. Created things <term>genita</term> <note>original: *genita*. This refers to things that are "begotten" or brought into existence, contrasting with the "unbegotten" or eternal Creator.</note> do not come from themselves, but are made by another. There are many created things, each evident to the senses and differing from one another, not at all being similar. Whatever things are brought into being proceed from another. There is, therefore, some Maker <term>factor</term> <note>The "Factor" or "Maker" in Hermetic thought is the divine architect/creator who brings form to the material world.</note> of these things, and He is uncreated <term>ingenitus</term>, so that He is more ancient than the things created. For we have said that created things flow from another. 

Nothing, however, can be more ancient than created things except that which is uncreated. Indeed, the Maker is more powerful, unique, and alone truly wise in all things, since nothing at all precedes Him. He also rules over the multitude, the magnitude, the action, the continuity, and the differences of all created things. Furthermore, created things are visible, while He is invisible; yet He acts for this very reason: so that He may become visible. Therefore, He is always creating. It is worthy to understand this, to marvel through understanding, and by marvelling...

## COMMENTARY.

*This fourteenth treatise asserts that all things perceived by the senses were made, and are continually being made: for just as they flow from another source who rules over all things as the Almighty, so also He continually sustains them, lest by their own natural tendency toward falling they rush into nothingness. Knowledge of Him alone makes one happy and blessed; He is God, the maker of all and the father. He alone is the begetter <term>genitor</term>, and all other things are begotten <term>genita</term> <note>original: *genitor* and *genita*. This terminology emphasizes the Hermetic view of God as the active source and the universe as the passive recipient of life.</note>. Between the begetter and the begotten, no middle state can be placed. These two are the universe: for all things consist of these two, the begetter and the begotten. Furthermore, he asserts that evil does not depend on God (just as rust on iron does not depend on the blacksmith) but follows the works created <note>This is a famous Hermetic defense of God's goodness, suggesting that "evil" is a natural byproduct of material existence, like rust, rather than an intentional creation of the Divine.</note>. And he raises us from human art to the understanding of divine art, showing that God himself sows immortality in heaven, change on earth, and life and motion in the whole world. This is the Epilogue. These few things, by way of arguments...*

The commentary explains that God is not the source of evil, comparing it to rust that naturally occurs on iron regardless of the blacksmith's skill.</summary>

### COMMENTARY.

*The first chapter teaches that all things belong to the one, and all things are one: belonging to the one, as from whom all things come; one, as all things are effects. In their cause they are one. It teaches that every human soul is immortal, but that this perhaps manifests in different ways; that all things descend from heaven; that which descends provides generation; that which ascends and tends upwards alone provides life. It teaches that very one, to whom all things belong and who is all things, moves the world and all the forms of the world from which the world was composed—which are fire, air, water, and earth. And just as all bodies make up the one body of the one world, so too he intends all the forms of things to create one "all-form" of the one world, which he calls the soul of the world <note>The Anima Mundi, a concept where the universe itself is a living being with a soul.</note>. Wherefore the world is "all-body" and "all-form"; and these are one body, one soul, one world, one God, from whom* <note>The text cuts off here, leading into the next page's discussion of the divine source.</note>

## CHAPTER II.

Heaven, therefore, is a sensible god <term>sensible god: a deity that can be perceived by the physical senses (like the sky and stars), in contrast to the "intelligible" God who can only be known by the mind</term>, the administrator of all bodies, whose increases and decreases the Sun and Moon have been allotted to govern. But of heaven itself, and of the soul itself, and of all things that are in the world, the governor is he who is the maker-god <note>original: *effector deus*. This refers to God as the ultimate cause or manufacturer of reality.</note> of all things. For from all the things mentioned above, of which he is the governor, a frequent influx <term>influx: the flowing of celestial power or influence from the higher spheres down into the material world</term> is carried through the world, and through the soul of all kinds and all species, and through the nature of things. The world, moreover, was prepared by God as a receptacle for all-formed species <note>original: *omniformium specierum*. This refers to the archetypal patterns or "forms" that give every creature its distinct shape and nature.</note>. By shaping nature through these species, he has led the world through the four elements <note>Earth, air, fire, and water.</note> all the way up to heaven. All things are to be pleasing to the sight of God; and all things, hanging from above, are divided into species, as I am about to speak...

# MERCVRII TRISM.

...[I am about] to speak <note>The text begins mid-sentence; the Latin "rus sum modo" is likely the conclusion of a word like *locuturus sum* (I am about to speak).</note> just now: The genera <term>genera: the general classes or categories of things, from which specific types arise</term> of all things follow their own species <term>species: the specific forms or individual types within a general class</term>, so that the genus is the totality, and the species is a small part of the genus. 

Therefore, there is a genus of gods and a genus of demons; likewise of men, and similarly of birds, and of all things which the world contains within itself; it generates species similar to itself. There is also another genus of living thing <note>original: *animalis*. In this philosophical context, this refers to anything possessing "anima" (soul or life-force), including plants, not just "animals" in the modern sense.</note>, a genus without senses indeed, yet not lacking a soul, whereby it rejoices in benefits and is diminished and damaged by adversity. I speak of all those things which live on earth by the health of their roots and stems, whose species are scattered throughout the whole earth. 

Heaven itself is full of God. The aforementioned genera inhabit [the world] up to the locations of those species whose forms are all immortal. For the species is a part of the genus—as man is a part of humanity—which must necessarily follow the quality of its own genus. From this it follows that although all genera are immortal, not all species are immortal. 

For regarding the genus of Divinity, both the genus itself and its species are immortal. But as for the genera of the rest, their eternity resides in the genus; although it may "die" in its individual species, it is nevertheless preserved by the fruitfulness of birth. And therefore species are mortal—just as man is mortal, while humanity is immortal. Yet, species of all genera are mixed into all genera...

<summary>Hermes explains the hierarchical relationship between universal "genera" (which are eternal) and individual "species" (which may be mortal), illustrating how humanity remains eternal as a category even though individual humans die.</summary>

It creates many connections with all other species, and indeed with nearly all of them by necessity. Because of this, he who has joined himself to the gods by his mind—the part by which he is linked to the gods—through divine religion <note>original: *diuina religione*</note>, approaches near to the gods. He who is joined to the demons approaches them. But those are truly human who are content with the middle-state of their own genus; and the remaining species of men will be similar to those classes of beings with whose species they have joined themselves.

## COMMENTARY.

*Chapter two. For a better understanding of the present matters, and some of the things that follow, it should by no means be hidden that Mercury <note>The author refers to Hermes Trismegistus by his Latin name, Mercurius. Hermes was believed to be an ancient Egyptian sage.</note> uses the word **animal** <term>animal: here used in its literal Latin sense of "an ensouled being," which includes anything with a "soul" (anima) such as plants or stars, not just creatures with fur or scales</term> with a far different meaning than we are accustomed to use; he does the same with the word **soul**. For in the second dialogue of the **Pimander** <note>The *Poimandres* is the first and most famous book of the Corpus Hermeticum, a collection of Greek wisdom texts</note>, he defines **soul** by **motion**. However, in the following chapter, he defines an **animal** as having both a **soul** and a **body**. Therefore, whatever possesses a motive force <note>original: *vim motricem*; the power to move itself or cause motion</note> possesses a soul, according to his specific way of speaking; and whatever possesses both a soul and a body is an animal. Thus, the **heaven**, the **world**, **plants**, and the **elements** are animals. But our custom is to call only that an "animal" which is an animated body endowed with **senses**, and we define a soul not only by motion, but by **life**, **sense**, **voluntary motion**, or **intellect**. Therefore, when we hear the word "animal," let us understand it in his way, not our own. But now, back to the dialogue. He maintains that the **heaven** and the **celestial body** relate to other sensible things <term>sensible: objects that can be perceived by the physical senses (sight, touch, etc.) rather than things only understood by the mind</term> just as **man** relates to other animals. Man is to other animals as an **animal god**; however, heaven is to other sensible things as a **sensible god**. But as for God, the ruler of all and the governor of all things that exist in the world, I would believe Him to be nothing other than*

The Lord and Shaper of all things, whom we rightly call God, created from Himself a second [being] who could be seen and felt. For necessity follows the things pleasing to God, and the effect accompanies His will. Nor is it credible that what has pleased God will ever displease Him, since He knew long beforehand both that it would happen and that it would be pleasing.

When he calls the world "the second God" <note>original: "secundum deum"</note> both here and in the sixth chapter, it is just as if you were to call "duality" <term>duitas</term> <note>the state of being two or twofold</note> a "second unity." For while duality is a single thing and a single binary <term>binarius</term> <note>the number two, representing the first step away from unity into multiplicity</note>, the Monad <term>monas</term> <note>the absolute "One" or the indivisible source in Neoplatonic and Hermetic philosophy</note> is absolutely one. The binary, however, is not absolutely one, but is one through participation and contraction—a "second" one. Thus, God is one, and is absolutely God; the world, however, is not God, but is God by participation, and the most beautiful trace <term>vestigium</term> <note>literally a "footprint" or mark left behind</note> of God among sensible things <note>objects that can be perceived by the senses</note>. This concludes the fourth part of the *Asclepius*.

## COMMENTARIES.

*The sixth chapter discusses how God is absolutely the first God; the world is the second god, not absolutely, but a god by <term>participation</term> <note>Participation is a philosophical concept where a lower being derives its qualities—like divinity or goodness—from a higher source.</note>, as it is the first image of the absolute God; and man is the third god by his participation in divinity, and the second image of God. God, however, is not an image, but the truth of all images. It states that man, by means of his soul, sense, spirit, and reason—as if by superior elements—is able to ascend into heaven. Yet, insofar as he is composed of fire, air, water, and earth, he is subject to death, and must leave behind all worldly things on earth, stripped of that divine part.*

*The measure according to which man ought to live is religion, which goodness follows; and this religion is seen to be perfect at last when, fortified by virtue, it despises the desires for all foreign things—possessions, the body, and all those things we long for, and finally, even the very sense of longing itself. For a man ought to be, and be called such—as his own judgment carries him—only insofar as the focus of his reason leads his soul; and so far as, through the contemplation of divinity, he joins that part which is mortal to himself, indeed out of the necessity of preserving the lower world...*

-># ASCLEPIUS #<-

Soon Hermes returns to the question of why man ought to learn the dimensions of the earth—that is, <term>geometry</term> <note>While we think of geometry as math, the text views it as a way to understand the divine proportions of creation.</note>—the qualities, quantities, the depths of the sea, the force of fire, and the nature of all these things. This constitutes the universal philosophy concerning numbers, the celestial spheres, and natural things; he learns them so that he may truly admire, adore, and praise the art and the divine mind, the craftsman <note>original: "artificem"</note> of all these things.*

*For this is pure philosophy, depending only on divine religion. This is <term>music</term>, this is harmony <note>original: "concentum"; referring to the Pythagorean idea that the universe functions like a perfectly tuned musical instrument.</note>: to know the order of all things, which each thing has obtained by divine reason. When this knowledge is brought together into a unified account <note>The OCR reads "vitiu," likely a printer's error for "unum" (unity) or "initium" (beginning).</note> regarding the Craftsman of all, it produces a certain harmony, most sweet and most true, like a divine melody. And philosophy, corrupted by no troublesome curiosity of the mind, should worship the divinity with a simple mind and soul, venerate his deeds, and give thanks to the will of God, which alone is most full of goodness. And he confirms the prophecy of Asclepius. This is the sixth partition.*

<margin>L</margin>

<term>matter</term> <note>original: "hyle," a Greek term for the raw, unformed substance of the universe.</note>, which we believe the Greeks call the world; and spirit accompanied the world, but not in the same way it accompanies God. For these elements from which the world is made are not God. Therefore, they did not exist as they are when they were not yet "born" <note>In this context, "born" or "generated" refers to the transition from potential existence to actual, formed existence.</note>. But they were already present even then within that source from which they were destined to be born. For we do not call things "unborn" only when they have not yet been born, but also those things which lack the fertility of generating, such that nothing can be born from them. 

Whatever things exist, therefore, in which the nature of generating is present—these are also "generable" <note>Capable of being produced or brought into existence.</note>, as are the things that can be born from them, even if those things were born from themselves. For there is no doubt that from those things which were born from themselves, those things from which all things arise can easily be born. 

God, therefore, is sempiternal; God is eternal, and He neither can be born, nor could He have been. He is, He was, and He will always be. This, then, is the nature of God: that which is entirely of itself. 

But <term>matter</term>—or the nature of the world—and spirit, although they seem to have been born from the beginning, nevertheless possess within themselves the power of being born and procreating, and the nature of fertility. For the beginning lies in the quality of nature, which possesses the power and nature of both conception and birth within itself. This nature, therefore, is capable of generating on its own without the conception of another. But truly, those things which have only the power of conceiving through the mingling of another nature must be distinguished in such a way that this place of the world, along with those things which are within it, would appear to be not yet <insert>born</insert>...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Hermes Trismegistus, Asclepius, and Ammon. <page-num>499</page-num>
-># ASCLEPIUS #<-

[spir]it <note>The Latin text "itus" completes the word "spiritus" from the previous page.</note>, which certainly contains within itself the force of all nature. But I speak of <term>place</term> <note>original: "locum"; in this philosophy, "place" is the necessary container or dimension that allows objects to exist and be perceived.</note> as that in which all things exist; for all these things could not have existed if a place were lacking that could sustain them all. For for all things that have existed, provision must be made for a place; for neither qualities, nor quantities, nor positions, nor effects could be distinguished for those things which are nowhere. 

Thus, therefore, even the world—although it was not "born" <note>In the sense of having a beginning in time; the text suggests the world is co-eternal with the principles that form it.</note>—nevertheless has within itself the nature of all things, seeing as it provides the most fertile wombs to all these things for conceiving. This, then, is the totality of quality and of <term>matter</term>, which is "creatable" <note>capable of being shaped or brought into specific form</note>, even if it has not been created. For just as the nature of matter is fertile with quality, so that same nature is equally fertile with <term>malice</term> <note>original: "malignitatis"; here referring to evil or the inherent "badness" found in the density of the material world.</note>. 

And I did not say, O Asclepius and Ammon (as is said by many), "Was God not able to cut away and turn away malice from the nature of things?" To those people, no answer at all should be given. However, for your sake, I will pursue what I had begun and provide an explanation. For they themselves say that God ought to have freed the world from malice in every way; for it is so present in the world that it seems to be like a limb of the world itself.

### COMMENTARY

*The seventh chapter contains a veiled philosophy concerning the birth of the world, matter* <note>original: "Hyle"; the raw, formless substance of the universe</note>*, the substance of the world, the accompanying spirit, and place. It states that all worldly things are within the world, and the world is within God; he calls that which contains them "place." Furthermore, he does not wish for the "place" of the world to be considered "born" (created in time); but he considers the world itself to be both born and unborn. It is "born," indeed, if you look at the craftsmanship of the creatures; but it is "unborn" if you look at the fundamental truth of that craftsmanship.*

*For matter and spirit—that is, the world—and a certain divine power moving through and diffused through all things, did not exist in the craftsmanship of the world when they were not yet born; but he says they were already present even then in that source from which they were destined to be born. But in what were they present, if not in that Divine Word* <note>original: "verbo"; the creative Logos or divine reason</note> *through which all things were made? And in whom, and what was made...*

<summary>Hermes explains that divine intellect, unlike sunlight, is never eclipsed by darkness, and the commentary explores how the world and matter pre-existed as potential within the Divine Word before creation.</summary>

From His divinity, nature was born, so that all things are as they are, and as they have been; and for all things to come hereafter, nature remains sufficient to be born from itself. ## COMMENTARY

*The eighth chapter encompasses the topic of the <term>ousiarchs <note>original: vsiarchis, from the Greek "ousia" (substance/essence) and "archē" (rule); refers to the spiritual governors of essential substances.</note></term>, the substantial principles whom he calls gods. He calls Jupiter the ousiarch of the heavens, and light the ousiarch of the sun. He posits thirty-six **horoscopes**, that is, "observers of the hours," who belong to the stars fixed forever in the same place. He names the leader of these **Pantomorphos**, which means the "All-Formed" <note>A name for a deity or principle that encompasses all shapes and forms.</note>. He establishes **Fortune** and **Fate** as the rulers of the seven wandering spheres <note>The seven "planets" of the ancient world: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>. He also posits an ousiarch of the air. However, these seem to be the fabrications of demons and certain vain disguises leading back toward pagan errors; those who dwell too long upon such things are forced toward vanity rather than being brought to perfection.*

*From here he returns to the contemplation of the Supreme God—who is unspeakable and unnamable, or rather, he who is named by the names of all things. He is most full of <term>fecundity <note>original: faecunditate; the power of being fertile or fruitfully creative.</note></term>, and from Him all things receive the quality that nothing can be barren. From this arises that love of procreating and the immense striving of nature; this contains nothing foul or disgraceful in itself, provided it is considered religiously, and provided the discourse concerning it is held and treated with no less reverence. For...*

<meta>catchword: ...it is</meta>

<summary>This page summarizes the Hermetic hierarchy of spiritual governors (ousiarchs) and the thirty-six decans, while the commentator warns against getting lost in these "pagan" astrological details instead of focusing on the Supreme God's creative fruitfulness.</summary>
<keywords>ousiarchs, Jupiter, Pantomorphos, Fortune, Fate, fecundity, procreation, planetary spheres, astrology</keywords>

->ASCLEPIUS.<-

...for this was granted to us in order to emulate <term>divine fecundity <note>original: divinae foecunditatis; the creative, life-giving power of God that allows for the generation of new life and the continuation of the species.</note></term>. But because the majority of men are ignorant of these mysteries, they profane divine laws and handle these matters insanely and irreverently—behaving like beasts, or as if they were raging and out of their minds. Therefore, out of a sense of shame, one should scarcely dare to think or speak of such things now; this is because the disordered behavior and irreverence of men toward the venerable <term>order of God <note>original: dei ordinationem; the divine structure or arrangement of the universe.</note></term> force themselves upon our senses and thoughts, rather than that beautiful, holy, and untainted divine order itself. Because it is granted to only a few to possess pure senses, I believe that one should think and speak about these matters only with those few. 

He soon adds that God granted intelligence and discipline to humans alone, so that the <term>immortal and divine part <note>original: particula eius immortalis, & diuina; the "spark" of the soul that originates from God and survives the body.</note></term> of the soul might avoid the vices it would otherwise easily fall into through its mixture with the physical body. For by reason of the body and its perishable nature, it is inevitable that cravings, desires, and other mental vices will affect the souls of men. This concludes the eighth section.

Asclepius, recognize this power. Just as the Lord and Father, or (what is greatest) God, is the maker of the celestial gods, so humanity is the maker of the gods who dwell in temples, <note>The "gods in temples" refers to the ancient practice of theurgy, where it was believed that statues could be "animated" or inhabited by divine spirits through specific rituals.</note> who are content with <term>human proximity <note>original: humana proximitate; the idea that these terrestrial gods choose to stay close to mankind to assist and interact with them.</note></term>, and who not only receive light but also give it. Not only does man move toward God, but he also strengthens the gods. Are you amazed, O Asclepius, or do you perhaps feel distrust, as many do?

**ASCLEPIUS.** I am confounded, O Trismegistus, but having freely assented to your words, I judge the human being to be most happy, having attained such great felicity.

**TRISMEGISTUS.** And not undeservedly is he worthy of wonder, who is the greatest of all. For the nature of all the celestial gods is manifest without confusion, having been propagated from the <term>purest part of nature <note>original: mundissima parte naturae; likely referring to the "aether" or the fifth element from which the stars and celestial beings were thought to be composed.</note></term>. Their visible forms are, as it were, only heads in place of a whole body. However, the species of gods which <term>humanity <note>original: humanitas; here referring to the creative capacity of the human race.</note></term> shapes is formed from a dual nature: from the divine nature, which is prior and much more divine, and from that which is within humans—that is, from the matter out of which they were fabricated. These gods are configured not only with heads alone, but with all their members and their entire bodies. Thus humanity, mindful of its own nature and origin, perseveres in that <term>imitation of divinity <note>original: divinitatis imitatione; the core Hermetic concept that man acts as a "second creator" on earth, mirroring God's creation of the cosmos.</note></term>. Just as the Father and Lord made the eternal gods so that they might be like Him, so humanity fashions its own gods in the likeness of its own...

And yet, since it is fitting for wise men to foreknow all things, it is not right for you to be ignorant of this: a time is coming when it will appear that the Egyptians have in vain served the divinity with a pious mind and diligent religion, and all their holy worship will fall into ruin and be frustrated. For the divinity is destined to return from earth to heaven. Egypt will be abandoned, and the land that was the seat of divinity, <term>widowed of its religion <note>original: religione uiduata; a powerful metaphor suggesting that without its rites and gods, the land loses its husband or protector.</note></term>, will be destitute of the presence of the gods. For when foreigners fill this region and land, there will be not only a neglect of religions, but (what is harder) it will be established by law—as if by statute—that religion, piety, and divine worship are forbidden. A penalty will be prescribed, and it will be prohibited...

And then, out of weariness with humanity, the world will no longer seem worthy of admiration or adoration. **TRISMEGISTUS.** For first, O Asclepius, all earthly things that exist are mortal. They are subjected to punishments after death that are all the more savage as they were perhaps zealously kept unpunished <note>The text suggests that crimes hidden or unpunished in the physical world face a more severe reckoning in the spiritual world to balance the scales of justice.</note> while they lived. For because the divinity has foreknowledge of all things, punishments will be rendered according to the qualities of the crimes, just as they truly are.

**ASCLEPIUS.** Who are worthy of greater punishments, O Trismegistus?

**TRISMEGISTUS.** Those who, condemned by human laws, lose their life violently, so that they seem not to have returned the soul owed to nature, but to have paid the penalty for their deeds. <note>Hermes suggests that a natural death is the "return" of the soul to its source, whereas an execution or violent death for a crime is a forced payment, depriving the soul of its natural exit.</note> On the other hand, for a just man, there is a defense in the religion of God and in the highest piety. For God protects such people from all evils. For the father and lord of all, who alone is all things, gladly shows himself to all. Not by revealing where he might be located in a place, nor what kind of "quality" he possesses, nor how "great" his quantity is, but by illuminating man by the sole <term>intelligence</term> <note>original: "intelligentia." In Hermetic philosophy, this is not just logic, but a higher spiritual intellect or "nous" capable of direct divine perception.</note> of the mind. He who, having shaken off the darkness of errors from his soul and perceived the clarity of truth, with his whole

-> # A S C L E P I V S. <-

Believe this Sun to be the second god, O <term>Asclepius</term> <note>The student to whom Hermes Trismegistus is speaking; in these texts, he represents a seeker of divine wisdom.</note>, who governs all other things and illuminates all the creatures of the world, whether they are animate <note>original: "animantia," meaning beings with souls.</note> or inanimate. For in every single part of a being that is always living, which exists within the world itself—just as in one and the same ever-living creature—there is no place for death. 

Therefore, the world itself must be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for it to live forever. The Sun, therefore, just like the world, is eternal; so too is he always the governor of vital things, or of all vitality, and their sustainer and dispenser. God is therefore the eternal governor of the living things, or the vital beings, that are in the world...

...governor, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. 
For he once dispensed life by an eternal law, providing life to all living beings in this manner which I shall describe. For in the very vitality of eternity, the world is moved; and within that vital eternity is the location of the world. For this reason, the world itself will never stand still, nor will it ever be destroyed, being surrounded and, as it were, bound by the perpetuity of living. He is, therefore, the dispenser of life to all things within him, and he is the place of all things governed under the sun. The movement of this world consists of a twofold effect: for the world itself is quickened <note>original: "uiuificatur," meaning to be made alive or animated.</note> from without by eternity, and it quickens all things that are within it, distinguishing them by numbers and by fixed and appointed times. All things are governed through the effect of the sun and the movement of the stars. All temporal things are written down by reason and divine law. Earthly time is recognized by the quality of the air and the variation of heat and cold, but celestial time is known by the revolutions of the stars returning to the same places in their temporal cycle; and the world is the receptacle <note>A "receptacle" here implies a vessel or container that holds and processes time.</note> of time, by whose course and movement the world is invigorated. Time, however, is maintained by order. Order and time cause the renewal of all things in the world through alternation.

## COMMENTARY.

*The tenth [part] concerning death and the examination of the soul when it has departed the body; that those whose lives were justly taken by human laws because of the magnitude of their crimes are more severely punished after death; that God is a defense for the righteous; concerning the divinity of the sun and the world. It posits the world as the first sensible <note>Meaning "perceptible to the senses" or "material."</note> god, and the sun as the second. It suggests the world will never be at rest and will never be destroyed. We, however, do not attribute the incommunicable name <note>A theological term referring to the unique name of God (often the Tetragrammaton) which cannot be applied to created things.</note> of God to either the sun or the world, and we believe the world is eventually to be dissolved. Therefore, these things—as the words of Hermes sound in their simple sense—display the error of the pagans. Nevertheless, by way of participation, we attribute divinity to them as being the excellent works of God.*

**This is the tenth partition.**

He cannot be moved by the impulse of any other nor by any change of place, since all things are in him, and he alone is in all things. ->M E R C V R I I  T R I S M.<-

...even more than that immobile eternity itself, into which the agitation <note>original: *agitatio*—in this context, it refers to the constant motion, flow, or "restless activity" of the temporal world.</note> of all ages returns, and from which the agitation of all ages takes its beginning. God, therefore, was stable, and eternity always existed alongside him in like manner, containing within itself the unborn world—which we rightly call <term>sensible<gloss>perceptible by the physical senses, as opposed to the purely intellectual or divine realm</gloss></term>—as an image of this God. Because of this, the world was made an imitator of eternity. 

Time, however, possesses the force and nature of its own stability, even though it is always in motion, by that very necessity of returning into itself. And so, although eternity is stable, immobile, and fixed, nevertheless, because it is always being recalled back into eternity by the mobility of time—and that agitation and mobility is turned by the logic of time—it results that eternity itself, while remaining immobile, appears to be moved only through the time in which it exists, and in which all agitation is contained. Thus it occurs that both eternity—which is stability—is moved, and the mobility of time becomes stable, fixed by the law of its course. 

In this way, it is also credible that God is moved within himself by that same immobility; for within the magnitude of his very stability, there is an immobile agitation. For the law of his magnitude is itself immobile. This, therefore, which is of such a nature—which is not subject to the senses—is infinite, incomprehensible, and immeasurable. It can neither be supported, nor carried, nor tracked down. For from where, and to where, and where, or in what manner...

We recognize that these are things only by the sense of touch. Whence it happens that many believe these are not **bodies**, but are **empty places**, which is impossible. 

For just as that which is said to be outside the world—if indeed there is anything (for I do not believe that either)—is understood to be full of intelligible things, that is, things similar to his own divinity; so also here, in this which is called the <term>sensible world<gloss>original: *sensibilis mundus*—the physical world that can be perceived through the senses</gloss></term>, it is most full of bodies and living beings suited to their own nature and quality. 

We do not see all their forms; some are excessively large, while others are very short, either because of the length of the distance between us, or because our sight is dull. Thus they appear as such to us, or perhaps because of their extreme shortness, they are believed by many not to exist at all. I speak now of the <term>demons<gloss>original: *daemonas*—in this context, intermediate spiritual beings, not "demons" in the modern evil sense</gloss></term>, whom I believe dwell with us, and the <term>heroes<gloss>original: *heroas*—exalted souls or semi-divine beings</gloss></term>, who dwell in the purest part of the air above us and the earth, where there is no place for clouds, nor any commotion from the movement of any celestial signs. 

Because of this, O Asclepius, you should never say that anything is **void**, unless you first specify what that thing is "void" of. For example, you might say a place is void of fire, or void of water...

->ASCLEPIUS<-

...and from things similar to these. Even if it were possible to imagine that a <term>void<gloss>original: *inane*—a space containing absolutely nothing</gloss></term> could exist apart from such things—whether that perceived void were small or large—it nonetheless could not be empty of <term>spirit<gloss>original: *spiritu*—here referring to an invisible, vital breath or pneuma that fills all space</gloss></term> and air.

In the same way, we must speak of **place**. This word on its own lacks meaning. For a "place" is only revealed by what it contains. If you take away the name of the object it holds, the meaning of the word is mutilated. This is why we correctly speak of a "place for water," a "place for fire," or other such things.

Just as it is impossible for a "void" to exist, so too "place" on its own cannot be defined. For if you propose a place without its contents, that place will appear empty—a thing I do not believe exists in the world. Since there is no such thing as a void, the nature of a place is not apparent by itself unless you add to it lengths, widths, or heights—just as we identify the dimensions of human bodies.

Because these things are so, O Asclepius, and you who are present: know that the <term>intelligible world<gloss>original: *mundus intelligibilis*—the spiritual realm of ideas and truth that exists beyond the reach of physical senses</gloss></term> (that is, God, who is recognized only by the mind's gaze) is incorporeal. No corporeal thing can be mixed with his nature—that is, nothing that can be measured by quality, quantity, or numbers. For within him, no such thing exists.

This world, then, which is called the <term>sensible world<gloss>original: *mundus sensibilis*—the physical, material universe perceived through the five senses</gloss></term>, is the receptacle for all sensible forms, qualities, or bodies—all of which [cannot exist] without...

-># ASCLEPIUS #<-

...whether they be bodies or incorporeal things, it is impossible for each individual form to be born exactly like another, given the differing points of hours and <term>climates<gloss>original: *climatum*—referring to geographical latitudes or astrological zones</gloss></term>. While the world changes in its rotation, the species itself is neither changed nor rotated. Thus, the forms of individual kinds remain permanent, yet within that same form, the individuals are unlike one another.

### COMMENTARIES

*The twelfth point argues that the "void" or "empty space" has no place in the nature of things; that <term>spirits<gloss>original: *dæmones*—intermediate beings between gods and humans, not necessarily evil</gloss></term> dwell with us around the earth, but due to their excessive <note>original: *subtilitatem*—referring to the fineness or rarity of their substance</note> subtlety, they are imperceptible to us. It states that the Heroes occupy a purer portion of the air. The name of "place" by itself is an empty concept, because a place exists only in relation to something else; without understanding the thing occupying it, what "place" is cannot be understood, and this is common to all relative terms. He establishes the existence of an <term>intelligible world<gloss>the world of divine ideas or archetypes, accessible only to the mind</term></gloss>, by which the <term>sensible world<gloss>the physical world perceived by the five senses</gloss></term> and all things within it are covered as if by a garment, inasmuch as the physical world is contained within the intelligible world. He argues that the forms of individuals within uniform <term>genera<gloss>the general categories or "kinds" of things, like "humanity" or "lions"</gloss></term> are all dissimilar, such as among men; and this occurs according to the moments and hours of the revolving circle over which **Phantomorphus** presides—whom he previously called the god of <term>horoscopes<gloss>original: *horoscopiorum*—referring to the "ascendant" or the specific timing of birth</gloss></term>. We, however, are ignorant of that god, and [accuse him] of folly...* <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword indicates the full word is "relinqui," likely suggesting that ignoring this god leads to being "left behind" in folly.</note>

<header>COMMENTARIES ON HERMES TRISMEGISTUS</header>

This thirteenth chapter suffers from the same impurity as the ninth chapter; in the very place where Hermes wishes man to be most divine and most admirable, in this he is certainly most impious and profane. This is because he invented idolatry, because he summoned demonic spirits and placed them into images, and added rituals and sacrifices. <note>The commentator is criticizing the "god-making" passage in the Hermetic text, where humans are said to animate statues with spirits.</note> He speaks of Aesculapius, Mercury, Isis, and Osiris, who were worshipped by the Egyptians; of the animals which the Egyptians held as sacred; and of the herbs, stones, aromatics, melodies, and hymns with which they would appease those spirits placed within the statues and images. Some <term>pythonics<gloss>originally referring to the priestesses of Apollo, here used to mean sorcerers or mediums who deal with spirits</gloss></term> (O unhappy age!) still tend to do this today, believing they hold spirits trapped either in rings or in small vessels—a most impure class of men, hostile to both God and men, and established as an enemy from the opposing side. Blessed Augustine argues against this profane error of impiety, and does so rightly, in his book *The City of God*, where he proves the truth in favor of the faith. <note>original: "De Civitate Dei"—Saint Augustine’s major work where he specifically refutes the *Asclepius* and its defense of pagan statues.</note> These things conclude the thirteenth chapter.

...[Tris]megistus, if the celestial gods rule over the whole universe, and the earthly gods dwell in individual things, what is it that we call Destiny <note>original: εἱμαρμένην (Heimarmene), the Greek philosophical term for the lot or fate assigned to each soul</note>? **TRIS.** O Asclepius, it is the necessity of all things that are done, always joined to itself by linked chains. It is, therefore, either the producer of things, or the supreme God, or it proceeds from God himself who was made the second God <note>The "second God" refers to the *Demiurge* or the Mind of the universe who carries out the creation</note>, or it is the discipline of all celestial and earthly things established by divine laws. Therefore, this Destiny <note>original: εἱμαρμένη</note> and Necessity are both joined to one another by an inseparable bond. The former, Destiny, brings forth the beginnings of all things, while Necessity truly compels toward the outcome those things which depend upon those beginnings. Order follows these—that is, the sequence and arrangement of time for things to be completed. For nothing exists without the composition of order. In all these things, this world is perfected. For the world itself is carried along by order, or rather, the whole world consists of order. Therefore, these three—Destiny <note>original: εἱμαρμένη, here glossed by the author as "fatum" or fate</note>, Necessity, and Order—are especially produced by the will of God, who governs the world by His law and by divine reason. From these, therefore, every act of willing or not-willing is completely turned away by divine decree: for they are neither moved by anger, nor are they bent by favor, but they serve the necessity of eternal reason; which eternity is unchangeable, immovable, and unbreakable. Fate <note>original: εἱμαρμένη (Heimarmene), the Greek term for the lot or destiny assigned to each being</note> is that which, like a sown seed, conceives the offspring of all things to come. Necessity follows, by which all things are driven to their effect by force. Third is Order, preserving the fabric of those things which Fate and Necessity arrange. This, therefore, is eternity, which neither began to be nor shall cease, and which is preserved in eternal motion, fixed by an immutable law of its course. It rises and falls often through alternating parts, so that, as the times vary, it rises in those same parts through which it had fallen. For such is the nature of a revolving circle, so tightly bound together, that you cannot know where the beginning of the rotation is, since all things always seem both to precede and follow one another. However, Chance and Fortune are mixed within all worldly affairs.

### COMMENTARY

**Chapter 14.** Concerning the Fates, which he calls Fate <note>original: εἱμαρμένην</note>, Necessity, and Order; others call them Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos <note>The three Fates of Greek mythology: the Spinner, the Allotter, and the Inflexible</note>. Regarding these matters, the pagans were no less prone to foolishness than they were regarding the rest of the gods they fashioned for themselves, inventing new and "wonderfully powerful" deities. But Mercury [Trismegistus] speaks of these more veiledly and sparingly, and somewhat ambiguously, as if these three were the predefinition and predestination of the divine mind, which the necessity of things (that they may exist) follows; and which, finally existing,

*existing, Order preserves them, just as it has been ordained by divine and eternal law, so that first is Fate, which is divine predefinition; second is the consequence of things; and third is preservation. And these three—either the divine law itself or those things accompanying the sequence of divine law—contain in an orderly fashion those things which are defined and according to the causes of nature. Yet Fate also permits undefined, unnatural, and indeterminate causes in contingent matters <note>original: "contingentibus rebus"; referring to events that happen by chance or are not strictly necessary</note>; but let others judge of these. And these things suffice for the present division.*

### CHAPTER 15

**W**e have spoken concerning each thing, as far as humanity was able, as it willed, and as divinity permitted; this alone remains for us, that, blessing God and praying, we return to the care of the body.
